﴿By those who range in ranks,﴾ ﴿and those who drive with a driving,﴾ ﴿and those who recite the reminder,﴾ ﴿indeed your God is One.﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and Lord of the easts.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of the stars,﴾ ﴿and as a protection from every rebellious devil.﴾ ﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly, and they are pelted from every side,﴾ ﴿repelled, and for them is a constant punishment.﴾ ﴿Except one who snatches a fragment, and he is pursued by a piercing flaming shooting star.﴾.

This surah is Meccan. The connection of its beginning with the end of Ya-Sin is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the Return and His power to revive the dead, and that He is the one who originates them, and when His will is directed at a thing it is, He mentioned His oneness, since what His will is directed at, in existence and non-existence, is not complete except by the Willer being one. This has been discussed in His saying: ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [21:22].

Allah swore by some of His creatures, saying: ﴿By those who range in ranks﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah and Masruq said: they are the angels, who line up in the sky in worship and remembrance in rows. It was also said: they spread their wings in the air, standing and awaiting the command of Allah. It was said: they are those among the children of Adam who are arranged in battle in the way of Allah, or in prayer and obedience. It was said: and the birds that spread their wings. "Those who drive" (al-zājirāt): Mujahid and al-Suddi said: the angels who drive the clouds and other creatures of Allah, exalted is He. Qatadah said: the verses of the Qur'an, because it contains the legal prohibitions; it was said: everything that is restrained from the disobedience of Allah. "Those who recite" (al-tāliyāt): the reciters. Mujahid said: the angels who recite His remembrance. Qatadah said: the children of Adam who recite His revealed speech, and His glorification and His magnification. Mujahid said: the angels who recite His remembrance. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that He swears by the souls of the diligent scholars, those who range their feet (al-ṣāffāt aqdāmahā) in tahajjud and all the other prayers and the rows of congregations; "those who drive" by admonition and advice; "those who recite" the verses of Allah, and "those who study" His laws; or by the souls of the reciters of the Qur'an in the way of Allah, which range the rows and drive the horses for jihad, and recite the remembrance along with that, not being distracted from it by those preoccupations. End of quote. He also said, meaning: the fa' of conjunction in "al-ṣāffāt" either indicates the sequence of its meanings in existence, as in the saying of the poet: "Alas for Ziyabah for al-Harith al-Sabih, then al-Ghanim, then al-Ayib", meaning the one who rose in the morning, then gained booty, then returned; or it indicates their sequence in degree in some respects, as when you say: take the better, then the best, and do the finer, then the finest; or it indicates the sequence of their described subjects in that, as when you say: may Allah have mercy on those who shave, then those who shorten. As for here, if you make the described subject singular, the fa' indicates the sequence of the ranks in degree; so if the singular is the angels, then the excellence belongs to the rank, then the driving, then the recitation; or the reverse. If you make the described subject plural, they are arranged in excellence, so the ranks are of excellence, the drivers are more excellent, and the reciters are of greater excellence; or the reverse. The meaning of the reverse in both places: you ascend from the more excellent to the excellent to the less excellent, or you begin with the lower, then the excellent, then the most excellent. Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq, al-A'mash, Abu 'Amr and Hamzah assimilated the three tā's (idghām). The sworn-upon sentence includes His oneness, exalted is He: He is One from all the aspects which the reflecting ones consider, a predicate after a predicate, according to the view of those who permit the enumeration of predicates; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and that is more laudatory: meaning, He is the Lord.

Abu Hayyan, al-Bahr al-Muhit, commentary on surah 37, verses 1–10 (part 2 of 2):

He mentioned the easts (al-mashariq) because they are the places where the lights rise, and seeing by them is more demanding; mentioning them makes mention of the wests (al-maghárib) unnecessary, since the wests are understood from the easts. There are three hundred and sixty easts, and likewise three hundred and sixty wests. The sun rises each day from one of these easts and sets in one of these wests, and it does not rise or set at the same point two days running. He used the dual in ﴿the Lord of the two easts and the Lord of the two wests﴾ [al-Rahman: 17], taking into account the easts and wests of summer and winter. Ibn 'Atiyya said: God intended the easts and wests of the sun, which, it is claimed, number one hundred and eighty in the year, from the longest days of the year to the shortest.

Then God informed of His power in adorning the sky with the stars, and of the arrangement of the adornment: that He made them a protection and a safeguard against the devil. End of quotation. The word zinah (adornment) is a verbal noun like sanah, and also a name for what something is adorned with, as liqah is the name for what the inkwell is fitted with. The majority read ﴿with the adornment of the stars﴾ with the genitive (idafah). This allows the verbal noun to be construed as an idafah to the agent, meaning that the stars adorned the sky, and as an idafah to the object, meaning that God adorned the stars. It also allows that the adornment is that with which something is adorned, with "the stars" as an explanation of the adornment, because the adornment is vague and applies to the stars and other things adorned with, or to what the stars adorn by their brightness and fixity. Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq (in one report from him), Abu Zur'ah, Ibn Thabbat and Talhah read: bi-zinatin (with tanwin), al-kawakibi (in the genitive) as an apposition to zinah. Ibn Thabbat and Masruq (in one report from each) and al-A'mash, Talhah and Abu Bakr read: bi-zinatin (with tanwin), al-kawakiba (in the accusative). This may be read with zinah as a verbal noun and al-kawakiba as the direct object, as in His saying ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger an orphan﴾ [al-Balad: 14]. It may also be read with al-kawakiba as an apposition to al-sama', meaning "We adorned the stars of the sky." Zayd ibn 'Ali read zinatin with tanwin and al-kawakibu in the nominative, either as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning "it is the stars," or as the agent of the verbal noun, meaning "that the stars adorned." Al-Farra' claimed that the nominative agent of a tanwinated verbal noun is not attested, while the Basrans permitted it, though rarely. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿with the adornment of the stars﴾ means "with the light of the stars." It has been said that their differing forms may also be intended, such as the shape of the Pleiades, the Big Dipper, Orion and others, along with their risings and their courses.

He singled out the nearest heaven (al-sama' al-dunya) for mention because it is the one seen by the eyes, and protection from the devils is only in it alone. The word ḥifẓan (as a safeguard) is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning "and We guarded it with a guarding," or as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) by adding a waw, or by postposing the governing verb, meaning "and for its protection We adorned it with the stars." It is also construed as a reflection of the sense of what came before, since the meaning is: "We created the stars as an adornment for the sky and as a safeguard." All these opinions are transmitted. As for al-marid (the rebellious), its explanation was given in His saying ﴿a rebellious devil﴾ [al-Nisa': 117] in Surat al-Nisa', where the word was ﴿marīdan﴾, whereas here it is ﴿mari'd﴾, in observance of the rhyme (fawasil).

﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly﴾ is a separate, independent sentence, narrating the condition of those who steal hearing, and that they are unable to listen or eavesdrop, being pelted with meteors and kept far from that. Except for the one who is given respite until he snatches a snatching and steals a stealing; then the angels promptly pursue him with the piercing meteor. It is not permissible for "they cannot listen" to be a descriptive clause or a resumptive answer to a questioner who asked why they are guarded from the devils, because the description, that they cannot listen, or the answer, would give no meaning to the guarding from the devils on either assumption. With the description, the meaning would become: "and a safeguard from every rebellious devil that neither hears nor eavesdrops," and likewise it would not fit as an answer. The view of one who said that the original is "so that they do not listen," with the lam and "an" deleted so the verb became nominative, is a strained opinion, and the speech of God is to be protected from it. The majority read: lā yassamma'ūna, negating their hearing, although they do eavesdrop, as in His saying ﴿Indeed they are removed from hearing﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 212]. It takes ila because it implies the sense of listening attentively. Ibn 'Abbas (in one report), Ibn Thabbat, 'Abdullah ibn Muslim, Talhah, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read: with shaddah on the sin and the mim, meaning lā yatasamma'ūna, the ta' being assimilated into the sin, and this implies negating eavesdropping. The apparent meaning of the hadiths is that they still eavesdrop, but they do not hear; and if any of them heard something, he would not escape guards and meteors, from the time of the sending of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and stoning was even more fitting in the Jahiliyyah. Since the fruit of eavesdropping is hearing, hearing is negated by negating eavesdropping in this reading, because its fruit, which is hearing, is absent. "The exalted assembly" (al-mala' al-a'la) includes the angels, while jinn and humans are "the lower assembly," since they are the inhabitants of the earth. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the noblest of the angels, and it was also reported from him that it is their book.

(And they are pelted) means they are shot at and stoned, ﴿from every side﴾, that is, from every direction from which they ascend to the sky. The meteor used as a missile is the one that people see falling, not the stars moving in the sky, because the motion of those is not seen, whereas this stone-throwing meteor is seen in its motion due to its nearness to us. This was said by Makki and al-Naqqash. Mahbub, from Ibn 'Amr, read: wa-yaqdhifūna (active voice), and duhūran is a verbal noun in the place of a circumstantial accusative (hal). Mujahid said: "expelled." It may also be an object of purpose, meaning "and if they are pelted, it is for expulsion," or a verbal noun of yuqdhafūna, since it implies the sense of expulsion, meaning "and they are driven away from every side with a driving away, and pelted from every side with a pelting." Either the figurative sense lies in yuqdhafūna or in duhūran. Ali, al-Sulami, Ibn Abi 'Abla, and al-Tabarani from his men, from Abu Ja'far, read: daḥūran, with a fatha on the dal, meaning a pelting that drives away, with a fatha on the dal. It may also be a verbal noun, like qabūl and wulūgh, except that these forms are reported to be restricted. Al-wāṣib means "the perpetual," as said by al-Suddi and Abu Salih, and it was discussed in Surat al-Nahl. It is said: "wasaba al-shay'u wuṣūban," meaning "it persisted." Mujahid said: "the painful," and from it comes al-waṣab (pain), as if the meaning is: they are stoned in this world and punished in the next. It is also possible that this perpetual punishment is theirs in this world, namely their being stoned perpetually and never attaining what they aim for of stealing hearing.

﴿Except one who snatches a snatching﴾: man (whoever) is a substitute for the pronoun in lā yassamma'ūna, and it may be in the accusative as an exception, meaning "the devils do not hear except the devil who snatches." Al-Jumhur read: khaṭifa, triliteral, with a kasra on the ta'. Al-Hasan and Qatadah read: with a kasra on the kha' and the ta' doubled. Abu Hatim said: it is said to be the dialect of Bakr ibn Wa'il and Tamim ibn Murrah. It was also read: khaṭṭifa, with a fatha on the kha' and a doubled kasra on the ta', which Ibn Khalawayh attributed to al-Hasan, Qatadah and 'Isa; and from al-Hasan also a reduced form. The original in these two readings is ikhtatafa; in the first, when it was made quiescent for assimilation and the kha' was quiescent, it was given a kasra to avoid two quiescent letters, so the alif of wasl was dropped and the ta' took a kasra following the kha's vowel. From Ibn 'Abbas: khiṭifa, with a kasra on both kha' and ta', lightened, following the vowel of the kha' to the vowel of the ta', as they said ni'im. It was also read: fa-atba'ahu, lightened and doubled. Al-thāqib: al-Suddi and Qatadah said it is the one piercing through with its light and its bright beam.

Surat al-Saffat is Meccan, and it has one hundred and eighty-two verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Indeed, We created them from sticky clay.﴾ Rather, you marvel and they mock. [Qur'an 37:11] ﴿And when they are reminded, they do not remember.﴾ [37:13] ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock.﴾ [37:14] ﴿And they say: this is nothing but clear magic.﴾ [37:15] ﴿When we die and become dust and bones, will we indeed be resurrected?﴾ [37:16] ﴿And our forefathers of old?﴾ [37:17] ﴿Say: yes, and you will be humbled.﴾ [37:18] ﴿It will be only one shout, and at once they will be looking.﴾ [37:19] ﴿And they will say: woe to us, this is the Day of Judgment.﴾ [37:20] ﴿This is the Day of Decision which you used to deny.﴾ [37:21] ﴿Gather those who did wrong, and their spouses, and what they used to worship,﴾ [37:22] ﴿besides Allah, and lead them to the path of Hellfire.﴾ [37:23] ﴿And stop them, for they are to be questioned.﴾ [37:24] ﴿What is wrong with you that you do not help one another?﴾ [37:25] ﴿Rather, today they are submitting.﴾ [37:26] ﴿And some of them turn to others, questioning one another.﴾ [37:27] ﴿They say: indeed you used to come to us from the right.﴾ [37:28] ﴿They say: rather, you were not believers.﴾ [37:29] ﴿We had no authority over you; rather, you were a transgressing people.﴾ [37:30] ﴿So the word of our Lord has come true against us; indeed we are to taste it.﴾ [37:31] ﴿So we led you astray, for we were ourselves astray.﴾ [37:32] ﴿Indeed, on that Day they will be sharers in the punishment.﴾ [37:33] ﴿Indeed, that is how We deal with the criminals.﴾ [37:34] ﴿Indeed, when it was said to them, "There is no god but Allah," they were arrogant.﴾ [37:35] ﴿And they said: shall we abandon our gods for a mad poet?﴾ [37:36] ﴿Rather, he has brought the truth and confirmed the messengers.﴾ [37:37] ﴿Indeed, you will taste the painful punishment.﴾ [37:38] ﴿And you will be recompensed only for what you used to do.﴾ [37:39] ﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah.﴾ [37:40] ﴿For them is a known provision,﴾ [37:41] ﴿fruits; and they will be honoured,﴾ [37:42] ﴿in Gardens of Bliss,﴾ [37:43] ﴿on couches facing one another.﴾ [37:44] ﴿A cup from a flowing spring will be passed around to them,﴾ [37:45] ﴿white, delicious to the drinkers,﴾ [37:46] ﴿in which there is no harm, nor will they be intoxicated by it.﴾ [37:47] ﴿And with them will be women of modest gaze, with beautiful eyes,﴾ [37:48] ﴿as if they were hidden eggs.﴾ [37:49] ﴿Then some of them will turn to others, questioning one another.﴾ [37:50] ﴿A speaker among them will say: indeed I had a companion,﴾ [37:51] ﴿who used to say: are you really among those who affirm?﴾ [37:52] ﴿When we die and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be held accountable?﴾ [37:53] ﴿He will say: will you look down?﴾ [37:54] ﴿So he looks down and sees him in the midst of the Hellfire.﴾ [37:55] ﴿He will say: by Allah, you nearly ruined me!﴾ [37:56] ﴿Had it not been for the favour of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forth.﴾ [37:57] ﴿Is it not that we will not die,﴾ [37:58] ﴿except our first death, and we will not be punished?﴾ [37:59] ﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph.﴾ [37:60] ﴿For the like of this let the workers work.﴾ [37:61] ﴿Is that better as a welcome, or the tree of Zaqqum?﴾ [37:62] ﴿Indeed, We made it a trial for the wrongdoers.﴾ [37:63] ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that springs from the root of Hellfire.﴾ [37:64] ﴿Its fruit is like the heads of devils.﴾ [37:65] ﴿Indeed they will eat from it and fill their bellies with it.﴾ [37:66] ﴿Then indeed for them upon it is a Allah.﴾ [37:74] ﴿And Noah called out to Us, and how excellent were the Answerers!﴾ [37:75] ﴿And We saved him and his family from the great distress.﴾ [37:76] ﴿And We made his descendants the stars,﴾ [37:88] ﴿and said: indeed I am sick.﴾ [37:89] ﴿So they turned away from him, retreating.﴾ [37:90] ﴿Then he slipped away to their gods and said: will you not eat?﴾ [37:91] ﴿What is wrong with you that you do not speak?﴾ [37:92] ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand.﴾ [37:93] ﴿Then they came to him hastening.﴾ [37:94]

Al-Zajr (التَّفْرِيقُ/الدفع): the pushing away of a thing by force and shouting. Al-Zajrah: the shout, from your saying: the shepherd zajara the camels and sheep, when he shouted at them and they returned to his voice. The poet said:

*Like the shouting of Abu 'Urwah to the beasts of prey when he feared they would mix with the sheep,*

meaning his calling out to them. Al-Thaqib: the very penetrating. Al-Lazib: that which clings to what is near it and sticks to it. Al-Ladhidh: that which is pleasant to taste; one says ladha al-shay' yaladhdhu, so it is ladhidh; and ladha in the pattern fa'ala, like talaba. The poet said:

*She delights in its taste, and you imagine in it, when you wake her after sleep.*

And he said:

*And a sweet one like the taste of Sarkhadi wine, which I left in the land of enemies, out of fear of misfortune.*

He means sleep.

And he said:

*By your delightful speech, which if you spoke with it to the lion of the wilderness, they would come swiftly.*

Al-Ghawl: a general term for harm; you say: ghala-hu kadha wa kadha, if it harmed him in secret. From it comes al-ghilah in the mind, and al-ghilah in nursing, and ghala-hu al-shay': it destroyed him and corrupted him. From it is the ghul that is in the lies of the Arabs and their proverbs: "Anger is the ghul of forbearance." The poet said:

*Our forefathers passed away living in comfort together, but a ghul took me in Mecca.*

That is: obstacles hindered me. And he said:

*Wine kept seizing us and taking away the first and the next.*

Wine made the drinker lose his mind (nazafat al-sharib al-khamr), and anzafa he: his mind went from intoxication, so he is nazif and munzif. The triliteral is transitive and the quadriliteral is intransitive, like kabbaytu al-rajul and akabba, and the wind scattered the clouds (qasha'at al-rih al-sahab), and qasha'a hawayahuma: meaning the two entered into the falling and scattering. The poet, who is al-Aswad, said:

*By my life, if you became drunk or sober, you would be the worst companions, the family of Abhar.*

And nuzifa al-sharib, with a damma on the z, and it is said: nuzifa al-matu'n: all his blood went out, in the passive. Nuzihat al-rakiyyah until its nazfah (its last of water): no water remained in it. It is said: anzafa al-rajul after his drink, and anzafa is shared between "became intoxicated" and "was exhausted." Al-Bayd: a known thing, and it is a collective noun; its singular is bayḍah, and it was named so for its whiteness, and it is pluralized as buyud. The poet said:

*In a barren desert, the camels seem like the sand grouse of sorrow whose young were eggs.*

Al-Zaqqum: a poisonous tree with a milk; if it touches a person's body, it swells and he dies from it in most cases; it grows in the barren lands bordering the desert. Al-Tazaqqum: swallowing with difficulty and effort. Shaba al-shay' bi al-shay' yashubuhu shawban: he mixed it and blended it. Rāgha yarūgh: he inclined secretly, from the trick (rawghat) of the fox. Zaffa: he hastened; and azaffa: he entered into zafif (hurrying), so its hamzah in it is not for transitivity; and azaffahu: he made him carry on the zafif. Al-Asma'i said: the hamzah in it is for transitivity. The poet, who is al-Farazdaq, said:

*So the leader of the she-camels came before their young ones, hurrying, and those behind him were hastening.*

* *

﴿By those who range in ranks,﴾ ﴿and those who drive with a driving,﴾ ﴿and those who recite the reminder,﴾ ﴿indeed your God is One.﴾ ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, and Lord of the easts.﴾ ﴿Indeed, We adorned the nearest heaven with an adornment of the stars,﴾ ﴿and as a protection from every rebellious devil.﴾ ﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly, and they are pelted from every side,﴾ ﴿repelled, and for them is a constant punishment.﴾ ﴿Except one who snatches a fragment, and he is pursued by a piercing flaming shooting star.﴾.

This surah is Meccan. The connection of its beginning with the end of Ya-Sin is that when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned the Return and His power to revive the dead, and that He is the one who originates them, and when His will is directed at a thing it is, He mentioned His oneness, since what His will is directed at, in existence and non-existence, is not complete except by the Willer being one. This has been discussed in His saying: ﴿If there were in them gods other than Allah, they would have been ruined﴾ [21:22].

Allah swore by some of His creatures, saying: ﴿By those who range in ranks﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah and Masruq said: they are the angels, who line up in the sky in worship and remembrance in rows. It was also said: they spread their wings in the air, standing and awaiting the command of Allah. It was said: they are those among the children of Adam who are arranged in battle in the way of Allah, or in prayer and obedience. It was said: and the birds that spread their wings. "Those who drive" (al-zājirāt): Mujahid and al-Suddi said: the angels who drive the clouds and other creatures of Allah, exalted is He. Qatadah said: the verses of the Qur'an, because it contains the legal prohibitions; it was said: everything that is restrained from the disobedience of Allah. "Those who recite" (al-tāliyāt): the reciters. Mujahid said: the angels who recite His remembrance. Qatadah said: the children of Adam who recite His revealed speech, and His glorification and His magnification. Mujahid said: the angels who recite His remembrance. Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that He swears by the souls of the diligent scholars, those who range their feet (al-ṣāffāt aqdāmahā) in tahajjud and all the other prayers and the rows of congregations; "those who drive" by admonition and advice; "those who recite" the verses of Allah, and "those who study" His laws; or by the souls of the reciters of the Qur'an in the way of Allah, which range the rows and drive the horses for jihad, and recite the remembrance along with that, not being distracted from it by those preoccupations. End of quote. He also said, meaning: the fa' of conjunction in "al-ṣāffāt" either indicates the sequence of its meanings in existence, as in the saying of the poet: "Alas for Ziyabah for al-Harith al-Sabih, then al-Ghanim, then al-Ayib", meaning the one who rose in the morning, then gained booty, then returned; or it indicates their sequence in degree in some respects, as when you say: take the better, then the best, and do the finer, then the finest; or it indicates the sequence of their described subjects in that, as when you say: may Allah have mercy on those who shave, then those who shorten. As for here, if you make the described subject singular, the fa' indicates the sequence of the ranks in degree; so if the singular is the angels, then the excellence belongs to the rank, then the driving, then the recitation; or the reverse. If you make the described subject plural, they are arranged in excellence, so the ranks are of excellence, the drivers are more excellent, and the reciters are of greater excellence; or the reverse. The meaning of the reverse in both places: you ascend from the more excellent to the excellent to the less excellent, or you begin with the lower, then the excellent, then the most excellent. Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq, al-A'mash, Abu 'Amr and Hamzah assimilated the three tā's (idghām). The sworn-upon sentence includes His oneness, exalted is He: He is One from all the aspects which the reflecting ones consider, a predicate after a predicate, according to the view of those who permit the enumeration of predicates; or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and that is more laudatory: meaning, He is the Lord.

Abu Hayyan, al-Bahr al-Muhit, commentary on surah 37, verses 1–10 (part 2 of 2):

He mentioned the easts (al-mashariq) because they are the places where the lights rise, and seeing by them is more demanding; mentioning them makes mention of the wests (al-maghárib) unnecessary, since the wests are understood from the easts. There are three hundred and sixty easts, and likewise three hundred and sixty wests. The sun rises each day from one of these easts and sets in one of these wests, and it does not rise or set at the same point two days running. He used the dual in ﴿the Lord of the two easts and the Lord of the two wests﴾ [al-Rahman: 17], taking into account the easts and wests of summer and winter. Ibn 'Atiyya said: God intended the easts and wests of the sun, which, it is claimed, number one hundred and eighty in the year, from the longest days of the year to the shortest.

Then God informed of His power in adorning the sky with the stars, and of the arrangement of the adornment: that He made them a protection and a safeguard against the devil. End of quotation. The word zinah (adornment) is a verbal noun like sanah, and also a name for what something is adorned with, as liqah is the name for what the inkwell is fitted with. The majority read ﴿with the adornment of the stars﴾ with the genitive (idafah). This allows the verbal noun to be construed as an idafah to the agent, meaning that the stars adorned the sky, and as an idafah to the object, meaning that God adorned the stars. It also allows that the adornment is that with which something is adorned, with "the stars" as an explanation of the adornment, because the adornment is vague and applies to the stars and other things adorned with, or to what the stars adorn by their brightness and fixity. Ibn Mas'ud, Masruq (in one report from him), Abu Zur'ah, Ibn Thabbat and Talhah read: bi-zinatin (with tanwin), al-kawakibi (in the genitive) as an apposition to zinah. Ibn Thabbat and Masruq (in one report from each) and al-A'mash, Talhah and Abu Bakr read: bi-zinatin (with tanwin), al-kawakiba (in the accusative). This may be read with zinah as a verbal noun and al-kawakiba as the direct object, as in His saying ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger an orphan﴾ [al-Balad: 14]. It may also be read with al-kawakiba as an apposition to al-sama', meaning "We adorned the stars of the sky." Zayd ibn 'Ali read zinatin with tanwin and al-kawakibu in the nominative, either as the predicate of an implied subject, meaning "it is the stars," or as the agent of the verbal noun, meaning "that the stars adorned." Al-Farra' claimed that the nominative agent of a tanwinated verbal noun is not attested, while the Basrans permitted it, though rarely. Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿with the adornment of the stars﴾ means "with the light of the stars." It has been said that their differing forms may also be intended, such as the shape of the Pleiades, the Big Dipper, Orion and others, along with their risings and their courses.

He singled out the nearest heaven (al-sama' al-dunya) for mention because it is the one seen by the eyes, and protection from the devils is only in it alone. The word ḥifẓan (as a safeguard) is in the accusative as a verbal noun, meaning "and We guarded it with a guarding," or as an object of purpose (maf'ul li-ajlihi) by adding a waw, or by postposing the governing verb, meaning "and for its protection We adorned it with the stars." It is also construed as a reflection of the sense of what came before, since the meaning is: "We created the stars as an adornment for the sky and as a safeguard." All these opinions are transmitted. As for al-marid (the rebellious), its explanation was given in His saying ﴿a rebellious devil﴾ [al-Nisa': 117] in Surat al-Nisa', where the word was ﴿marīdan﴾, whereas here it is ﴿mari'd﴾, in observance of the rhyme (fawasil).

﴿They cannot listen to the exalted assembly﴾ is a separate, independent sentence, narrating the condition of those who steal hearing, and that they are unable to listen or eavesdrop, being pelted with meteors and kept far from that. Except for the one who is given respite until he snatches a snatching and steals a stealing; then the angels promptly pursue him with the piercing meteor. It is not permissible for "they cannot listen" to be a descriptive clause or a resumptive answer to a questioner who asked why they are guarded from the devils, because the description, that they cannot listen, or the answer, would give no meaning to the guarding from the devils on either assumption. With the description, the meaning would become: "and a safeguard from every rebellious devil that neither hears nor eavesdrops," and likewise it would not fit as an answer. The view of one who said that the original is "so that they do not listen," with the lam and "an" deleted so the verb became nominative, is a strained opinion, and the speech of God is to be protected from it. The majority read: lā yassamma'ūna, negating their hearing, although they do eavesdrop, as in His saying ﴿Indeed they are removed from hearing﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 212]. It takes ila because it implies the sense of listening attentively. Ibn 'Abbas (in one report), Ibn Thabbat, 'Abdullah ibn Muslim, Talhah, al-A'mash, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read: with shaddah on the sin and the mim, meaning lā yatasamma'ūna, the ta' being assimilated into the sin, and this implies negating eavesdropping. The apparent meaning of the hadiths is that they still eavesdrop, but they do not hear; and if any of them heard something, he would not escape guards and meteors, from the time of the sending of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and stoning was even more fitting in the Jahiliyyah. Since the fruit of eavesdropping is hearing, hearing is negated by negating eavesdropping in this reading, because its fruit, which is hearing, is absent. "The exalted assembly" (al-mala' al-a'la) includes the angels, while jinn and humans are "the lower assembly," since they are the inhabitants of the earth. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the noblest of the angels, and it was also reported from him that it is their book.

(And they are pelted) means they are shot at and stoned, ﴿from every side﴾, that is, from every direction from which they ascend to the sky. The meteor used as a missile is the one that people see falling, not the stars moving in the sky, because the motion of those is not seen, whereas this stone-throwing meteor is seen in its motion due to its nearness to us. This was said by Makki and al-Naqqash. Mahbub, from Ibn 'Amr, read: wa-yaqdhifūna (active voice), and duhūran is a verbal noun in the place of a circumstantial accusative (hal). Mujahid said: "expelled." It may also be an object of purpose, meaning "and if they are pelted, it is for expulsion," or a verbal noun of yuqdhafūna, since it implies the sense of expulsion, meaning "and they are driven away from every side with a driving away, and pelted from every side with a pelting." Either the figurative sense lies in yuqdhafūna or in duhūran. Ali, al-Sulami, Ibn Abi 'Abla, and al-Tabarani from his men, from Abu Ja'far, read: daḥūran, with a fatha on the dal, meaning a pelting that drives away, with a fatha on the dal. It may also be a verbal noun, like qabūl and wulūgh, except that these forms are reported to be restricted. Al-wāṣib means "the perpetual," as said by al-Suddi and Abu Salih, and it was discussed in Surat al-Nahl. It is said: "wasaba al-shay'u wuṣūban," meaning "it persisted." Mujahid said: "the painful," and from it comes al-waṣab (pain), as if the meaning is: they are stoned in this world and punished in the next. It is also possible that this perpetual punishment is theirs in this world, namely their being stoned perpetually and never attaining what they aim for of stealing hearing.

﴿Except one who snatches a snatching﴾: man (whoever) is a substitute for the pronoun in lā yassamma'ūna, and it may be in the accusative as an exception, meaning "the devils do not hear except the devil who snatches." Al-Jumhur read: khaṭifa, triliteral, with a kasra on the ta'. Al-Hasan and Qatadah read: with a kasra on the kha' and the ta' doubled. Abu Hatim said: it is said to be the dialect of Bakr ibn Wa'il and Tamim ibn Murrah. It was also read: khaṭṭifa, with a fatha on the kha' and a doubled kasra on the ta', which Ibn Khalawayh attributed to al-Hasan, Qatadah and 'Isa; and from al-Hasan also a reduced form. The original in these two readings is ikhtatafa; in the first, when it was made quiescent for assimilation and the kha' was quiescent, it was given a kasra to avoid two quiescent letters, so the alif of wasl was dropped and the ta' took a kasra following the kha's vowel. From Ibn 'Abbas: khiṭifa, with a kasra on both kha' and ta', lightened, following the vowel of the kha' to the vowel of the ta', as they said ni'im. It was also read: fa-atba'ahu, lightened and doubled. Al-thāqib: al-Suddi and Qatadah said it is the one piercing through with its light and its bright beam.

(p. 354) ﴿So ask them: are they harder to create, or those We have created? Indeed, We created them from clinging clay.﴾ ﴿Rather, you marvel, and they mock.﴾ ﴿And when they are reminded, they do not remember.﴾ ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock it.﴾ ﴿And they say, "This is nothing but manifest magic."﴾ ﴿"When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?"﴾ ﴿"And our forefathers of old?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Yes, and you will be humbled."﴾ ﴿It will be but a single blast, and behold, they will be looking.﴾ ﴿And they will say, "Woe to us! This is the Day of Recompense."﴾ ﴿"This is the Day of Judgment, which you used to deny."﴾

*Al-istifta'* is a kind of asking. The hamza (the interrogative particle), although it has moved to the meaning of affirmation (taqrir, an assertion posed as a question), is originally for the meaning of interrogation, i.e., "ask them." The pronoun refers to the polytheists of Makkah. It was said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu al-Ashadd ibn Kaladah, and he was given this kunya (byname) because of the severity of his strength and power. In this affirmative interrogation, the comparison in strength is made between them and those others whom He created: the nations, the jinn, the angels, the celestial spheres and the earths. In the Mushaf of Abdullah (the codex of Ibn Mas'ud), it reads: *am man 'addadna* ("or those whom We have counted"), which is an explanation of *man khalaqna* ("those whom We have created"), meaning: those We have counted among the rows (of creatures) and what comes after them of created beings. The rational is given precedence over the non-rational in His words *man khalaqna*, and He restricted Himself to the agent in *khalaqna* ("We created"), without mentioning the object of the creation, being content with what preceded it. It is as if He said: "or those of the strange and wondrous created things." Al-A'mash read *aman* with the mim lightened and without *am*, making it a second interrogative, also affirmative, so the two are two independent clauses in affirmation. *Man* is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is omitted, its estimate being *ashaddu* ("harder"). On the reading *am man huwa*, it is one affirmation, and its parallel is His words: ﴿Are you harder to create, or the sky?﴾ [al-Nazi'at 27]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Ashaddu khalqan* may mean *aqwa khalqan* ("stronger in creation"), from their saying *shadid al-khalq* ("of strong creation") and *fi khalqihi shiddah* ("in His creation there is strength"), and *asa'bu khalqan* ("more difficult to create"). And *ashaddu khalqan* or *ashaqqahu* may mean *aqwa khalqan*, from their saying *shadid al-khalq*, and *fi khalqihi shiddah*, on the sense of refutation, for their denial of resurrection and the second creation. Whoever finds it easy to create these great creatures, and for whom their invention is not difficult, creating mankind is easier for him." Their being created from *tin lazib* is either a testimony against them of weakness and softness, because what is made from clay is not described as hard and strong; or an argument against them that the clinging clay from which they were created is dust. So from where do they deny that they should be created from dust like it? They said: ﴿When we are dust?﴾ [al-Ra'd 5]. This meaning is supported by what follows concerning their denial of resurrection. End of quotation. What appears is the first possibility. It has been said that ﴿those whom We have created﴾ refers to the past nations, as in His words: ﴿How many generations have We destroyed before them who were mightier in force than them?﴾ [Qaf 36], and His words: ﴿And they were mightier than you in strength﴾ [al-Tawbah 69]. He attributed the creation from clay to them, while the one created from it was their father Adam, since they were his offspring. Al-Tabari said: "The son of Adam was created from earth, water, fire and air, and all of this when mixed becomes clinging clay, which adheres to whatever is near it." It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that *al-lazib* was read with a kasra, meaning "the noble and the good."

The majority read ﴿Rather, you marvel﴾ with the second-person ta' (of address), meaning: at the power of God over these great creations, while they mock you and your wonder and what you show them of the signs of God's power; or: you marvel at their denial of resurrection, while they mock the matter of resurrection; or: you marvel at their turning away from the truth and their blindness to guidance, and that they should be disbelievers despite what you have brought from God. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Sa'dan and Ibn Miqsam read it with the first-person ya' (of speaker). It is related from 'Ali, 'Abdullah, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Shaqiq and al-A'mash. Shurayh the judge denied this reading and said: "God does not marvel." Ibrahim said: "Shurayh was self-satisfied with his knowledge, and 'Abdullah was more knowledgeable than him," meaning 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. The apparent meaning is that the first-person pronoun refers to God Most High, and marvel is not permissible for God Most High, because it is a shock that affects the one who marvels at something. But it has come in a hadith that marvel is attributed to God Most High, and it is interpreted as an attribute of action that God manifests in the manner of the one marvelled at, whether in magnification or belittlement, until people become marvelling at it. So the meaning is: "Rather, I marvel at their misguidance and evil deeds, and I have made it a marvel for those who look at it and at what is joined with it of My law and My guidance." Al-Zamakhshari said: "That is, My great signs and the abundance of My creations have reached such a point that I marvel at them; how then should My servants, these people, for their ignorance and obstinacy, mock My signs? Or: I marvel that they deny resurrection from one whose deeds are these, while they mock the one who describes God as capable of it." He said: "Marvel is stripped of its literal sense to mean magnification, or marvel is imagined and presumed." It has been said: the pronoun refers to the Messenger, meaning: "Say: 'Rather, I marvel.'" Makki and 'Ali ibn Sulayman said: "And they mock your prophethood and the truth that you possess."

The majority read ﴿Rather, you marvel﴾ with the second-person ta' (of address), meaning: at the power of God over these great creations, while they mock you and your wonder and what you show them of the signs of God's power; or: you marvel at their denial of resurrection, while they mock the matter of resurrection; or: you marvel at their turning away from the truth and their blindness to guidance, and that they should be disbelievers despite what you have brought from God. He said: "Marvel is stripped of its literal sense to mean magnification, or marvel is imagined and presumed." It has been said: the pronoun refers to the Messenger, meaning: "Say: 'Rather, I marvel.'" Makki and 'Ali ibn Sulayman said: "And they mock your prophethood and the truth that you possess."

﴿And when they are reminded﴾ and admonished, ﴿they do not remember﴾, and do not heed. Jannah ibn Hubaysh mentioned the reading *dhakaru* with the kaf lightened. It is related that Rukanah, a man of the polytheists of Makkah, met the Messenger (ﷺ) on a deserted mountain while he was tending his flock; he was one of the strongest of people. The Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: "O Rukanah, do you see, if I wrestle you down, will you believe in me?" He said: "Yes." So he threw him down three times. Then he showed him signs of a tree calling and coming to him, but he did not believe. He came to Makkah and said: "O Banu Hashim, you have bewitched the people of the earth with your companion!" So this verse was revealed concerning him and his like: ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock it.﴾ Mujahid and Qatadah said: *yastaskhiruna* ("they mock") is in the form *istaf'ala*, which has the sense of the bare form (*yaskharuna*). It has also been said that it has the sense of seeking, meaning they seek to be among those who mock. Al-Zamakhshari said: "They exaggerate in mockery, or one of them urges another to mock it." It was read *yastashiruna* with the unpointed ha' (ḥ), and this refers to what Rukanah said: "I will certainly bewitch the Messenger." The reference by *hadha* ("this") is to what appeared at his hands, peace be upon him, of the extraordinary miraculous.

The difference over the vowelling of the mim in *mitna* ("we have died") has been mentioned earlier, whether kasra or damma. Whoever reads *a-idha* ("when") with the interrogative, the answer to *idha* is omitted, meaning *nub'athu* ("shall we be resurrected?"), and this is indicated by ﴿indeed we are resurrected﴾; or it is stripped of the sense of condition and remains a pure adverb of time, and the governing verb is estimated: "Shall we be resurrected when we have died?" Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Ibn 'Amir and Nafi' in the narration of Qalun read it with sukun, so it is a conjunction (*harf 'atf*), and whoever reads it with fatha says *qaluu* ("they said") and the conjunction has the interrogative hamza entering upon it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Awa-aba'una* is conjoined to the position of *inna* and its noun, or to the pronoun in *mab'uthuna*." What allowed conjoining to it is the separation by the interrogative hamza, and the meaning is: "Will our forefathers also be resurrected?" as an added emphasis of improbability, meaning that they are older, so their resurrection is more remote and more absurd. So when you say: "Did Zayd stand, or 'Amr?" then 'Amr is an inceptive noun with an omitted predicate for the reason we mentioned. ﴿And you will be humbled﴾, that is, abased. This is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*), whose governing element is omitted, its estimate being: "Yes, you will be resurrected." He added to the answer that their resurrection would be while they are stained with abasement and humiliation. The condition is not omitted with its answer remaining, except when the verb is apocopated (jussed) in what is called the answer of command and prohibition, and what is mentioned with them according to some, but if it is inceptive (ibtida'), then omitting it is not permissible.

In His words ﴿which you used to deny﴾ there is rebuke and reproach for them.

It is related that Rukanah, a man of the polytheists of Makkah, met the Messenger (ﷺ) on a deserted mountain while he was tending his flock; he was one of the strongest of people. The Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: "O Rukanah, do you see, if I wrestle you down, will you believe in me?" He said: "Yes." So he threw him down three times. It was read *yastashiruna* with the unpointed ha' (ḥ), and this refers to what Rukanah said: "I will certainly bewitch the Messenger." The reference by *hadha* ("this") is to what appeared at his hands, peace be upon him, of the extraordinary miraculous.

The difference over the vowelling of the mim in *mitna* ("we have died") has been mentioned earlier, whether kasra or damma. Whoever reads *a-idha* ("when") with the interrogative, the answer to *idha* is omitted, meaning *nub'athu* ("shall we be resurrected?"), and this is indicated by ﴿indeed we are resurrected﴾; or it is stripped of the sense of condition and remains a pure adverb of time, and the governing verb is estimated: "Shall we be resurrected when we have died?" The majority read *a-wa-aba'una* with the fatha on the waw in *awa* ("or"). Abu Ja'far, Shaybah, Ibn 'Amir and Nafi' in the narration of Qalun read it with sukun, so it is a conjunction (*harf 'atf*), and whoever reads it with fatha says *qaluu* ("they said") and the conjunction has the interrogative hamza entering upon it. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Awa-aba'una* is conjoined to the position of *inna* and its noun, or to the pronoun in *mab'uthuna*." What allowed conjoining to it is the separation by the interrogative hamza, and the meaning is: "Will our forefathers also be resurrected?" as an added emphasis of improbability, meaning that they are older, so their resurrection is more remote and more absurd. End of quotation. As for his saying that it is conjoined to the position of *inna* and its noun, the school of Sibawayh is contrary to that, because your saying *inna Zaydan qa'imun wa-'Amrun* contains a noun in the nominative on the basis of the inception, with its predicate omitted. As for his saying "or to the pronoun in *mab'uthuna*" and so on, it is not permissible to conjoin it to the pronoun, because the interrogative hamza enters only upon sentences, not upon a single word; if it were conjoined to a single word, the verb would govern the single word through the mediation of the conjunction particle, and the interrogative hamza's preceding element does not govern what follows it. So his saying *awa-aba'una* is an inceptive noun (mubtada'), whose predicate is omitted, its estimate being *mab'uthuna* ("resurrected"), and what precedes it indicates it. So when you say: "Did Zayd stand, or 'Amr?" then 'Amr is an inceptive noun with an omitted predicate for the reason we mentioned. Their interrogation contained denial and improbability, so God commanded His Prophet to answer them with "Yes."

﴿And you will be humbled﴾, that is, abased. This is a circumstantial clause (*jumlah haliyyah*), whose governing element is omitted, its estimate being: "Yes, you will be resurrected." He added to the answer that their resurrection would be while they are stained with abasement and humiliation. Ibn Wathhab read *na'im* with the kasra on the ʿayn, and the disagreement over it has been mentioned in Surat al-A'raf; it is a metonymy for the resurrection. ﴿It will be but a single blast﴾, that is, a shout, and it is the second blast. Since their resurrection arises from the blast, the blast is called that by metaphor. Al-Zamakhshari said: "It is ambiguous (*mubhamah*), clarified by its predicate." He and Ibn Malik often say that the pronoun is explained by the predicate, and Ibn Malik counted among this His words: ﴿It is nothing but our worldly life﴾ [al-An'am 29], and we discussed this with him in the commentary on *al-Tashil*. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Fa-innama* is the answer to an implied condition, its estimate being: 'When that is the case, then it is but a single blast.'" End of quotation. The clause of the condition is often implied before the fa' when the estimate is permissible, and there is no necessity for that. The condition is not omitted with its answer remaining, except when the verb is apocopated (jussed) in what is called the answer of command and prohibition, and what is mentioned with them according to some, but if it is inceptive (ibtida'), then omitting it is not permissible.

*Yanzurun* is from *al-nazar* ("looking"), meaning: "then behold, they are seeing clearly," or from *al-intizar* ("waiting"), meaning: "then they are awaiting what will be done to them and what they will be commanded." The apparent meaning is that His words ﴿Woe to us!﴾ are part of the speech of some of the disbelievers to others, up to the end of the two clauses, in which they acknowledged that it is the Day of Recompense and that it is the Day of Distinction, and some of them addressed others. Abu Hatim paused at His words ﴿Woe to us!﴾ and made ﴿This is the Day of Recompense﴾ to the end part of the speech of God to them, or of the angels. It has been said that ﴿This is the Day of Recompense﴾ is part of the speech of the disbelievers, and ﴿This is the Day of Distinction﴾ is not part of their speech, but the meaning is: it is said to them, "This is the Day of Distinction." *Yawm al-Din* ("the Day of Recompense") is the Day of requital and exchange, and *Yawm al-Fasl* ("the Day of Distinction") is the Day of separating between the groups of guidance and the groups of error. In His words ﴿which you used to deny﴾ there is rebuke and reproach for them.

(p. 354) ﴿So ask them: are they harder to create, or those We have created? Indeed, We created them from clinging clay.﴾ ﴿Rather, you marvel, and they mock.﴾ ﴿And when they are reminded, they do not remember.﴾ ﴿And when they see a sign, they mock it.﴾ ﴿And they say, "This is nothing but manifest magic."﴾ ﴿"When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?"﴾ ﴿"And our forefathers of old?"﴾ ﴿Say: "Yes, and you will be humbled."﴾ ﴿It will be but a single blast, and behold, they will be looking.﴾ ﴿And they will say, "Woe to us! This is the Day of Recompense."﴾ ﴿"This is the Day of Judgment, which you used to deny."﴾

*Al-istifta'* is a kind of asking. The hamza (the interrogative particle), although it has moved to the meaning of affirmation (taqrir, an assertion posed as a question), is originally for the meaning of interrogation, i.e., "ask them." The pronoun refers to the polytheists of Makkah. It was said that the verse was revealed concerning Abu al-Ashadd ibn Kaladah, and he was given this kunya (byname) because of the severity of his strength and power. In this affirmative interrogation, the comparison in strength is made between them and those others whom He created: the nations, the jinn, the angels, the celestial spheres and the earths. In the Mushaf of Abdullah (the codex of Ibn Mas'ud), it reads: *am man 'addadna* ("or those whom We have counted"), which is an explanation of *man khalaqna* ("those whom We have created"), meaning: those We have counted among the rows (of creatures) and what comes after them of created beings. The rational is given precedence over the non-rational in His words *man khalaqna*, and He restricted Himself to the agent in *khalaqna* ("We created"), without mentioning the object of the creation, being content with what preceded it. It is as if He said: "or those of the strange and wondrous created things." Al-A'mash read *aman* with the mim lightened and without *am*, making it a second interrogative, also affirmative, so the two are two independent clauses in affirmation. *Man* is the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is omitted, its estimate being *ashaddu* ("harder"). On the reading *am man huwa*, it is one affirmation, and its parallel is His words: ﴿Are you harder to create, or the sky?﴾ [al-Nazi'at 27]. Al-Zamakhshari said: "*Ashaddu khalqan* may mean *aqwa khalqan* ("stronger in creation"), from their saying *shadid al-khalq* ("of strong creation") and *fi khalqihi shiddah* ("in His creation there is strength"), and *asa'bu khalqan* ("more difficult to create"). And *ashaddu khalqan* or *ashaqqahu* may mean *aqwa khalqan*, from their saying *shadid al-khalq*, and *fi khalqihi shiddah*, on the sense of refutation, for their denial of resurrection and the second creation. Whoever finds it easy to create these great creatures, and for whom their invention is not difficult, creating mankind is easier for him." Their being created from *tin lazib* is either a testimony against them of weakness and softness, because what is made from clay is not described as hard and strong; or an argument against them that the clinging clay from which they were created is dust. So from where do they deny that they should be created from dust like it? They said: ﴿When we are dust?﴾ [al-Ra'd 5]. This meaning is supported by what follows concerning their denial of resurrection. End of quotation. What appears is the first possibility. It has been said that ﴿those whom We have created﴾ refers to the past nations, as in His words: ﴿How many generations have We destroyed before them who were mightier in force than them?﴾ [Qaf 36], and His words: ﴿And they were mightier than you in strength﴾ [al-Tawbah 69]. He attributed the creation from clay to them, while the one created from it was their father Adam, since they were his offspring. Al-Tabari said: "The son of Adam was created from earth, water, fire and air, and all of this when mixed becomes clinging clay, which adheres to whatever is near it." It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that *al-lazib* was read with a kasra, meaning "the noble and the good."

The majority read ﴿Rather, you marvel﴾ with the second-person ta' (of address), meaning: at the power of God over these great creations, while they mock you and your wonder and what you show them of the signs of God's power; or: you marvel at their denial of resurrection, while they mock the matter of resurrection; or: you marvel at their turning away from the truth and their blindness to guidance, and that they should be disbelievers despite what you have brought from God. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Sa'dan and Ibn Miqsam read it with the first-person ya' (of speaker). It is related from 'Ali, 'Abdullah, Ibn 'Abbas, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Wathhab, Talhah, Shaqiq and al-A'mash. Shurayh the judge denied this reading and said: "God does not marvel." Ibrahim said: "Shurayh was self-satisfied with his knowledge, and 'Abdullah was more knowledgeable than him," meaning 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. The apparent meaning is that the first-person pronoun refers to God Most High, and marvel is not permissible for God Most High, because it is a shock that affects the one who marvels at something. But it has come in a hadith that marvel is attributed to God Most High, and it is interpreted as an attribute of action that God manifests in the manner of the one marvelled at, whether in magnification or belittlement, until people become marvelling at it. So the meaning is: "Rather, I marvel at their misguidance and evil deeds, and I have made it a marvel for those who look at it and at what is joined with it of My law and My guidance." Al-Zamakhshari said: "That is, My great signs and the abundance of My creations have reached such a point that I marvel at them; how then should My servants, these people, for their ignorance and obstinacy, mock My signs? Or: I marvel that they deny resurrection from one whose deeds are these, while they mock the one who describes God as capable of it." He said: "Marvel is stripped of its literal sense to mean magnification, or marvel is imagined and presumed." It has been said: the pronoun refers to the Messenger, meaning: "Say: 'Rather, I marvel.'" Makki and 'Ali ibn Sulayman said: "And they mock your prophethood and the truth that you possess."

﴿And when they are reminded﴾ and admonished, ﴿they do not remember﴾, and do not heed. Jannah ibn Hubaysh mentioned the reading *dhakaru* with the kaf lightened. It is related that Rukanah, a man of the polytheists of Makkah, met the Messenger (ﷺ) on a deserted mountain while he was tending his flock; he was one of the strongest of people. The Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: "O Rukanah, do you see, if I wrestle you down, will you believe in me?" He said: "Yes." So he threw him down three times. Then he showed him signs of a tree calling and coming to him, but he did not believe. He came to Makkah and said: "O Banu Hashim, you have bewitched the people of the earth with your companion!" **Verses 22–39**

﴿Gather those who did wrong, and their spouses, and what they used to worship﴾ ﴿besides God, and guide them to the path of the Blazing Fire﴾ ﴿and stop them, for they are to be questioned﴾ ﴿"What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?"﴾ ﴿Nay, today they are in full submission﴾ ﴿and they turn to one another, questioning each other﴾ ﴿They will say, "You used to come to us from the right side."﴾ ﴿They will say, "Nay, you were not believers﴾ ﴿and we had no authority over you. Rather, you were a rebellious people﴾ ﴿so the word of our Lord has come true against us: we are indeed going to taste (the punishment)﴾ ﴿and we led you astray, for we were ourselves astray"﴾ ﴿So on that Day they will share in the punishment﴾ ﴿Indeed, that is how We deal with the criminals﴾ ﴿Indeed, when it was said to them, "There is no god but God," they behaved arrogantly﴾ ﴿and they said, "Are we to abandon our gods for a mad poet?"﴾ ﴿Nay, he has brought the truth and confirmed the messengers﴾ ﴿Indeed, you are going to taste the painful punishment﴾ ﴿and you will be recompensed only for what you used to do.﴾

(Gather) is an address from God to the angels, or the angels addressing one another, i.e., gather together the wrongdoers and their unbelieving women; this is said by Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Rummani preferred it. "Their kinds and their companions," also said by 'Amr ibn 'Abbas, or "their likes among the sinners": the people of fornication with the people of fornication, the people of theft, or "their companions," the devils. 'Isa ibn Sulayman al-Hijazi read (wa-azwajuhum) in the nominative, as a conjunction with the pronoun in (zalamu), i.e., "and their spouses did wrong." (Fahduhum) means: make them know and drive them to the path of the Fire, until they roast in it; al-Jahim is one of the levels of Jahannam. (Qifuhum) is as He said: ﴿If you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire﴾ [al-An'am: 27], and it is a rebuke to them. (Innahum mas'uluna) — 'Isa read (annahum) with a fatha on the hamza. 'Abd Allah said: they will be asked about drinking cold water, in mockery of them; and also from him: they will be asked about "There is no god but God." The majority said: and about their deeds, and they will be made to stand before their ugliness. And in a hadith: "The feet of a servant will not move until he is asked about five things: his youth, how he spent it; his life, how he consumed it; his wealth, how he earned it and how he spent it; and what he did with what he knew." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is possible that the meaning is in the manner of what he explained with His saying ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?﴾, i.e., they are asked about their refusal to help one another, and this is in the form of rebuke for refusing. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is mockery of them and a rebuke to them for their inability to help one another, after they had been, in the world, mutually supportive and helpful. Al-Tha'labi said: (What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?) is the reply of Abu Jahl when he said at Badr: ﴿We are a united force, victorious﴾ [al-Qamar: 44]. It was also read: (la tanasarun), with one ta' and with two ta's, and with the assimilation of one into the other.

﴿Nay, today they are in full submission﴾: i.e., some of them have surrendered to one another and forsaken one another out of helplessness; each one of them is submissive and not victorious.

﴿and they turn to one another, questioning each other﴾: Qatadah said: they are jinn and humans, and their questioning is in the sense of reproach, regret and wrath. They said: i.e., the humans said to the jinn. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: or the weak among humans, the unbelievers, said to their leaders and chiefs. "The right side" (al-yamin) is the bodily limb, and is not intended here. It was said: it was borrowed for the direction of good, or for strength and force, or for the direction of desires, or for the direction of deception and misguidance, showing that it is right guidance, or for the oath. Each of these metaphors has a basis.

As for its being borrowed for the direction of good: the right limb is the nobler and more blessed of the two limbs; they used to take omens by it even in the case of the "sanih" (a bird flying from right to left), they shook hands, they gave and received with it, and they handled most matters with it, and did the finest things with it; it was assigned to the recorder of good deeds, and the believer takes his book with it, whereas the left is the opposite. As for its being borrowed for strength and force: blows are struck with it, so the meaning is: you overpower us with your strength and drive us onto the path of error. As for its being borrowed for the direction of desires: the right side is the heavier side of a person and the liver is on it, while the left side has the heart and its cunning and is lighter; and one who is defeated turns onto his left side, since it is the lighter of his two sides. As for its being borrowed for the direction of deception and misguidance: it is as if they likened the words of the seducers to the omens which they regard as praiseworthy, as if the deception in their seduction were the most praiseworthy thing. As for the oath: they swear to them and come to them as those swearing to the goodness of what they lead them to.

(They said), i.e., those addressed, either the jinn or the leaders of unbelief: ﴿Nay, you were not believers﴾, i.e., we did not confirm you in unbelief; rather, of your own selves you refused faith. Al-Zamakhshari said: you turned away, despite your having been empowered and having been tested, "Nay, you were a people upon unbelief, not compelled," and we had no authority over you by which we might strip you of your power and testing; rather, you were a people who freely chose rebellion. End. The terms "empowerment" and "choice" are the vocabulary of the Mu'tazilah, following their doctrine.

﴿so the word of our Lord has come true against us﴾: i.e., the word of our Lord became binding upon us, that is, His threat to us of punishment. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿we are indeed going to taste (the punishment)﴾ is their report that they, all of them, the leaders and the followers, will taste the punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: so the word of our Lord was binding upon us, ﴿we are indeed going to taste﴾, meaning God's threat that we will surely taste His punishment, since He knows our state and that we deserve the punishment for it. Had he related the threat as it is, he would have said: "Indeed you are going to taste," but he shifted it to the first-person speaker, because they are speaking about themselves, and similar is the saying of the poet:

"Hawazin has claimed that my wealth is small"

Had he related their saying, he would have said: "your wealth is small." And from this is the saying of one who makes another swear to the swearer: "I will surely go out," and "let us surely go out": the hamza is for relating the swearer's words, and the ta' is for the one making the oath turning toward the oath. End.

﴿and we led you astray﴾: we called you to error, and there was in you a readiness for it, so you went astray.

﴿for we were ourselves astray﴾: so we wanted you to share with us in error.

﴿So on that Day they will share in the punishment﴾: i.e., on the day when they questioned one another and reproached one another in speech. This is a report from Him, exalted is He, that just as they shared in error, they share in what follows from it of punishment. (Indeed, that is how) i.e., like this deed with these, We deal with every criminal; thus his punishment follows from his crime. Then He informed about their greatest crime, which is associating partners with God, and their arrogance against His monotheism and singling Him out for divinity. Then He mentioned what they slandered the Messenger with, which is attributing to him poetry and madness, and that they would not abandon their gods for him or for what he brought; thus they combined denial of the Oneness with denial of the Message. Their saying (a mad poet) is a jumble in their speech and confusion in their error, for a poet is one who has such understanding, acuity and quickness of perception that he orders strange meanings and shapes them in the mold of striking words, whereas one who is mad cannot attain any of that.

Then God turned away from their speech and informed that the truth has come, namely the affirmation of what does not perish; so what he brought is not poetry, but the truth about which there is no doubt. Then He informed that he confirmed those messengers who preceded him, since he and they were upon one way in calling the nations to monotheism and to abandoning the worship of other than Him. 'Abd Allah read (wa-saddaqa) with the dal lightened, and (al-mursaluna) with waw in the nominative, i.e., the messengers confirmed in announcing him and that he would come at the end of them. The majority read ﴿la-dhA'iqu al-'adhab﴾ with the nun dropped for the annexation; and Abu al-Sammal, and Aban, from Tha'labah, from 'Asim, read it with the nun dropped because of the meeting of the definite article's lam and the accusative 'adhab. Just as some dropped the tanwin for that in the reading of one who read "Ahadu Allah." Ibn 'Atiyyah reported from Abu al-Sammal that he read "la-dha'iqun" with tanwin and "al-'adhaba" in the accusative, and this is construed as meaning a plural, otherwise the singular would not agree with the plural pronoun in (innakum), and the poet's saying:

"I found him unwilling to be pleased, and not remembering God except a little"

It was also read: "la-dha'iquna" with the nun, and "al-'adhaba" in the accusative. And: "What you are recompensed with is only the like of your deeds, since it is the fruit of your deeds."

ﷻ

**Verses 22–39**

Rather, you were a rebellious people﴾ ﴿so the word of our Lord has come true against us: we are indeed going to taste (the punishment)﴾ ﴿and we led you astray, for we were ourselves astray"﴾ ﴿So on that Day they will share in the punishment﴾ ﴿Indeed, that is how We deal with the criminals﴾ ﴿Indeed, when it was said to them, "There is no god but God," they behaved arrogantly﴾ ﴿and they said, "Are we to abandon our gods for a mad poet?"﴾ ﴿Nay, he has brought the truth and confirmed the messengers﴾ ﴿Indeed, you are going to taste the painful punishment﴾ ﴿and you will be recompensed only for what you used to do.﴾

(Gather) is an address from God to the angels, or the angels addressing one another, i.e., gather together the wrongdoers and their unbelieving women; this is said by Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Rummani preferred it. "Their kinds and their companions," also said by 'Amr ibn 'Abbas, or "their likes among the sinners": the people of fornication with the people of fornication, the people of theft, or "their companions," the devils. 'Isa ibn Sulayman al-Hijazi read (wa-azwajuhum) in the nominative, as a conjunction with the pronoun in (zalamu), i.e., "and their spouses did wrong." (Fahduhum) means: make them know and drive them to the path of the Fire, until they roast in it; al-Jahim is one of the levels of Jahannam. (Qifuhum) is as He said: ﴿If you could see when they are made to stand over the Fire﴾ [al-An'am: 27], and it is a rebuke to them. (Innahum mas'uluna) — 'Isa read (annahum) with a fatha on the hamza. 'Abd Allah said: they will be asked about drinking cold water, in mockery of them; and also from him: they will be asked about "There is no god but God." The majority said: and about their deeds, and they will be made to stand before their ugliness. And in a hadith: "The feet of a servant will not move until he is asked about five things: his youth, how he spent it; his life, how he consumed it; his wealth, how he earned it and how he spent it; and what he did with what he knew." Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it is possible that the meaning is in the manner of what he explained with His saying ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?﴾, i.e., they are asked about their refusal to help one another, and this is in the form of rebuke for refusing. Al-Zamakhshari said: this is mockery of them and a rebuke to them for their inability to help one another, after they had been, in the world, mutually supportive and helpful. Al-Tha'labi said: (What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?) is the reply of Abu Jahl when he said at Badr: ﴿We are a united force, victorious﴾ [al-Qamar: 44]. It was also read: (la tanasarun), with one ta' and with two ta's, and with the assimilation of one into the other.

﴿Nay, today they are in full submission﴾: i.e., some of them have surrendered to one another and forsaken one another out of helplessness; each one of them is submissive and not victorious.

﴿and they turn to one another, questioning each other﴾: Qatadah said: they are jinn and humans, and their questioning is in the sense of reproach, regret and wrath. They said: i.e., the humans said to the jinn. Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: or the weak among humans, the unbelievers, said to their leaders and chiefs. "The right side" (al-yamin) is the bodily limb, and is not intended here. It was said: it was borrowed for the direction of good, or for strength and force, or for the direction of desires, or for the direction of deception and misguidance, showing that it is right guidance, or for the oath. Each of these metaphors has a basis.

As for its being borrowed for the direction of good: the right limb is the nobler and more blessed of the two limbs; they used to take omens by it even in the case of the "sanih" (a bird flying from right to left), they shook hands, they gave and received with it, and they handled most matters with it, and did the finest things with it; it was assigned to the recorder of good deeds, and the believer takes his book with it, whereas the left is the opposite. As for its being borrowed for strength and force: blows are struck with it, so the meaning is: you overpower us with your strength and drive us onto the path of error. As for its being borrowed for the direction of desires: the right side is the heavier side of a person and the liver is on it, while the left side has the heart and its cunning and is lighter; and one who is defeated turns onto his left side, since it is the lighter of his two sides. As for its being borrowed for the direction of deception and misguidance: it is as if they likened the words of the seducers to the omens which they regard as praiseworthy, as if the deception in their seduction were the most praiseworthy thing. As for the oath: they swear to them and come to them as those swearing to the goodness of what they lead them to.

(They said), i.e., those addressed, either the jinn or the leaders of unbelief: ﴿Nay, you were not believers﴾, i.e., we did not confirm you in unbelief; rather, of your own selves you refused faith. Al-Zamakhshari said: you turned away, despite your having been empowered and having been tested, "Nay, you were a people upon unbelief, not compelled," and we had no authority over you by which we might strip you of your power and testing; rather, you were a people who freely chose rebellion. End. The terms "empowerment" and "choice" are the vocabulary of the Mu'tazilah, following their doctrine.

﴿so the word of our Lord has come true against us﴾: i.e., the word of our Lord became binding upon us, that is, His threat to us of punishment. The apparent meaning is that His saying ﴿we are indeed going to taste (the punishment)﴾ is their report that they, all of them, the leaders and the followers, will taste the punishment. Al-Zamakhshari said: so the word of our Lord was binding upon us, ﴿we are indeed going to taste﴾, meaning God's threat that we will surely taste His punishment, since He knows our state and that we deserve the punishment for it. Had he related the threat as it is, he would have said: "Indeed you are going to taste," but he shifted it to the first-person speaker, because they are speaking about themselves, and similar is the saying of the poet:

"Hawazin has claimed that my wealth is small"

Had he related their saying, he would have said: "your wealth is small." And from this is the saying of one who makes another swear to the swearer: "I will surely go out," and "let us surely go out": the hamza is for relating the swearer's words, and the ta' is for the one making the oath turning toward the oath. End.

﴿and we led you astray﴾: we called you to error, and there was in you a readiness for it, so you went astray.

﴿for we were ourselves astray﴾: so we wanted you to share with us in error.

﴿So on that Day they will share in the punishment﴾: i.e., on the day when they questioned one another and reproached one another in speech. This is a report from Him, exalted is He, that just as they shared in error, they share in what follows from it of punishment. (Indeed, that is how) i.e., like this deed with these, We deal with every criminal; thus his punishment follows from his crime. Then He informed about their greatest crime, which is associating partners with God, and their arrogance against His monotheism and singling Him out for divinity. Then He mentioned what they slandered the Messenger with, which is attributing to him poetry and madness, and that they would not abandon their gods for him or for what he brought; thus they combined denial of the Oneness with denial of the Message. Their saying (a mad poet) is a jumble in their speech and confusion in their error, for a poet is one who has such understanding, acuity and quickness of perception that he orders strange meanings and shapes them in the mold of striking words, whereas one who is mad cannot attain any of that.

Then God turned away from their speech and informed that the truth has come, namely the affirmation of what does not perish; so what he brought is not poetry, but the truth about which there is no doubt. Then He informed that he confirmed those messengers who preceded him, since he and they were upon one way in calling the nations to monotheism and to abandoning the worship of other than Him. 'Abd Allah read (wa-saddaqa) with the dal lightened, and (al-mursaluna) with waw in the nominative, i.e., the messengers confirmed in announcing him and that he would come at the end of them. The majority read ﴿la-dhA'iqu al-'adhab﴾ with the nun dropped for the annexation; and Abu al-Sammal, and Aban, from Tha'labah, from 'Asim, read it with the nun dropped because of the meeting of the definite article's lam and the accusative 'adhab. Just as some dropped the tanwin for that in the reading of one who read "Ahadu Allah." Ibn 'Atiyyah reported from Abu al-Sammal that he read "la-dha'iqun" with tanwin and "al-'adhaba" in the accusative, and this is construed as meaning a plural, otherwise the singular would not agree with the plural pronoun in (innakum), and the poet's saying:

"I found him unwilling to be pleased, and not remembering God except a little"

It was also read: "la-dha'iquna" with the nun, and "al-'adhaba" in the accusative. And: "What you are recompensed with is only the like of your deeds, since it is the fruit of your deeds."

It was also read: (la tanasarun), with one ta' and with two ta's, and with the assimilation of one into the other.

﴿Nay, today they are in full submission﴾: i.e., some of them have surrendered to one another and forsaken one another out of helplessness; each one of them is submissive and not victorious.

"The right side" (al-yamin) is the bodily limb, and is not intended here.
