﴿As if they were hidden eggs﴾. He likened them, the majority say, to the hidden ostrich eggs in its nest, which is the nest-hollow, and its color is white with a fine yellowness, and women are likened to it, so he said:

"Glowing of cheeks"; and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

"And an egg of a tent whose dwelling is not approached; I enjoyed with it some pleasure, not hastily.
Like the virgin of al-Maqana, whiteness with yellowness, nourished by flowing water unmixed."

Al-Suddi and Ibn Jubayr said: he likened their colors to the color of the inner shell of the egg, which is the membrane of the egg, and it is what is hidden within a covering. Al-Tabari preferred this and said: as for the outer shell of the egg, it is not hidden. From Ibn ʿAbbas: "the hidden egg" is the protected jewel, but the wording rejects this view. A group said: it is a general comparison of the whole woman to the whole egg, intending by that the proportion of the woman's parts, and that each part of her in its goodness relative to its kind is like the relation of another of her parts to its kind; so the proportion of her hair to her eye is balanced, since both are complete in their kind, and the egg is the most proportionate of things in its parts, since in its visual beauty it is one; as one of the men of letters said in love-poetry:

"Her limbs are proportioned, so you see no discord in them, but they came in measure."

Their questioning in Paradise is questioning of ease and luxury, recounting their bliss, the state of the world, faith and its fruit. ﴿Then approached﴾ is coordinated with ﴿a cup is passed around among them﴾, and the meaning: they drink and converse over the drink, as is the custom of drinking in this world.

The poet said:

"Nothing of pleasures remains but the conversations of the noble over wine."

It is brought in the past tense for the truthfulness of the report, as if it had already occurred. Then Allah related of one of them what He related, recalling thereby His blessing upon him, in that He guided him to faith and to belief in the occurrence of resurrection, reward and punishment; and this is an example of guarding oneself against evil companions and keeping distance from them. Ibn ʿAbbas and others said: this speaker and his companion were of humankind. A group said: they are the two in His saying ﴿Woe to me! I wish I had not taken so-and-so as a friend﴾ [al-Furqan: 28]. Mujahid said: he was a human and a jinn among the disbelieving devils. Al-Jumhur read ﴿مِنَ المُصَدِّقِينَ﴾ (among the believers) with a light ṣād, from taṣdīq (belief); and a group read it with a shadda, from taṣaddaq (giving charity). Qurrah ibn Thaʿlaba al-Nahrani said: they were two partners with eight thousand dirhams; one of them worshipped Allah while being negligent in trade and reflection, and the other was occupied with his wealth; so he separated from his partner because of his negligence. Whenever he bought a house, a slave-girl, a garden, or the like, he displayed it to the believer and boasted over him, so the believer would give charity of something similar in order to buy in Paradise; and so what Allah intended happened to them in the Hereafter. Al-Zamakhshari said: it was revealed concerning a man who gave his wealth in charity for the sake of Allah, then became needy, and asked some of his brothers for help. He said: "Where is your wealth?" He said: "I gave it in charity so that Allah would compensate me in the Hereafter with something better than it." He said: "Are you truly among those who believe in the Day of Religion, or among those who give charity seeking reward? By Allah, I will not give you anything."

﴿Are we indeed to be recompensed?﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and al-Suddi said: "to be requited and called to account"; it was also said: "to be governed and subjected to rule," from the saying "danahu": he governed him; and from the hadith: "The wise is the one who governs his soul." The apparent meaning is that the pronoun in ﴿he said: Would you like to look?﴾ refers to the speaker in ﴿a speaker said﴾. It was said: in the speech there is an omission; the meaning being: he said to this speaker those present of the angels: "Your companion here is being punished in hell," and at that he said: ﴿Would you like to look?﴾. The address in ﴿Would you like to look?﴾ may be to the angels, or to his companions in Paradise with whom he was conversing, or to his servants; and this is the apparent meaning. When his companion denied resurrection, he knew that he was in the Fire, and so he said: ﴿Would you like to look?﴾ toward the Fire, so that I may show you that companion? According to this view, the speech requires no omission, nor a statement of the angels: "Your companion is being punished in hell." It was said: in Paradise there are openings through which its people look at the people of the Fire. It was also said: the speaker of ﴿Would you like to look?﴾ is God Most High. It was said: some of the angels say to the people of Paradise: "Rather, do you wish to look, so that you may know where your station is compared to the station of the people of the Fire?"

Al-Jumhur read ﴿مُطَّلِعُونَ﴾ with a shadda on the open ṭā' and a fatha on the nūn, and ﴿اطَّلَعَ﴾ with a shadda on the ṭā' as a past verb. Abu ʿAmr, in the transmission of Husayn al-Ju'fi, read: muṭlaʿūna, with a sukun on the ṭā' and a fatha on the nūn, then ﴿أُطْلِعَ﴾ with a damma on the hamza, a sukun on the ṭā', and a kasra on the lam as a past verb in the passive voice; this is the reading of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Muhaysin, ʿAmmar ibn Abi ʿAmmar, and Abu Siraj. It was also read: fa-aṭṭali'u, with a shadda, as a present verb in the subjunctive after the interrogative. It was read: muṭli'ūna, with lightening, fa-aṭla'a lightened as a past verb, and fa-aṭli'u lightened as a present subjunctive. Abu al-Barhatham and ʿAmmar ibn Abi ʿAmmar, as transmitted by Khalaf from ʿAmmar, read: muṭli'ūnī with a lightened ṭā' and a kasra on the nūn, then ﴿أُطْلِعَ﴾ as a past passive verb. Abu Hatim and others rejected this reading, because it combines the plural nūn with the first-person ya'. The correct form would be muṭṭali'ī, as he said, or mukhrijiyya-hum. Abu al-Fath justified it by treating the active participle as having the function of the present tense, and al-Tabari cited for this the poet's line:

"I do not know, while every opinion of mine is an opinion: will Shurahi hand me over to my people?"

Al-Farra' said: he means Shurahil. Al-Zamakhshari said: he means "muṭṭali'ūna iyyāya" (looking at me), placing the attached pronoun in the position of the detached one, as in his saying:

"They are the doers of good and those who command it."

Or he likened the active participle in this to the present tense due to their affinity, as if he said: "taṭṭali'ūna" (you look), and this is weak, occurring only in poetry. End of quote. The second explanation is Abu al-Fath's explanation; the first explanation is not permissible, because it is not among the positions of the detached pronoun, so the attached pronoun would be placed in its position; it is not permissible to say: "Hind, Zayd is hitting her" (with the attached pronoun), nor "Zayd is hitting me" in that sense. Al-Zamakhshari's speech indicates its permissibility, but the better is Abu al-Fath's explanation, and it has come from it: "amuslimunī ilā qawmī sharāḥī"; and the saying of another:

﴿فَأُطْلِعَ﴾ is the reading in which the verb is in the passive, so its pronoun (the one who looks) is the unnamed object, and the verb is transitive by means of the hamza (the causative prefix). One says: "Zayd rose (ṭalaʿa)," and "someone else made him rise (aṭlaʿahu)."

The poet's verse:

"So is there a youth among the nobles of the people who will carry me,
and no one carries me except the son of a porter?"

And the other said:

"and it is not one who tires me."

These are verses in which the tanwin (nunation, the "n" sound added to nouns) stands together with the ya' of the first person (the speaker's "my"). Likewise the nun of the plural (nūn al-jamʿ) stands with it, treating the nun as if it were tanwin, because both drop out in the idafa (genitive annexation).

It is said: ṭalaʿa ʿalaynā fulān and iṭṭalaʿa have the same meaning.

The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: ṭalaʿa and iṭṭalaʿa mean "appeared and became visible." Iṭṭalaʿa iṭṭilāʿan means "came forward," and it is used in the passive form. The meaning is: "Are you coming forward? Then he will be made to come forward." If the verbal noun (maṣdar) is made the substitute for the subject, as in "iṭṭalaʿa al-iṭṭilāʿ," or the omitted preposition (ḥarf al-jarr) is made the substitute, meaning "iṭṭalaʿa bihi," that is possible, because iṭṭalaʿa is intransitive (lāzim), just as aqbala is. End of quote.

We have already mentioned that aṭṭalaʿa is made transitive by the hamza from the intransitive ṭalaʿa. As for his saying "or the omitted preposition, i.e., iṭṭalaʿa bihi," this is not permissible. The object of the passive verb (the substitute for the subject) may not be omitted, because it takes the place of the subject. Just as the subject may not be omitted without its governing verb, so it is with this. If you say "Zayd is helped (mamdūd)" or "Zayd is angered (maghḍūb)," meaning "by him" or "at him," it is not allowed.

Sawāʾ al-Jaḥīm means its middle. You say: "I became exhausted until my middle (sawāʾī) was cut off." Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was called sawāʾ because the distance from it to all its sides is equal, meaning the middle of the Blazing Fire.

Khalīl al-ʿAṣrī said: he saw him, and his condition had changed. Had God not made him know it, he would not have recognized him. At that point he said to him: ﴿By God, you almost ruined me!﴾, meaning "you almost destroyed me by your misguidance." Inna is a light form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy form (thaqīla), with which the oath is introduced. Tallāhi is an oath in which there is wonder at his (the believer's) safety from it (the fire), when his companion had almost brought him to ruin.

﴿And were it not for the blessing of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forward﴾ (for punishment), just as you have been brought forward. This blessing is His granting him success in faith and in keeping away from an evil companion.

﴿Then are we not going to die﴾: Zayd ibn ʿAlī read it as "bimā'itīn" (with a different word). The apparent view is that this is from the speech of the speaker (the believer), addressing his companion in a tone of reproach. That is: we, the people of Paradise, are not going to die. But the first death was ours in this world. This is unlike the people of the Fire, who at every moment wish for death.

﴿And we shall not be punished﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ 138], as are the people of the Fire; rather, we are always in bliss. In his saying this, he may be giving him a rebuke, scolding him and grieving him with what God has bestowed on him of entering Paradise, teaching him that his state in the Hereafter differs from his state (in this world), just as they differed in this world, in that there is no reward after death. What appeared to him was the opposite: he is punished for his disbelief in God and his denial of resurrection.

It is also possible that this is an address from the speaker to his companions, when he saw what had befallen his companion. He made them stand before His blessings, may He be exalted, in the eternity of their abiding in Paradise and their bliss in it.

His saying "(inna hādhā)" connects, according to this interpretation too, up to His saying ﴿the workers﴾, not clearly as an address to his companions.

It is also possible that his speech ended at His saying ﴿you almost ruined me﴾, and that ﴿Then are we not going to die﴾ up to "punished" is part of his speech and the speech of his companions. Likewise "(inna hādhā)" up to ﴿the workers﴾, meaning: "this matter in which we are, of bliss and deliverance from the Fire."

It has been said: it is from the speech of God, may He be exalted, confirming their words, affirming them, and addressing the Messenger of God and his community. This is strengthened by His saying ﴿For the like of this let the workers work﴾. The Hereafter is not a place of work, and this statement by the believer in the Hereafter does not fit, except as a figurative usage, as if he were saying: "For the like of this, the workers should work."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: what the hamza of interrogation is coordinated with is omitted, and its meaning is: "Are we to be immortal?" That is, "blessed." So: "then we are not going to die, nor be punished." End of quote.

It has already been established in his view that when the hamza of interrogation precedes and a coordinating particle comes after it, the pronoun is placed in a position that makes the hamza and the particle stand in the places they occupy. The position of the majority is that the coordinating particle is the one put first in the underlying structure, with the hamza after it. But since the hamza has the right to begin the sentence, it was placed first. So the underlying order, according to the majority, is as stated. As for al-Zamakhsharī, he has returned to the position of the majority, and the discussion with him on this point has already been presented.

Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 37, verse 40–61 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah.﴾ ﴿Those will have a known provision﴾ ﴿—fruits; and they will be honoured﴾ ﴿in Gardens of Bliss﴾ ﴿upon couches, facing one another.﴾ ﴿A cup will be passed around among them from a flowing spring﴾ ﴿white, delicious to those who drink﴾ ﴿—no harm in it, nor will they be intoxicated by it.﴾ ﴿And with them will be maidens restraining their gaze, with beautiful wide eyes﴾ ﴿as if they were hidden eggs.﴾ ﴿Then they will approach one another, questioning.﴾ ﴿A speaker among them will say, "I had a companion﴾ ﴿who used to say, 'Are you really among those who believe?﴾ ﴿When we have died and become dust and bones, will we indeed be recompensed?'"﴾ ﴿He will say, "Would you like to look?"﴾ ﴿So he looks and sees him in the midst of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿He will say, "By Allah, you nearly brought me to ruin!﴾ ﴿Had it not been for the favour of my Lord, I would surely have been among those brought forth."﴾ ﴿Are we not to die﴾ ﴿except our first death, and are we not to be punished?﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is the great triumph.﴾ ﴿For the like of this let the workers work.﴾ (p-359)

﴿Except the servants of Allah﴾ is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'). Having mentioned some of the states of the disbelievers and their punishment, he mentioned some of the states of the believers and their bliss. And ﴿the sincere ones﴾ is an adjective of praise, because their being servants of Allah necessarily entails that they are sincere. He described ﴿provision﴾ as ﴿known﴾, i.e., with them. Their eyes are gladdened by the provision that is poured out for them, and by the fact that their desires come to them according to what they wish. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Known by its qualities with which it was created: good taste, fragrance, delight, and fine appearance." It was also said: "known in its time," like His saying, ﴿And for them is their provision therein morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 62]. From Qatadah: "The known provision is Paradise," but His saying ﴿in Gardens of Bliss﴾ contradicts this. End of quote. (﴿fruits﴾) is a substitute for (﴿provision﴾), and it refers to that which is enjoyed and not eaten for sustaining health; meaning that all their provision is fruits, since they have no need to sustain health with staple foods, for they are sound bodies created for eternity, so everything they eat is for the sake of enjoyment. Ibn Miqsam read: ﴿mukarramun﴾, with a fatha on the kaf and a shadda on the ra'.

He first mentioned the provision, which is what bodies enjoy, and secondly the honour, which is what souls enjoy; and "provision" with "without humiliation" is an emphatic phrase. Then he mentioned the place in which they are, namely the Gardens of Bliss. Then the noblest of the place, which is the couches. Then the pleasure of intimacy, that some of them face others, which is the most complete and most intimate joy. Then the drink, and that they do not take it themselves, but cups are passed around to them. Then he described what is passed around to them in terms of goodness and the absence of corruptions. Then he mentioned the completion of bodily pleasure and concluded with it, just as he began with bodily pleasure in the provision; and it is the most eloquent of delights, namely intimacy with women.

Al-Jumhur read ﴿عَلى سُرُرٍ﴾ (ʿalā sururin) with a damma on the ra'; Abu al-Sammal read it with a fatha, which is the dialect of some of Tamim, and Kalb, who open what is a plural of the pattern fu'ul from a geminate when it is a noun. The grammarians differed regarding the adjective: some analogized it to the noun and so opened, saying that with the fatha of the lam according to that second dialect in the noun; and some restricted that to the noun, which is where the transmission in that dialect occurs. It was said: "muqabala" means that they do not look at the back of one another. In a hadith: "At times curtains are lifted from them, so some of them look at others; and there is no doubt that most of their times are in their palaces."

﴿Yutaf﴾ (is passed around) is in the passive voice, and the agent is omitted; it is affirmed in another verse in His saying ﴿And there will circulate among them immortal youths﴾ [al-Insan: 19], ﴿and there will circulate among them servants of theirs﴾ [al-Tur: 24]; and perhaps they are those who died from the children of the polytheists before reaching the age of obligation. In Sahih al-Bukhari, they are the servants of the people of Paradise. The kas (cup) is the glass vessel in which there is wine or the like of intoxicating drinks, and it is not called a kas unless it contains that. He has called wine itself a kas, naming the thing by the name of its container. The poet said:

"And a cup I drank for pleasure, and another by which I sought a cure."

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, and al-Akhfash said: every kas in the Qur'an is wine. It was said: kas is a specific form among vessels, which is anything whose mouth is wide and which has no handle, and it is not considered whether it is for wine or not.

﴿From a flowing spring﴾, i.e., from a flowing drink, or from a flowing spring, which is that which flows on the face of the earth as water flows. (White) is an adjective of the cup or of the wine. Al-Hasan said: the wine of Paradise is whiter than milk. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah: ṣafrāʾ (yellow), as one of the later poets said:

"Yellow, the sorrows do not descend upon its courtyard; if a stone touched it, it would become joy."

(Delicious) is an adjective applied to the verbal noun for emphasis, or by omission, i.e., possessing delight, or as a feminine of ladhdha in the sense of ladhidh (delicious). (p-360)

﴿No harm in it﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said: it is a headache. Ibn ʿAbbas also said, as did Mujahid and Ibn Zayd: a pain in the stomach. End of quote. The term includes all kinds of corruption arising from drinking wine, so all of them are negated: colic, headache, drowsiness, rowdiness, idle talk, and sinful speech, and the like. Since intoxication is the greatest of its harms, he singled it out by mention, saying ﴿nor will they be intoxicated by it.﴾ The two Haramis and the two Iraqi readers read it with a damma on the ya' and a fatha on the za' here, and in al-Waqiʿa, "and with the departing of the intellect"; Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i explained it with a kasra on both; ʿAsim with a fatha here and a kasra in al-Waqiʿa; Ibn Abi Ishaq with a fatha on the ya' and a kasra on the za'; and Talha with a fatha on the ya' and a damma on the za'.

Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd said: ﴿restraining the gaze﴾: they restrain their gaze to their husbands, and their gaze does not extend to a non-spouse, by His saying, "ʿUruban" (loving, equal in age). The poet said:

"Of the maidens restraining their gaze, if a gnat crawled above the cheek, its trace would appear upon it."

The second explanation is Abu al-Fath's explanation; the first explanation is not permissible, because it is not among the positions of the detached pronoun, so the attached pronoun would be placed in its position; it is not permissible to say: "Hind, Zayd is hitting her" (with the attached pronoun), nor "Zayd is hitting me" in that sense. Al-Zamakhshari's speech indicates its permissibility, but the better is Abu al-Fath's explanation, and it has come from it: "amuslimunī ilā qawmī sharāḥī"; and the saying of another:

﴿فَأُطْلِعَ﴾ is the reading in which the verb is in the passive, so its pronoun (the one who looks) is the unnamed object, and the verb is transitive by means of the hamza (the causative prefix). One says: "Zayd rose (ṭalaʿa)," and "someone else made him rise (aṭlaʿahu)."

The poet's verse:

"So is there a youth among the nobles of the people who will carry me,
and no one carries me except the son of a porter?"

And the other said:

"and it is not one who tires me."

These are verses in which the tanwin (nunation, the "n" sound added to nouns) stands together with the ya' of the first person (the speaker's "my"). Likewise the nun of the plural (nūn al-jamʿ) stands with it, treating the nun as if it were tanwin, because both drop out in the idafa (genitive annexation).

It is said: ṭalaʿa ʿalaynā fulān and iṭṭalaʿa have the same meaning.

The author of al-Lawāmiḥ said: ṭalaʿa and iṭṭalaʿa mean "appeared and became visible." Iṭṭalaʿa iṭṭilāʿan means "came forward," and it is used in the passive form. The meaning is: "Are you coming forward? Then he will be made to come forward." If the verbal noun (maṣdar) is made the substitute for the subject, as in "iṭṭalaʿa al-iṭṭilāʿ," or the omitted preposition (ḥarf al-jarr) is made the substitute, meaning "iṭṭalaʿa bihi," that is possible, because iṭṭalaʿa is intransitive (lāzim), just as aqbala is. End of quote.

We have already mentioned that aṭṭalaʿa is made transitive by the hamza from the intransitive ṭalaʿa. As for his saying "or the omitted preposition, i.e., iṭṭalaʿa bihi," this is not permissible. The object of the passive verb (the substitute for the subject) may not be omitted, because it takes the place of the subject. Just as the subject may not be omitted without its governing verb, so it is with this. If you say "Zayd is helped (mamdūd)" or "Zayd is angered (maghḍūb)," meaning "by him" or "at him," it is not allowed.

Sawāʾ al-Jaḥīm means its middle. You say: "I became exhausted until my middle (sawāʾī) was cut off." Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was called sawāʾ because the distance from it to all its sides is equal, meaning the middle of the Blazing Fire.

Khalīl al-ʿAṣrī said: he saw him, and his condition had changed. Had God not made him know it, he would not have recognized him. At that point he said to him: ﴿By God, you almost ruined me!﴾, meaning "you almost destroyed me by your misguidance." Inna is a light form (mukhaffafa) of the heavy form (thaqīla), with which the oath is introduced. Tallāhi is an oath in which there is wonder at his (the believer's) safety from it (the fire), when his companion had almost brought him to ruin.

﴿And were it not for the blessing of my Lord, I would have been among those brought forward﴾ (for punishment), just as you have been brought forward. This blessing is His granting him success in faith and in keeping away from an evil companion.

﴿Then are we not going to die﴾: Zayd ibn ʿAlī read it as "bimā'itīn" (with a different word). The apparent view is that this is from the speech of the speaker (the believer), addressing his companion in a tone of reproach. That is: we, the people of Paradise, are not going to die. But the first death was ours in this world. This is unlike the people of the Fire, who at every moment wish for death.

﴿And we shall not be punished﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ 138], as are the people of the Fire; rather, we are always in bliss. In his saying this, he may be giving him a rebuke, scolding him and grieving him with what God has bestowed on him of entering Paradise, teaching him that his state in the Hereafter differs from his state (in this world), just as they differed in this world, in that there is no reward after death. What appeared to him was the opposite: he is punished for his disbelief in God and his denial of resurrection.

It is also possible that this is an address from the speaker to his companions, when he saw what had befallen his companion. He made them stand before His blessings, may He be exalted, in the eternity of their abiding in Paradise and their bliss in it.

His saying "(inna hādhā)" connects, according to this interpretation too, up to His saying ﴿the workers﴾, not clearly as an address to his companions.

It is also possible that his speech ended at His saying ﴿you almost ruined me﴾, and that ﴿Then are we not going to die﴾ up to "punished" is part of his speech and the speech of his companions. Likewise "(inna hādhā)" up to ﴿the workers﴾, meaning: "this matter in which we are, of bliss and deliverance from the Fire."

It has been said: it is from the speech of God, may He be exalted, confirming their words, affirming them, and addressing the Messenger of God and his community. This is strengthened by His saying ﴿For the like of this let the workers work﴾. The Hereafter is not a place of work, and this statement by the believer in the Hereafter does not fit, except as a figurative usage, as if he were saying: "For the like of this, the workers should work."

Al-Zamakhsharī said: what the hamza of interrogation is coordinated with is omitted, and its meaning is: "Are we to be immortal?" That is, "blessed." So: "then we are not going to die, nor be punished." End of quote.

It has already been established in his view that when the hamza of interrogation precedes and a coordinating particle comes after it, the pronoun is placed in a position that makes the hamza and the particle stand in the places they occupy. The position of the majority is that the coordinating particle is the one put first in the underlying structure, with the hamza after it. But since the hamza has the right to begin the sentence, it was placed first. So the underlying order, according to the majority, is as stated. As for al-Zamakhsharī, he has returned to the position of the majority, and the discussion with him on this point has already been presented.

[p. 363] When the story of the believer and his companion had ended, and this had come about as a digression (*istitrad*) from one matter to another, he returned to the mention of Paradise and the provision that God has prepared in it for its people. He said: ﴿Is that better as a welcome (nuzul), or the tree of zaqqum?﴾ The *nuzul* is what is prepared for guests. He placed the provision of Paradise on a par with ﴿the tree of zaqqum﴾. Since the known provision produces pleasure and joy, and the tree of zaqqum produces pain and distress, there is no common ground between them in terms of goodness. The purpose is to make Quraysh and the disbelievers affirm and to bring them to acknowledge two things, one of which is clearly false. If the statement were a genuine question, it would not be valid, since no one could imagine that there is any good in the tree of zaqqum, such that it would be equated with the provision of Paradise. Rather, because the believer chose what leads to the provision of Paradise, and the disbeliever chose what leads to the tree of zaqqum, this was said as a rebuke to the disbelievers and to make them acknowledge the evil of their choice.

﴿Indeed We made it a trial for the wrongdoers.﴾ Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Suddi said: this refers to Abu Jahl and his peers. When it was revealed, Abu Jahl said to the disbelievers, "Muhammad says that the Fire grows trees, while it consumes them and destroys them." Thus they were tempted by this, along with all their followers. Abu Jahl also said: "The zaqqum is only dates with butter, and we eat it." It is said that its root is at the bottom of Hell, and its branches rise up to its levels. The word *talʿ* (spathe, the flower cluster of the palm), which is the palm tree, is used metaphorically for what this tree bears, and its *talʿ* is likened to the fruit of a well-known tree called in Yemen *al-Astan*, whose fruit is called "the heads of the devils." Al-Nabighah mentioned it in his verse:

*She turns away from black astan-trees whose lower parts are...*
*Walking like the gait of wandering slave-women carrying bundles of firewood.*

It is a rough, bitter tree of repulsive appearance, and the Arabs named its fruit thus by comparison with the heads of the devils; later it became a standard by which things were likened. It is also said that it is a tree called *al-sawm*, which Saʿidah ibn Jawbah al-Hudhali mentioned in his verse:

*Assigned to guard the branches of the sawm, watching them,*
*Gazing from the lookouts, his belly torn, weak with fear.*

It is also said that the devils are a kind of serpent with crests, and from this comes the verse:

*A short-hipped woman swears whenever I swear,*
*Like the devil of the hima-tree, I know her.*

It is also said that it is likened to what is widely known among people of the aversion and ugliness of the heads of devils, even though they are not seen. For this reason they depict the devil in the most hideous forms. When they see a disheveled person with bristling hair, they say, "His face is like the face of a devil, and his head like the head of a devil." This is in contrast to the angel, whose beautiful appearance they liken to it. Just as Imru' al-Qays likened the sharp, blue-tinged blades to the fangs of the ghouls in his verse:

*And sharpened blades, blue, like the fangs of ghouls,*

though he had not seen those fangs. All of this is an imaginative comparison (*tashbih takhyili*). The pronoun in ﴿from it﴾ refers to the tree, i.e., from its *talʿ*. The majority read ﴿la-shawban﴾ with a fatha on the shin; Shaybân al-Nahwi read it with a damma. al-Zajjaj said: the fatha is for the verbal noun and the damma for the noun, meaning that it is a verb in the sense of a passive participle, i.e., *mashub* (mixed), like *al-naqs* in the sense of *al-manqus*. It was explained as mixing. *Hamim* is water that is extremely hot. It is also said that what is meant here is their drink, which is the mud of putrefaction, their pus and what flows from them. Since He mentioned that they fill their bellies from the tree of zaqqum because of the hunger that afflicts them, or because they are compelled to eat and fill their bellies as an increase in their punishment, He then mentioned what they are given to drink, because of the intensity of their thirst, which is what is mixed for them from the *hamim*. Since filling the stomach follows eating immediately, the conjunction used in His words ﴿then they are filling﴾ is *fa* (then/immediately). Since drinking is often delayed after eating, the word *thumma* (then, implying an interval) is used. Or, when their bellies have been filled with the fruit of the tree, which is hot and burns their bellies and makes them thirsty, their drink is delayed for a time so that they may increase in suffering through thirst, in addition to their suffering, and then they are given what is even hotter, more painful and more hateful.

﴿Then indeed their return is to the Hellfire.﴾ When He has taken them from their dwellings, in which they were lodged in the Fire, to the tree of zaqqum to eat from it, to fill themselves, and to drink from the *hamim*, and [when the sense of] their return to their dwellings is considered, *thumma* is used to indicate this. Return indicates movement, at the time of eating and drinking, to a place other than the place of those two. Then He mentioned their condition regarding the imitation of their fathers. The pronoun refers to Quraysh, and that this imitation was the cause of their deserving those hardships, i.e., they found their fathers astray, so they followed them in their error, hastening in this without anything holding them back. Then He informed about the misguidance of most of those who came before, from the nations, even though their eras were never without the sending of messengers and their warning of the consequences of denial. In His words ﴿So look﴾ there is an indication of their destruction and the evil of their end. He excepted from His servants the sincere ones, and they are the minority, which is the counterpart of His words ﴿most of the earlier ones﴾. The meaning is: except the servants of God, for they were saved.

When He mentioned the misguidance of the earlier ones, and mentioned the first of them in fame, namely the people of Noah, peace be upon him, this included several things: his supplication against his people, his request for salvation, and his seeking help. God answered him in all of this with an answer by which He reached his aim. The *lam* in ﴿then indeed how excellent﴾ is the response to an oath, like the verse:

*By God, you two are indeed excellent lords whom I have found.*

The object of praise is omitted, and its implied meaning is: "then indeed how excellent are We as those who respond." He used the plural form for majesty and grandeur, as in His words ﴿So We determined, and how excellent are the determiners﴾ [al-Mursalat 23], and ﴿the great distress﴾. al-Suddi said: it is drowning, and from it comes the denial of the disbelievers and the boarding of the water and its terror. They are a clearly defined category belonging to the family, which cannot be understood otherwise. Ibn Abbas and Qatadah said: all the people of the earth are from the descendants of Noah. In a hadith: "He, peace be upon him, recited ﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾ and said: Sam, Ham and Japheth." al-Tabari said: the Arabs are from the offspring of Sam, the Sudanese from the offspring of Ham, and the Turks and others from the offspring of Japheth. Another group said: God preserved the descendants of Noah and extended his line, and people are not confined to his offspring; rather, among the nations are those who do not trace back to him.

﴿And We left upon him among the later ones﴾, i.e., among those who remain forever. The object of *taraknā* is omitted, and its implied meaning is "a good and beautiful commendation at the end of time," as said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi. *Salam* (peace) is in the nominative as a new subject (*mubtada'*), and God greeted him with peace so that mankind would follow this, and no one among the worlds would mention him with evil. God greeted him in recompense for his long patience with the words of the disbelievers and their harm to him. al-Zamakhshari said: ﴿And We left upon him among the later ones﴾ and this phrase, which is ﴿Peace upon Noah among the worlds﴾, means: they greet him with greeting and pray for him, and it is from reported speech, like your saying: "I read a surah which We sent down." End of quote. This is the view of al-Farra' and others among the Kufan grammarians, and this is the one on which it is left. It is as if he said: "And We left upon Noah a greeting by which he is greeted until the Day of Resurrection." End. In the reading of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud) it is *salaman* in the accusative. The meaning of ﴿among the worlds﴾ is that this greeting is established and affirmed among all of them, continuing upon him among the angels and both groups (jinn and humankind), who all greet him to the last of them. Then He gave the reason for this greeting: that he was a doer of good, and then He gave the reason for his doing good: that he was a believer. This indicates the greatness of faith and its station with God.

﴿Then We drowned the others﴾, i.e., those among his people who denied him. When He mentioned his greetings and the salvation of his household, since they were believers, He mentioned the destruction of the others by drowning.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 37, verses 83–98:**

﴿And indeed, among his followers was Abraham.﴾ ﴿When he came to his Lord with a sound heart.﴾ ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship?"﴾ ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God, that you desire?﴾ ﴿So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾ ﴿Then he glanced at the stars.﴾ ﴿And said, "Indeed, I am ill."﴾ ﴿So they turned away from him, retreating.﴾ ﴿Then he went secretly to their gods and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ ﴿"What is wrong with you that you do not speak?"﴾ ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand.﴾ ﴿Then they came toward him, hastening.﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you worship what you carve?"﴾ ﴿"And God created you and what you make."﴾ ﴿They said, "Build for him a structure and throw him into the blazing fire."﴾ ﴿So they intended a scheme against him, but We made them the lowest.﴾

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿مِن شِيعَتِهِ﴾ ("among his followers") refers to Noah. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi. The meaning is: among those who followed him in the fundamentals of religion and monotheism, even though their sacred laws differed, or whose laws mostly agreed. Or it means: among those who followed him in steadfastness in God's religion and in patience against those who denied. Between Noah and Abraham there were two thousand and six hundred and forty years, and between them were the prophets Hud and Salih, peace be upon them both.

Al-Farra' said: the pronoun in ﴿مِن شِيعَتِهِ﴾ refers to Muhammad. The more well-known usage is that the later in time is a follower (shi'ah) of the earlier. The reverse occurs in the verse of al-Kumayt:

*"I have none but the family of Ahmad as followers, and I have none but the path of truth as a path."*

Here he made them followers of himself.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "To what does the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) relate?" I say: it relates to what is contained in the word shi'ah of the sense of following (al-mushayaʿah). That is: indeed, among those who followed him in his religion and his piety, at the time when he came to his Lord with a sound heart, was Abraham. Or it relates to an omitted verb, which is "remember" (udhkur). End of quotation.

As for the first analysis, it is not permitted, because it involves separating the governing element from the governed by a foreign element, namely the words ﴿لَإبْراهِيمَ﴾, since these are foreign to "among his followers" and to "when". Moreover, the restriction is increased, since he has taken it as "among those who followed him when he came to Abraham." Also, the emphatic lam (lām al-tawkīd) prevents what precedes it from governing what follows it. If you say, "Indeed, one who strikes with the sword against us, Zayd," and you intend, "striking Zayd is indeed coming against us," it is not permitted. As for his taking it as "remember," this is the standard view among the grammarians (al-muʿribīn, those who analyse i'rab, grammatical case and structure).

His coming to his Lord with a sound heart means his sincerity in religion for God. The soundness of his heart means his freedom from polytheism, doubt, and the defects that afflict hearts, such as rancour, envy, malice, deceit, pride and the like. ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr said: "He never openly displayed anything." It has been said: "Sound" means free from polytheism, and there is no sense in restricting it.

Regarding the accusative case of ﴿أئِفْكًا﴾, the grammarians permitted several possibilities:

First: it is the object of ﴿تُرِيدُونَ﴾ ("you desire"), and the reproach is directed at his people. The interrogative is for confirmation (istifhām taqrīr). Ibn ʿAtiyyah mentioned only this possibility, and al-Zamakhshari also mentioned it. He said: he explained the falsehood (ifk) by his saying, "gods other than God," so that they are a falsehood in themselves.

Second: it is an object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlih), meaning: "Do you desire gods other than God out of falsehood?" "Gods" (ālihah) is then the direct object, and he placed it first out of concern for it. He placed the object of purpose before the direct object, because it was more important to him to confront them with the fact that they were in falsehood and vanity in their polytheism. Al-Zamakhshari began with this possibility.

Third: it is a circumstantial element (ḥāl), meaning: "Do you desire gods other than God, as liars?" This is what al-Zamakhshari said. He made the verbal noun a circumstantial element, which is not common except with the particle *ammā*, as in *ammā ʿilman fa-ʿālimun* ("as for knowledge, he is knowledgeable").

﴿So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾ is an interrogative of rebuke, warning and threat. That is: what is your opinion of Him who deserves to be worshipped, since He is the Lord of the worlds, that you have abandoned His worship and made the idols equal to Him? Or: what is your opinion of His action toward you, with your punishment, since you have worshipped other than Him? It is like when you say, "You have wronged so-and-so; what do you expect him to do to you, other than the evil you have done to him?"

When he rebuked them for worshipping other than God, he wished to show them that their idols neither benefit nor harm. So he devised a plan to make himself alone against them, so that he might break them and show them their condition and their helplessness.

﴿Then he glanced at the stars﴾: the apparent meaning is that he intended the knowledge of the planets and the influences attributed to them, which God had given them. The apparent meaning is that his glance was into them, that is, into their knowledge, or into their book which contained their states and their judgements. It has been said: they used to practise this, so he came to them from the direction in which they practised it, and gave them the impression that by a sign in the science of the stars he had deduced that he was sick, that is, that he was close to sickness. It has been said: it was the plague, which was the most prevalent illness among them at that time, and they feared contagion and fled from him to their festival. For this reason he said ﴿So they turned away from him, retreating﴾. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, and they left him in the house of the idols, and he did what he did. This coming was not from them directly, but after their coming from their own place, there took place those exchanges mentioned in the surah "Iqtarab."

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 37, verses 83–98:**

﴿And indeed, among his followers was Abraham.﴾ ﴿When he came to his Lord with a sound heart.﴾ ﴿When he said to his father and his people, "What is it that you worship?"﴾ ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God, that you desire?﴾ ﴿So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾ ﴿Then he glanced at the stars.﴾ ﴿And said, "Indeed, I am ill."﴾ ﴿So they turned away from him, retreating.﴾ ﴿Then he went secretly to their gods and said, "Will you not eat?"﴾ ﴿"What is wrong with you that you do not speak?"﴾ ﴿Then he turned upon them, striking with the right hand.﴾ ﴿Then they came toward him, hastening.﴾ ﴿He said, "Do you worship what you carve?"﴾ ﴿"And God created you and what you make."﴾ ﴿They said, "Build for him a structure and throw him into the blazing fire."﴾ ﴿So they intended a scheme against him, but We made them the lowest.﴾

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿مِن شِيعَتِهِ﴾ ("among his followers") refers to Noah. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi. The meaning is: among those who followed him in the fundamentals of religion and monotheism, even though their sacred laws differed, or whose laws mostly agreed. Or it means: among those who followed him in steadfastness in God's religion and in patience against those who denied. Between Noah and Abraham there were two thousand and six hundred and forty years, and between them were the prophets Hud and Salih, peace be upon them both.

Al-Farra' said: the pronoun in ﴿مِن شِيعَتِهِ﴾ refers to Muhammad. The more well-known usage is that the later in time is a follower (shi'ah) of the earlier. The reverse occurs in the verse of al-Kumayt:

*"I have none but the family of Ahmad as followers, and I have none but the path of truth as a path."*

Here he made them followers of himself.

Al-Zamakhshari said: If you ask, "To what does the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) relate?" I say: it relates to what is contained in the word shi'ah of the sense of following (al-mushayaʿah). That is: indeed, among those who followed him in his religion and his piety, at the time when he came to his Lord with a sound heart, was Abraham. Or it relates to an omitted verb, which is "remember" (udhkur). End of quotation.

Moreover, the restriction is increased, since he has taken it as "among those who followed him when he came to Abraham." Also, the emphatic lam (lām al-tawkīd) prevents what precedes it from governing what follows it. If you say, "Indeed, one who strikes with the sword against us, Zayd," and you intend, "striking Zayd is indeed coming against us," it is not permitted. As for his taking it as "remember," this is the standard view among the grammarians (al-muʿribīn, those who analyse i'rab, grammatical case and structure).

It has been said: "Sound" means free from polytheism, and there is no sense in restricting it.

Then will you not reason?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 138] ﴿And indeed, Jonah was among the messengers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 139] ﴿When he fled to the laden ship.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 140] ﴿And he drew lots and was among the losers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 141] ﴿Then the fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 142] ﴿And had he not been of those who exalt [Allah],﴾ [Al-Saffat: 143] ﴿he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 144] ﴿So We cast him onto the open land while he was ill.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 145] ﴿And We caused to grow over him a gourd vine.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 146] ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 147] ﴿And they believed, so We let them enjoy [worldly life] for a time.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 148] ﴿So ask them, "Does your Lord have daughters while they have sons?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 149] ﴿Or did We create the angels female while they were witnesses?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 150] ﴿Unquestionably, it is from their own falsehood that they say,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 151] ﴿"Allah has begotten," and indeed, they are liars.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 152] ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 153] ﴿What is [wrong] with you? How do you judge?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 154] ﴿Will you not be reminded?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 155] ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 156] ﴿Then bring your Book, if you should be truthful.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 157] ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship. But the jinn know that they will be brought [to punishment].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 158] ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they describe,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 159] ﴿except the chosen servants of Allah.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 160] ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship﴾ [Al-Saffat: 161] ﴿cannot lead [anyone] astray,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 162] ﴿except one who is to burn in Hell.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 163] ﴿And there is none of us but that he has a known position.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 164] ﴿And indeed, we are those who line up [in ranks].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 165] ﴿And indeed, we are those who exalt [Allah].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 166] ﴿And indeed, they were saying,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 167] ﴿"If we had with us a reminder from the former peoples,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 168] ﴿we would have been sincere servants of Allah."﴾ [Al-Saffat: 169] ﴿But they disbelieved in it, so they will come to know.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 170] ﴿And Our word had already preceded for Our servants, the messengers,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 171] ﴿that indeed they would be the victorious.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 172] ﴿And indeed, Our soldiers—they will be the victors.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 173] ﴿So turn away from them for a time.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 174] ﴿And observe them, for they will see.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 175] ﴿Then is it Our punishment they are hastening?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 176] ﴿But when it descends in their courtyard, evil is the morning of those who were warned.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 177] ﴿So turn away from them for a time.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 178] ﴿And observe, for they will see.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 179] ﴿Exalted is your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 180] ﴿And peace upon the messengers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 181] ﴿And praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 182]

Talla al-rajulu al-rajula: he threw him down on his side; it was also said: he placed him down with force. Sa'ida ibn Huwba said:
"And he laid him down for the forehead and the mouth."

Al-jabinan: the two sides of the forehead on either side. The plural of jabin as ajbun is anomalous; its regular form in the paucal would be ajbina, like kathib and akthiba, and in the plural jabanat and jubun, like kuthubat and kutub.

Al-dhabh (sacrifice): the name of what is slaughtered, like al-ri'y (pasture) is the name of what is grazed.

Abaqa: he fled. Sahama: he cast lots. Al-mudhda': the overturned one. Al-hut: the fish, a known creature.

Alama: he did what one is blamed for. The poet said:
"How many a blameworthy one was not struck with blame, and how many a wrongdoer has no sin."

Al-ara': open, spacious land with no trees and no known landmarks. The poet said:
"I raised a leg whose stumbling I do not fear, and I cast off my garments into the wide open land."

Al-yaqtin: yafil (a pattern) like al-yafsid, from qatana: he remained in the place. It refers to plants that do not stand on a stalk of wood, such as melon, colocynth and cucumber vines. Al-sahah: the courtyard; its plural is sukh. The poet said:
"Thus it was the same whether they did not let their camels graze, or they let them graze and the courtyards were dusty."

[p. 369]

﴿He said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me.﴾ ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy.﴾ ﴿And when he reached with him [the age of] exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast."﴾ ﴿And when they had both submitted and he put him down upon his forehead,﴾ ﴿We called to him, "O Abraham,﴾ ﴿you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this was the clear trial.﴾ ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ ﴿And We left for him [favorable mention] among later generations:﴾ ﴿"Peace upon Abraham."﴾ ﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ ﴿And We gave him good tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are doers of good and those who clearly wrong themselves.﴾.

When Allah saved him from them and from the fire into which they threw him, he resolved to part from them. He expressed his migration to the land of Syria as going to his Lord, as he said: ﴿Indeed, I am migrating to my Lord﴾ [Al-Ankabut: 26], so that he could worship his Lord freely and supplicate to Him without meeting anyone who would disturb him. He emigrated from the land of Babil (Babylon), from the kingdom of Namrud (Nimrod), to Syria. It was also said: to the land of Egypt. The view of those who say that his going does not mean emigration, but rather meeting Allah after being burned, believing that he would die in the fire, is far-fetched; they say he said this before being thrown into the fire. As for ﴿He will guide me﴾, it means to Paradise, as Qatada held; because his saying ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous﴾ refutes this view, since one who believes he will die in the fire would not pray that Allah grant him a righteous son. ("He will guide me") means He will grant me success in what is good for me.

﴿From among the righteous﴾ means a son who will be counted among the righteous. The word hibah (gift) is mostly used for a child, though it has also come for a brother, as in His saying ﴿And We gave him, from Our mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 53]. The good tidings included that the child would be male, that he would reach the age of puberty, and that he would be described as forbearing. What forbearance is greater than his saying, when his father had presented the sacrifice to him: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast﴾.

﴿When he reached with him [the age of] exertion﴾: between this clause and the one before it there is an omitted element, whose sense is: so a child was born to him and grew up.

﴿When he reached﴾ means that he reached the point of walking with his father in his affairs and needs. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: al-sa'y here means work, worship and assistance. Qatada said: al-sa'y is walking on foot, meaning exertion with full capacity. On this al-Zamakhshari said: it cannot be connected to balagha (reached) in the sense that both of them reached the limit of exertion together, nor to al-sa'y, because its origin is a verbal noun which cannot precede what depends on it. He denied that it is an explanation, as if, when he said ﴿When he reached with him the exertion﴾, meaning the limit at which he could exert himself, it was asked: "With whom?" and he answered: "With his father." The reason for specifying the father is that he was the gentlest of people and the most compassionate toward him and toward others, and he would not impose on him the kind of demand that would be hard for him, since he had not yet become firm in his speech and his father did not require him to return. At that time he was thirteen years old. End of quote.

﴿He said, "O my son"﴾: a call of tenderness and compassion.

﴿Indeed, I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you﴾, meaning by a command from Allah, and this is indicated by ﴿do as you are commanded﴾. The dreams of prophets are revelation, like wakefulness. His mentioning the dream to him was a way of making him bear that great trial. He consulted him with the words ﴿so see what you think﴾, although it was a binding command from Allah, so that he would know what he had in him for accepting this great test, would strengthen him if he grew anxious, would prepare his soul to face this trial, and would calm his soul regarding what was unavoidable, since being surprised by a trial before one is aware of it is harder on the soul. What he saw was in a dream and not in wakefulness, like the dream of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the dream of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of entering the Sacred Mosque; this shows that the states of the prophets, in wakefulness and in sleep, are equal in truthfulness and mutually supporting. It is said: when the angels gave the good tidings of a forbearing boy, he said: "Then he is the one to be sacrificed to Allah." When he reached the limit of exertion with him, it was said to him: "Fulfil your vow." It is said: on the night of Tarwiyah he saw someone saying to him: "Allah commands you to sacrifice this son of yours." When he woke in the morning, he reflected on it throughout the day until evening, wondering whether this dream was from Allah; hence the day was named Tarwiyah (reflection). When he saw the same thing the following evening, he knew it was from Allah; hence the day was named Arafah (knowledge). Then he saw the same in the third night, and he resolved to slaughter him; hence it was named the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr).

The majority of reciters read (ترى) "tara" with a fatha on the ta and the ra. Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), al-Aswad ibn Yazid, Ibn Wathhab, Talha, al-A'mash, Mujahid, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma on the ta and a kasra on the ra. Al-Dahhak and al-A'mash also read it with a damma on the ta and a fatha on the ra. The first is from opinion (al-ra'y); the second means: what do you show me and what do you present so that I may consider it? The third means: what is it that comes to your imagination and falls into your heart? (انظر) is suspended, and (ماذا) is an interrogative. If (ذا) is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," then (ما) is the subject, and the verb after (ذا) is its relative clause. If (ذا) is part of a compound, then it is in the position of an object of the verb after it. The clause, together with the interrogative that is the object of the verb following it, is in the position of an object of (انظر). Since the father's address was (يا بني) out of tenderness, the son addressed him as (يا أبت) out of reverence and honor.

﴿Do as you are commanded﴾: meaning do what you are commanded to do. The object has been omitted, though it is in the accusative case; the original is ما تؤمر به, then the particle was dropped and the pronoun became attached in the accusative, so its deletion was permitted because the conditions for deletion are present. Al-Zamakhshari said: or ما أمرك, with the verbal noun attached to the object that has no named agent; there is disagreement over this. Is it held that a verbal noun that governs can be formed in the passive so that what follows it becomes an object without a named agent, or is that not so?

﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast﴾: the speech of one who has been given forbearance, patience, and obedience to the command of Allah, and contentment with what Allah has decreed.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 37, verses 99–113 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿When they had both submitted﴾, meaning, to the command of God. It is said: "istaslama" and "salama" have the same meaning. The majority read *aslama*. ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud), ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, al-Aʿmash and al-Thawri read *sallama*, meaning they entrusted the matter to Him in His decree and His destiny. It is also read *istaslama*, in three readings. Qatada said, regarding *aslama*, that "this one submitted his son, and this one submitted himself," making *aslama* transitive. Others made it intransitive, meaning: they both yielded to the command of God and humbled themselves before Him.

﴿And he laid him down upon his forehead﴾, meaning he cast him down on one of his sides upon the ground, while carrying out the matter with patience and resolve. This took place at the rock that is in Mina. Al-Hasan said it was at the spot overlooking the mosque of Mina. Al-Dahhak said it was at the place of sacrifice where sacrifices are made today.

The answer to *lamma* ("when") is omitted and is to be supplied after ﴿and he laid him down upon his forehead﴾, meaning: We gave them a great reward. This was said by some of the Basran grammarians. Or it is to be supplied after ﴿the vision﴾, meaning: what happened, which speech conveys but which description cannot encompass, of their rejoicing and their praising God for what He bestowed upon them, in many words that al-Zamakhshari mentioned in his customary oratorical manner. Or it is to be supplied before ﴿and he laid him down﴾, its estimate being ﴿When they had both submitted and he laid him down﴾. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and it is in their view like the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*So when we passed through the courtyard of the tribe and he turned aside*

The Kufans said: the answer is affirmative, and it is ﴿We called out to him﴾, with the *waw* being extra. A group said: it is ﴿and he laid him down﴾, with the *waw* being extra. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned in the story of Ibrahim and his son, and what passed between them of words and deeds, detailed accounts, the correctness of which God knows best; they may be found in his book. The *an* (that) is explanatory, meaning ﴿you have fulfilled the vision﴾. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *wa-nadaynahu qad saddaqta* ("and We called out to him, you have fulfilled"), omitting *an*. It is also read *sadaqta*, with the *dal* lightened. Fayyad read *al-Riyya*, with a kasra on the *ra'* and assimilation, and *taṣdiq al-ru'ya* (the confirmation of the vision). Al-Zamakhshari said: He exerted his utmost effort and did what the slaughterer does: laying him down on his side and drawing the blade across his throat. But God, glorified is He, brought about what prevented the blade from passing through it, and this does not detract from Ibrahim's act. Do you not see that he is not called disobedient or negligent? Rather he is called obedient and striving, as if the blade had passed through and cut the veins, and let the blood flow. This is not a case of abrogation (*naskh*, the cancellation of a ruling) affecting the one commanded before the act, nor before the time of the act, in any way, as some minds might leap to, until one becomes occupied with speech about it. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ may mean with your heart, in the sense: your vision was in your sight a true vision from God, and you acted according to it when you believed in it and held its truth. It may also mean: you confirmed in your heart what the vision produced in your soul, as if he said: you have fulfilled its right through action. End of quote.

﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers﴾. This is a reason for the granting of the relief that God bestowed upon them after hardship, and the attainment of their desire after despair.

﴿Indeed, this﴾, meaning what Ibrahim was commanded to do, namely the slaughter of his son, ﴿was surely the manifest trial﴾, meaning the clear test in which the sincere are distinguished from others. Or it was the clear tribulation, whose difficulty is such that no tribulation is harder than it.

﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was the ram that Abel offered, which was accepted from him, and which was grazing in Paradise until Isma'il was ransomed with it. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan also said: he was ransomed with a mountain goat that came down upon him from the *sarw* (a tree). The majority said: it was a white ram, with curved horns, of a fine shape, and it was described as great. Mujahid said: because it was accepted with certainty. ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd said: because a tradition (*sunna*) was established through it, and it became an enduring religious practice until the end of time. al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: because it was from God. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: because it was not from lineage, but from creation (*al-takwin*). Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr said: its greatness was that it was one of the rams of Paradise, pastured there for forty autumns. In His saying ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ there is evidence that Ibrahim did not slaughter his son, since he was ransomed. A group said: the slaughter took place and then he was restored. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this is a manifest lie. Another group said: Ibrahim did not see in his dream only the passing of the blade, so he assumed it was a complete slaughter and carried it out accordingly. When what he saw occurred, the abrogation occurred. He said: there is no disagreement, since Ibrahim, peace be upon him, passed the blade over the throat of his son and it did not cut. End of quote. What the Qur'an indicates is that He ﴿laid him down upon his forehead﴾ only, and it is not reported in any authentic hadith that "he passed the blade over the throat of his son."

﴿And We left for him among later generations﴾ up to ﴿the believers﴾. Its parallel was explained earlier, at the end of the story of Noah, before the story of Ibrahim here. Here He said "thus," without "indeed" (*inna*), being content with the mention of that before and after.

﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. The apparent meaning is that this is a good news different from that earlier good news. The gentle boy promised to Ibrahim is Isma'il, and he is the one who was sacrificed, not Isaac. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, Muʿawiya ibn Abi Sufyan, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi, al-Shaʿbi, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and a group of the Successors (*tabiʿun*). They relied on the apparent sense of these verses, and on his saying, peace be upon him: "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones." And on the saying of a Bedouin to him: "O son of the two sacrificed ones," and he smiled, peace be upon him, meaning Isma'il and his father ʿAbdullah. ʿAbd al-Muttalib had vowed to sacrifice one of his sons, and the lot fell upon ʿAbdullah, but his maternal uncles prevented it and said to him: ransom your son with a hundred camels, so he ransomed him with them. And in what God revealed to Musa in a long hadith: "As for Isma'il, he was generous with the blood of himself." ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz asked a Jew who had become Muslim about this, and he said: "Indeed a Jew knows it, but they envy you, O Arabs." The two horns of the ram were hung in the Kaʿba. Al-Asmaʿi asked Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla about the sacrificed one, and he said: "O Asmaʿi, where has your reason strayed from you? When was Isaac in Mecca? And he is the one who built the House with his father, and the place of sacrifice is in Mecca." End of quote.

God described him with patience in His saying ﴿And Isma'il and Idris and Dhu al-Kifl, each of them was among the patient﴾ [al-Anbiya': 85], which is his patience over the slaughter. And with truthfulness of promise in His saying ﴿Indeed he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam: 54], because he promised his father from himself patience over the slaughter, and fulfilled it. Al-Tabari mentioned that Ibn ʿAbbas said: the sacrificed one is Isma'il, and the Jews claim that it is Isaac, and the Jews lied. Among the strongest evidences used is that God gave Ibrahim good news of Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob. So if the sacrificed one were Isaac, then that announcement would not correspond to reality, and that is impossible in God's announcements, may He be exalted.

A group went to the view that the sacrificed one is Isaac, among them al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, Ibn Masʿud, ʿAli, ʿAtaʾ, ʿIkrima, Kaʿb, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, and Ibn ʿAbbas in one narration. And the command to sacrifice him was in Syria (al-Sham). ʿAtaʾ and Muqatil said: in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was also said: in the Hijaz, and he came with his father upon al-Buraq. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and Ibn ʿAbbas in one narration said: the command to sacrifice him was in Syria, at the Maqam (the Station of Ibrahim). Ibn ʿAbbas said: the good news in His saying ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac﴾ is the good news of his prophethood. They said: God informed of His friend Ibrahim, when he migrated to Syria, that he asked Him for a son, then He followed that good news with a gentle boy, then He mentioned his vision of slaughtering that boy who had been announced. This is indicated by the letter of Jacob to Joseph, peace be upon them both: "From Jacob, Israel of God, son of Isaac, sacrificed one of God, son of Ibrahim, friend of God." Whoever makes the sacrificed one Isaac makes this good news a good news of his prophethood, as we mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas. They said: it is not permissible for God to give him good news of both his birth and his prophethood together, because the testing by slaughtering him would not be valid while he knows that he will be a prophet. Whoever makes him Isma'il makes the good news about his son Isaac. The word *nabiyyan* ("a prophet") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) (p-372), which is a *hal muqaddara* (a state that is future with respect to the time of the main verb). If Isaac is the sacrificed one, and this good news was of the birth of Isaac, then al-Zamakhshari raised this as a question. He said: If you say: there is a difference between this and His saying ﴿Enter it, abiding forever﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. That is because the one entered exists together with the entering, but abiding forever does not exist together with both, so you estimated two estimates for the abiding, and it was correct. But the thing given good news of is not like that, since it is known at the time the good news exists, and the non-existence of the one given good news necessitates the non-existence of its state, because a state is an ornament that subsists only with its bearer. This one given good news, who is Isaac, when he came into existence, prophethood was not yet present with his existence, but was delayed from him for a long period. So how can he be made a prophet as a state to be estimated? A state is a description of the doer and the object at the time the act exists from or upon them. So abiding forever, though it is not their description at the time of entering Paradise, its estimate is their description, because the meaning is: estimating abiding forever. But prophethood is not like that, since there is no way for it to be existent at the time of the existence of the good news of Isaac, because Isaac does not exist. I say: this is a question fine in its thread and narrow in its path. What resolves the problem is that it is necessary to estimate an omitted genitive construction, which is His saying ﴿And We gave him good news﴾ with the existence of Isaac as a prophet, meaning: that he would come into existence with his prophethood estimated. So the governing element of the state is the existence, not the act of giving good news. By this, the parallel to His saying ﴿Enter it, abiding forever﴾ [al-Zumar: 73] returns. ﴿From among the righteous﴾ is a second state, and its coming is for the sake of praise and commendation, because every prophet must be among the righteous. End of quote.

﴿And We blessed him and Isaac﴾, meaning We poured upon them both the blessings of religion and of this world, and by bringing forth the prophets of the Children of Israel from his loins.

﴿And among their offspring is one who does good and one who clearly wrongs himself﴾. In this there is a warning to the Jews, and to whoever was among their offspring who did not believe in Muhammad ﷺ. In it there is also evidence that a righteous person may beget a wicked one, and no defect or deficiency attaches to him because of that.
