As for ﴿He will guide me﴾, it means to Paradise, as Qatada held; because his saying ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous﴾ refutes this view, since one who believes he will die in the fire would not pray that Allah grant him a righteous son. ("He will guide me") means He will grant me success in what is good for me.

﴿From among the righteous﴾ means a son who will be counted among the righteous. The word hibah (gift) is mostly used for a child, though it has also come for a brother, as in His saying ﴿And We gave him, from Our mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 53]. The good tidings included that the child would be male, that he would reach the age of puberty, and that he would be described as forbearing. What forbearance is greater than his saying, when his father had presented the sacrifice to him: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast﴾.

﴿When he reached with him [the age of] exertion﴾: between this clause and the one before it there is an omitted element, whose sense is: so a child was born to him and grew up.

﴿When he reached﴾ means that he reached the point of walking with his father in his affairs and needs. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: al-sa'y here means work, worship and assistance. Qatada said: al-sa'y is walking on foot, meaning exertion with full capacity. On this al-Zamakhshari said: it cannot be connected to balagha (reached) in the sense that both of them reached the limit of exertion together, nor to al-sa'y, because its origin is a verbal noun which cannot precede what depends on it. He denied that it is an explanation, as if, when he said ﴿When he reached with him the exertion﴾, meaning the limit at which he could exert himself, it was asked: "With whom?" and he answered: "With his father." The reason for specifying the father is that he was the gentlest of people and the most compassionate toward him and toward others, and he would not impose on him the kind of demand that would be hard for him, since he had not yet become firm in his speech and his father did not require him to return. At that time he was thirteen years old. End of quote.

﴿He said, "O my son"﴾: a call of tenderness and compassion.

﴿Indeed, I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you﴾, meaning by a command from Allah, and this is indicated by ﴿do as you are commanded﴾. The dreams of prophets are revelation, like wakefulness. His mentioning the dream to him was a way of making him bear that great trial. He consulted him with the words ﴿so see what you think﴾, although it was a binding command from Allah, so that he would know what he had in him for accepting this great test, would strengthen him if he grew anxious, would prepare his soul to face this trial, and would calm his soul regarding what was unavoidable, since being surprised by a trial before one is aware of it is harder on the soul. What he saw was in a dream and not in wakefulness, like the dream of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the dream of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of entering the Sacred Mosque; this shows that the states of the prophets, in wakefulness and in sleep, are equal in truthfulness and mutually supporting. It is said: when the angels gave the good tidings of a forbearing boy, he said: "Then he is the one to be sacrificed to Allah." When he reached the limit of exertion with him, it was said to him: "Fulfil your vow." It is said: on the night of Tarwiyah he saw someone saying to him: "Allah commands you to sacrifice this son of yours." When he woke in the morning, he reflected on it throughout the day until evening, wondering whether this dream was from Allah; hence the day was named Tarwiyah (reflection). When he saw the same thing the following evening, he knew it was from Allah; hence the day was named Arafah (knowledge). Then he saw the same in the third night, and he resolved to slaughter him; hence it was named the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr).

The majority of reciters read (ترى) "tara" with a fatha on the ta and the ra. Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), al-Aswad ibn Yazid, Ibn Wathhab, Talha, al-A'mash, Mujahid, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma on the ta and a kasra on the ra. Al-Dahhak and al-A'mash also read it with a damma on the ta and a fatha on the ra. The first is from opinion (al-ra'y); the second means: what do you show me and what do you present so that I may consider it? The third means: what is it that comes to your imagination and falls into your heart? (انظر) is suspended, and (ماذا) is an interrogative. If (ذا) is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," then (ما) is the subject, and the verb after (ذا) is its relative clause. If (ذا) is part of a compound, then it is in the position of an object of the verb after it. The clause, together with the interrogative that is the object of the verb following it, is in the position of an object of (انظر). Since the father's address was (يا بني) out of tenderness, the son addressed him as (يا أبت) out of reverence and honor.

﴿Do as you are commanded﴾: meaning do what you are commanded to do. The object has been omitted, though it is in the accusative case; the original is ما تؤمر به, then the particle was dropped and the pronoun became attached in the accusative, so its deletion was permitted because the conditions for deletion are present. Al-Zamakhshari said: or ما أمرك, with the verbal noun attached to the object that has no named agent; there is disagreement over this. Is it held that a verbal noun that governs can be formed in the passive so that what follows it becomes an object without a named agent, or is that not so?

﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast﴾: the speech of one who has been given forbearance, patience, and obedience to the command of Allah, and contentment with what Allah has decreed.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 37, verses 99–113 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿When they had both submitted﴾, meaning, to the command of God. It is said: "istaslama" and "salama" have the same meaning. The majority read *aslama*. ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud), ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, al-Aʿmash and al-Thawri read *sallama*, meaning they entrusted the matter to Him in His decree and His destiny. It is also read *istaslama*, in three readings. Qatada said, regarding *aslama*, that "this one submitted his son, and this one submitted himself," making *aslama* transitive. Others made it intransitive, meaning: they both yielded to the command of God and humbled themselves before Him.

﴿And he laid him down upon his forehead﴾, meaning he cast him down on one of his sides upon the ground, while carrying out the matter with patience and resolve. This took place at the rock that is in Mina. Al-Hasan said it was at the spot overlooking the mosque of Mina. Al-Dahhak said it was at the place of sacrifice where sacrifices are made today.

The answer to *lamma* ("when") is omitted and is to be supplied after ﴿and he laid him down upon his forehead﴾, meaning: We gave them a great reward. This was said by some of the Basran grammarians. Or it is to be supplied after ﴿the vision﴾, meaning: what happened, which speech conveys but which description cannot encompass, of their rejoicing and their praising God for what He bestowed upon them, in many words that al-Zamakhshari mentioned in his customary oratorical manner. Or it is to be supplied before ﴿and he laid him down﴾, its estimate being ﴿When they had both submitted and he laid him down﴾. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and it is in their view like the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*So when we passed through the courtyard of the tribe and he turned aside*

The Kufans said: the answer is affirmative, and it is ﴿We called out to him﴾, with the *waw* being extra. A group said: it is ﴿and he laid him down﴾, with the *waw* being extra. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned in the story of Ibrahim and his son, and what passed between them of words and deeds, detailed accounts, the correctness of which God knows best; they may be found in his book. The *an* (that) is explanatory, meaning ﴿you have fulfilled the vision﴾. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *wa-nadaynahu qad saddaqta* ("and We called out to him, you have fulfilled"), omitting *an*. It is also read *sadaqta*, with the *dal* lightened. Fayyad read *al-Riyya*, with a kasra on the *ra'* and assimilation, and *taṣdiq al-ru'ya* (the confirmation of the vision). Al-Zamakhshari said: He exerted his utmost effort and did what the slaughterer does: laying him down on his side and drawing the blade across his throat. But God, glorified is He, brought about what prevented the blade from passing through it, and this does not detract from Ibrahim's act. Do you not see that he is not called disobedient or negligent? Rather he is called obedient and striving, as if the blade had passed through and cut the veins, and let the blood flow. This is not a case of abrogation (*naskh*, the cancellation of a ruling) affecting the one commanded before the act, nor before the time of the act, in any way, as some minds might leap to, until one becomes occupied with speech about it. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ may mean with your heart, in the sense: your vision was in your sight a true vision from God, and you acted according to it when you believed in it and held its truth. It may also mean: you confirmed in your heart what the vision produced in your soul, as if he said: you have fulfilled its right through action. End of quote.

﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers﴾. This is a reason for the granting of the relief that God bestowed upon them after hardship, and the attainment of their desire after despair.

﴿Indeed, this﴾, meaning what Ibrahim was commanded to do, namely the slaughter of his son, ﴿was surely the manifest trial﴾, meaning the clear test in which the sincere are distinguished from others. Or it was the clear tribulation, whose difficulty is such that no tribulation is harder than it.

﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was the ram that Abel offered, which was accepted from him, and which was grazing in Paradise until Isma'il was ransomed with it. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan also said: he was ransomed with a mountain goat that came down upon him from the *sarw* (a tree). The majority said: it was a white ram, with curved horns, of a fine shape, and it was described as great. Mujahid said: because it was accepted with certainty. ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd said: because a tradition (*sunna*) was established through it, and it became an enduring religious practice until the end of time. al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: because it was from God. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: because it was not from lineage, but from creation (*al-takwin*). Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr said: its greatness was that it was one of the rams of Paradise, pastured there for forty autumns. In His saying ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ there is evidence that Ibrahim did not slaughter his son, since he was ransomed. A group said: the slaughter took place and then he was restored. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this is a manifest lie. Another group said: Ibrahim did not see in his dream only the passing of the blade, so he assumed it was a complete slaughter and carried it out accordingly. When what he saw occurred, the abrogation occurred. He said: there is no disagreement, since Ibrahim, peace be upon him, passed the blade over the throat of his son and it did not cut. End of quote. What the Qur'an indicates is that He ﴿laid him down upon his forehead﴾ only, and it is not reported in any authentic hadith that "he passed the blade over the throat of his son."

﴿And We left for him among later generations﴾ up to ﴿the believers﴾. Its parallel was explained earlier, at the end of the story of Noah, before the story of Ibrahim here. Here He said "thus," without "indeed" (*inna*), being content with the mention of that before and after.

﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. The apparent meaning is that this is a good news different from that earlier good news. The gentle boy promised to Ibrahim is Isma'il, and he is the one who was sacrificed, not Isaac. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, Muʿawiya ibn Abi Sufyan, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi, al-Shaʿbi, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and a group of the Successors (*tabiʿun*). They relied on the apparent sense of these verses, and on his saying, peace be upon him: "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones." And on the saying of a Bedouin to him: "O son of the two sacrificed ones," and he smiled, peace be upon him, meaning Isma'il and his father ʿAbdullah. ʿAbd al-Muttalib had vowed to sacrifice one of his sons, and the lot fell upon ʿAbdullah, but his maternal uncles prevented it and said to him: ransom your son with a hundred camels, so he ransomed him with them. And in what God revealed to Musa in a long hadith: "As for Isma'il, he was generous with the blood of himself." ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz asked a Jew who had become Muslim about this, and he said: "Indeed a Jew knows it, but they envy you, O Arabs." The two horns of the ram were hung in the Kaʿba. Al-Asmaʿi asked Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla about the sacrificed one, and he said: "O Asmaʿi, where has your reason strayed from you? When was Isaac in Mecca? And he is the one who built the House with his father, and the place of sacrifice is in Mecca." End of quote.

God described him with patience in His saying ﴿And Isma'il and Idris and Dhu al-Kifl, each of them was among the patient﴾ [al-Anbiya': 85], which is his patience over the slaughter. And with truthfulness of promise in His saying ﴿Indeed he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam: 54], because he promised his father from himself patience over the slaughter, and fulfilled it. Al-Tabari mentioned that Ibn ʿAbbas said: the sacrificed one is Isma'il, and the Jews claim that it is Isaac, and the Jews lied. Among the strongest evidences used is that God gave Ibrahim good news of Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob. So if the sacrificed one were Isaac, then that announcement would not correspond to reality, and that is impossible in God's announcements, may He be exalted.

A group went to the view that the sacrificed one is Isaac, among them al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, Ibn Masʿud, ʿAli, ʿAtaʾ, ʿIkrima, Kaʿb, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, and Ibn ʿAbbas in one narration. And the command to sacrifice him was in Syria (al-Sham). ʿAtaʾ and Muqatil said: in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was also said: in the Hijaz, and he came with his father upon al-Buraq. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and Ibn ʿAbbas in one narration said: the command to sacrifice him was in Syria, at the Maqam (the Station of Ibrahim). Ibn ʿAbbas said: the good news in His saying ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac﴾ is the good news of his prophethood. They said: God informed of His friend Ibrahim, when he migrated to Syria, that he asked Him for a son, then He followed that good news with a gentle boy, then He mentioned his vision of slaughtering that boy who had been announced. This is indicated by the letter of Jacob to Joseph, peace be upon them both: "From Jacob, Israel of God, son of Isaac, sacrificed one of God, son of Ibrahim, friend of God." Whoever makes the sacrificed one Isaac makes this good news a good news of his prophethood, as we mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas. They said: it is not permissible for God to give him good news of both his birth and his prophethood together, because the testing by slaughtering him would not be valid while he knows that he will be a prophet. Whoever makes him Isma'il makes the good news about his son Isaac. The word *nabiyyan* ("a prophet") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) (p-372), which is a *hal muqaddara* (a state that is future with respect to the time of the main verb). If Isaac is the sacrificed one, and this good news was of the birth of Isaac, then al-Zamakhshari raised this as a question. He said: If you say: there is a difference between this and His saying ﴿Enter it, abiding forever﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. That is because the one entered exists together with the entering, but abiding forever does not exist together with both, so you estimated two estimates for the abiding, and it was correct. But the thing given good news of is not like that, since it is known at the time the good news exists, and the non-existence of the one given good news necessitates the non-existence of its state, because a state is an ornament that subsists only with its bearer. This one given good news, who is Isaac, when he came into existence, prophethood was not yet present with his existence, but was delayed from him for a long period. So how can he be made a prophet as a state to be estimated? A state is a description of the doer and the object at the time the act exists from or upon them. So abiding forever, though it is not their description at the time of entering Paradise, its estimate is their description, because the meaning is: estimating abiding forever. But prophethood is not like that, since there is no way for it to be existent at the time of the existence of the good news of Isaac, because Isaac does not exist. I say: this is a question fine in its thread and narrow in its path. What resolves the problem is that it is necessary to estimate an omitted genitive construction, which is His saying ﴿And We gave him good news﴾ with the existence of Isaac as a prophet, meaning: that he would come into existence with his prophethood estimated. So the governing element of the state is the existence, not the act of giving good news. By this, the parallel to His saying ﴿Enter it, abiding forever﴾ [al-Zumar: 73] returns. ﴿From among the righteous﴾ is a second state, and its coming is for the sake of praise and commendation, because every prophet must be among the righteous. End of quote.

﴿And We blessed him and Isaac﴾, meaning We poured upon them both the blessings of religion and of this world, and by bringing forth the prophets of the Children of Israel from his loins.

﴿And among their offspring is one who does good and one who clearly wrongs himself﴾. In this there is a warning to the Jews, and to whoever was among their offspring who did not believe in Muhammad ﷺ. In it there is also evidence that a righteous person may beget a wicked one, and no defect or deficiency attaches to him because of that.

[p. 368]

﴿He said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me.﴾ ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy.﴾ ﴿And when he reached with him [the age of] exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast."﴾ ﴿And when they had both submitted and he put him down upon his forehead,﴾ ﴿We called to him, "O Abraham,﴾ ﴿you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this was the clear trial.﴾ ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ ﴿And We left for him [favorable mention] among later generations:﴾ ﴿"Peace upon Abraham."﴾ ﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ ﴿And We gave him good tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are doers of good and those who clearly wrong themselves.﴾ ﴿And We certainly bestowed favor upon Moses and Aaron.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 114] ﴿And We saved them and their people from the great distress.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 115] ﴿And We helped them, so they were the victors.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 116] ﴿And We gave them the clear Book.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 117] ﴿And We guided them to the straight path.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 118] ﴿And We left for them [favorable mention] among later generations:﴾ [Al-Saffat: 119] ﴿"Peace upon Moses and Aaron."﴾ [Al-Saffat: 120] ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 121] ﴿Indeed, they were among Our believing servants.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 122] ﴿And indeed, Elias was among the messengers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 123] ﴿When he said to his people, "Will you not fear Allah?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 124] ﴿Do you call upon Baal and leave the best of creators,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 125] ﴿Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your first forefathers?"﴾ [Al-Saffat: 126] ﴿But they denied him, so indeed, they will be brought [to punishment].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 127] ﴿Except the chosen servants of Allah.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 128] ﴿And We left for him [favorable mention] among later generations:﴾ [Al-Saffat: 129] ﴿"Peace upon the family of Yasin."﴾ [Al-Saffat: 130] ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 131] ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 132] ﴿And indeed, Lot was among the messengers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 133] ﴿When We saved him and his family, all of them,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 134] ﴿except an old woman among those who remained behind.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 135] ﴿Then We destroyed the others.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 136] ﴿And indeed, you pass by them in the morning﴾ [Al-Saffat: 137] ﴿and at night. Then will you not reason?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 138] ﴿And indeed, Jonah was among the messengers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 139] ﴿When he fled to the laden ship.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 140] ﴿And he drew lots and was among the losers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 141] ﴿Then the fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 142] ﴿And had he not been of those who exalt [Allah],﴾ [Al-Saffat: 143] ﴿he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 144] ﴿So We cast him onto the open land while he was ill.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 145] ﴿And We caused to grow over him a gourd vine.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 146] ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 147] ﴿And they believed, so We let them enjoy [worldly life] for a time.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 148] ﴿So ask them, "Does your Lord have daughters while they have sons?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 149] ﴿Or did We create the angels female while they were witnesses?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 150] ﴿Unquestionably, it is from their own falsehood that they say,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 151] ﴿"Allah has begotten," and indeed, they are liars.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 152] ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 153] ﴿What is [wrong] with you? How do you judge?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 154] ﴿Will you not be reminded?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 155] ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 156] ﴿Then bring your Book, if you should be truthful.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 157] ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship. But the jinn know that they will be brought [to punishment].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 158] ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they describe,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 159] ﴿except the chosen servants of Allah.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 160] ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship﴾ [Al-Saffat: 161] ﴿cannot lead [anyone] astray,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 162] ﴿except one who is to burn in Hell.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 163] ﴿And there is none of us but that he has a known position.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 164] ﴿And indeed, we are those who line up [in ranks].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 165] ﴿And indeed, we are those who exalt [Allah].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 166] ﴿And indeed, they were saying,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 167] ﴿"If we had with us a reminder from the former peoples,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 168] ﴿we would have been sincere servants of Allah."﴾ [Al-Saffat: 169] ﴿But they disbelieved in it, so they will come to know.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 170] ﴿And Our word had already preceded for Our servants, the messengers,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 171] ﴿that indeed they would be the victorious.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 172] ﴿And indeed, Our soldiers—they will be the victors.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 173] ﴿So turn away from them for a time.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 174] ﴿And observe them, for they will see.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 175] ﴿Then is it Our punishment they are hastening?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 176] ﴿But when it descends in their courtyard, evil is the morning of those who were warned.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 177] ﴿So turn away from them for a time.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 178] ﴿And observe, for they will see.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 179] ﴿Exalted is your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 180] ﴿And peace upon the messengers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 181] ﴿And praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 182]

Talla al-rajulu al-rajula: he threw him down on his side; it was also said: he placed him down with force. Sa'ida ibn Huwba said:
"And he laid him down for the forehead and the mouth."

Al-jabinan: the two sides of the forehead on either side. The plural of jabin as ajbun is anomalous; its regular form in the paucal would be ajbina, like kathib and akthiba, and in the plural jabanat and jubun, like kuthubat and kutub.

Al-dhabh (sacrifice): the name of what is slaughtered, like al-ri'y (pasture) is the name of what is grazed.

Abaqa: he fled. Sahama: he cast lots. Al-mudhda': the overturned one. Al-hut: the fish, a known creature.

Alama: he did what one is blamed for. The poet said:
"How many a blameworthy one was not struck with blame, and how many a wrongdoer has no sin."

Al-ara': open, spacious land with no trees and no known landmarks. The poet said:
"I raised a leg whose stumbling I do not fear, and I cast off my garments into the wide open land."

Al-yaqtin: yafil (a pattern) like al-yafsid, from qatana: he remained in the place. It refers to plants that do not stand on a stalk of wood, such as melon, colocynth and cucumber vines. Al-sahah: the courtyard; its plural is sukh. The poet said:
"Thus it was the same whether they did not let their camels graze, or they let them graze and the courtyards were dusty."

[p. 369]

﴿He said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me.﴾ ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy.﴾ ﴿And when he reached with him [the age of] exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast."﴾ ﴿And when they had both submitted and he put him down upon his forehead,﴾ ﴿We called to him, "O Abraham,﴾ ﴿you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this was the clear trial.﴾ ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ ﴿And We left for him [favorable mention] among later generations:﴾ ﴿"Peace upon Abraham."﴾ ﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ ﴿And We gave him good tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are doers of good and those who clearly wrong themselves.﴾.

When Allah saved him from them and from the fire into which they threw him, he resolved to part from them. He expressed his migration to the land of Syria as going to his Lord, as he said: ﴿Indeed, I am migrating to my Lord﴾ [Al-Ankabut: 26], so that he could worship his Lord freely and supplicate to Him without meeting anyone who would disturb him. He emigrated from the land of Babil (Babylon), from the kingdom of Namrud (Nimrod), to Syria. It was also said: to the land of Egypt. The view of those who say that his going does not mean emigration, but rather meeting Allah after being burned, believing that he would die in the fire, is far-fetched; they say he said this before being thrown into the fire. As for ﴿He will guide me﴾, it means to Paradise, as Qatada held; because his saying ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous﴾ refutes this view, since one who believes he will die in the fire would not pray that Allah grant him a righteous son. ("He will guide me") means He will grant me success in what is good for me.

﴿From among the righteous﴾ means a son who will be counted among the righteous. The word hibah (gift) is mostly used for a child, though it has also come for a brother, as in His saying ﴿And We gave him, from Our mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 53]. The good tidings included that the child would be male, that he would reach the age of puberty, and that he would be described as forbearing. What forbearance is greater than his saying, when his father had presented the sacrifice to him: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast﴾.

﴿When he reached with him [the age of] exertion﴾: between this clause and the one before it there is an omitted element, whose sense is: so a child was born to him and grew up.

﴿When he reached﴾ means that he reached the point of walking with his father in his affairs and needs. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: al-sa'y here means work, worship and assistance. Qatada said: al-sa'y is walking on foot, meaning exertion with full capacity. On this al-Zamakhshari said: it cannot be connected to balagha (reached) in the sense that both of them reached the limit of exertion together, nor to al-sa'y, because its origin is a verbal noun which cannot precede what depends on it. He denied that it is an explanation, as if, when he said ﴿When he reached with him the exertion﴾, meaning the limit at which he could exert himself, it was asked: "With whom?" and he answered: "With his father." The reason for specifying the father is that he was the gentlest of people and the most compassionate toward him and toward others, and he would not impose on him the kind of demand that would be hard for him, since he had not yet become firm in his speech and his father did not require him to return. At that time he was thirteen years old. End of quote.

﴿He said, "O my son"﴾: a call of tenderness and compassion.

﴿Indeed, I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you﴾, meaning by a command from Allah, and this is indicated by ﴿do as you are commanded﴾. The dreams of prophets are revelation, like wakefulness. His mentioning the dream to him was a way of making him bear that great trial. He consulted him with the words ﴿so see what you think﴾, although it was a binding command from Allah, so that he would know what he had in him for accepting this great test, would strengthen him if he grew anxious, would prepare his soul to face this trial, and would calm his soul regarding what was unavoidable, since being surprised by a trial before one is aware of it is harder on the soul. What he saw was in a dream and not in wakefulness, like the dream of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the dream of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of entering the Sacred Mosque; this shows that the states of the prophets, in wakefulness and in sleep, are equal in truthfulness and mutually supporting. It is said: when the angels gave the good tidings of a forbearing boy, he said: "Then he is the one to be sacrificed to Allah." When he reached the limit of exertion with him, it was said to him: "Fulfil your vow." It is said: on the night of Tarwiyah he saw someone saying to him: "Allah commands you to sacrifice this son of yours." When he woke in the morning, he reflected on it throughout the day until evening, wondering whether this dream was from Allah; hence the day was named Tarwiyah (reflection). When he saw the same thing the following evening, he knew it was from Allah; hence the day was named Arafah (knowledge). Then he saw the same in the third night, and he resolved to slaughter him; hence it was named the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr).

The majority of reciters read (ترى) "tara" with a fatha on the ta and the ra. Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), al-Aswad ibn Yazid, Ibn Wathhab, Talha, al-A'mash, Mujahid, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma on the ta and a kasra on the ra. Al-Dahhak and al-A'mash also read it with a damma on the ta and a fatha on the ra. The first is from opinion (al-ra'y); the second means: what do you show me and what do you present so that I may consider it? The third means: what is it that comes to your imagination and falls into your heart? (انظر) is suspended, and (ماذا) is an interrogative. If (ذا) is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," then (ما) is the subject, and the verb after (ذا) is its relative clause. If (ذا) is part of a compound, then it is in the position of an object of the verb after it. The clause, together with the interrogative that is the object of the verb following it, is in the position of an object of (انظر). Since the father's address was (يا بني) out of tenderness, the son addressed him as (يا أبت) out of reverence and honor.

﴿Do as you are commanded﴾: meaning do what you are commanded to do. The object has been omitted, though it is in the accusative case; the original is ما تؤمر به, then the particle was dropped and the pronoun became attached in the accusative, so its deletion was permitted because the conditions for deletion are present. Al-Zamakhshari said: or ما أمرك, with the verbal noun attached to the object that has no named agent; there is disagreement over this. Is it held that a verbal noun that governs can be formed in the passive so that what follows it becomes an object without a named agent, or is that not so?

﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast﴾: the speech of one who has been given forbearance, patience, and obedience to the command of Allah, and contentment with what Allah has decreed.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 37, verses 99–113 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿When they had both submitted﴾, meaning, to the command of God. It is said: "istaslama" and "salama" have the same meaning. The majority read *aslama*. ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud), ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, al-Aʿmash and al-Thawri read *sallama*, meaning they entrusted the matter to Him in His decree and His destiny. It is also read *istaslama*, in three readings. Qatada said, regarding *aslama*, that "this one submitted his son, and this one submitted himself," making *aslama* transitive. Others made it intransitive, meaning: they both yielded to the command of God and humbled themselves before Him.

﴿And he laid him down upon his forehead﴾, meaning he cast him down on one of his sides upon the ground, while carrying out the matter with patience and resolve. This took place at the rock that is in Mina. Al-Hasan said it was at the spot overlooking the mosque of Mina. Al-Dahhak said it was at the place of sacrifice where sacrifices are made today.

The answer to *lamma* ("when") is omitted and is to be supplied after ﴿and he laid him down upon his forehead﴾, meaning: We gave them a great reward. This was said by some of the Basran grammarians. Or it is to be supplied after ﴿the vision﴾, meaning: what happened, which speech conveys but which description cannot encompass, of their rejoicing and their praising God for what He bestowed upon them, in many words that al-Zamakhshari mentioned in his customary oratorical manner. Or it is to be supplied before ﴿and he laid him down﴾, its estimate being ﴿When they had both submitted and he laid him down﴾. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and it is in their view like the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*So when we passed through the courtyard of the tribe and he turned aside*

The Kufans said: the answer is affirmative, and it is ﴿We called out to him﴾, with the *waw* being extra. A group said: it is ﴿and he laid him down﴾, with the *waw* being extra. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned in the story of Ibrahim and his son, and what passed between them of words and deeds, detailed accounts, the correctness of which God knows best; they may be found in his book. The *an* (that) is explanatory, meaning ﴿you have fulfilled the vision﴾. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *wa-nadaynahu qad saddaqta* ("and We called out to him, you have fulfilled"), omitting *an*. It is also read *sadaqta*, with the *dal* lightened. Fayyad read *al-Riyya*, with a kasra on the *ra'* and assimilation, and *taṣdiq al-ru'ya* (the confirmation of the vision). Al-Zamakhshari said: He exerted his utmost effort and did what the slaughterer does: laying him down on his side and drawing the blade across his throat. But God, glorified is He, brought about what prevented the blade from passing through it, and this does not detract from Ibrahim's act. Do you not see that he is not called disobedient or negligent? Rather he is called obedient and striving, as if the blade had passed through and cut the veins, and let the blood flow. This is not a case of abrogation (*naskh*, the cancellation of a ruling) affecting the one commanded before the act, nor before the time of the act, in any way, as some minds might leap to, until one becomes occupied with speech about it. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ may mean with your heart, in the sense: your vision was in your sight a true vision from God, and you acted according to it when you believed in it and held its truth. It may also mean: you confirmed in your heart what the vision produced in your soul, as if he said: you have fulfilled its right through action. End of quote.

﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers﴾. This is a reason for the granting of the relief that God bestowed upon them after hardship, and the attainment of their desire after despair.

﴿Indeed, this﴾, meaning what Ibrahim was commanded to do, namely the slaughter of his son, ﴿was surely the manifest trial﴾, meaning the clear test in which the sincere are distinguished from others. Or it was the clear tribulation, whose difficulty is such that no tribulation is harder than it.

﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was the ram that Abel offered, which was accepted from him, and which was grazing in Paradise until Isma'il was ransomed with it. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan also said: he was ransomed with a mountain goat that came down upon him from the *sarw* (a tree). The majority said: it was a white ram, with curved horns, of a fine shape, and it was described as great. Mujahid said: because it was accepted with certainty. ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd said: because a tradition (*sunna*) was established through it, and it became an enduring religious practice until the end of time. al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: because it was from God. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: because it was not from lineage, but from creation (*al-takwin*). Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr said: its greatness was that it was one of the rams of Paradise, pastured there for forty autumns. In His saying ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ there is evidence that Ibrahim did not slaughter his son, since he was ransomed. A group said: the slaughter took place and then he was restored. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this is a manifest lie. Another group said: Ibrahim did not see in his dream only the passing of the blade, so he assumed it was a complete slaughter and carried it out accordingly. When what he saw occurred, the abrogation occurred. He said: there is no disagreement, since Ibrahim, peace be upon him, passed the blade over the throat of his son and it did not cut. End of quote. What the Qur'an indicates is that He ﴿laid him down upon his forehead﴾ only, and it is not reported in any authentic hadith that "he passed the blade over the throat of his son."

﴿And We left for him among later generations﴾ up to ﴿the believers﴾. Its parallel was explained earlier, at the end of the story of Noah, before the story of Ibrahim here. Here He said "thus," without "indeed" (*inna*), being content with the mention of that before and after.

﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. The apparent meaning is that this is a good news different from that earlier good news. The gentle boy promised to Ibrahim is Isma'il, and he is the one who was sacrificed, not Isaac. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, Muʿawiya ibn Abi Sufyan, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi, al-Shaʿbi, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and a group of the Successors (*tabiʿun*). They relied on the apparent sense of these verses, and on his saying, peace be upon him: "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones." And on the saying of a Bedouin to him: "O son of the two sacrificed ones," and he smiled, peace be upon him, meaning Isma'il and his father ʿAbdullah. ʿAbd al-Muttalib had vowed to sacrifice one of his sons, and the lot fell upon ʿAbdullah, but his maternal uncles prevented it and said to him: ransom your son with a hundred camels, so he ransomed him with them. And in what God revealed to Musa in a long hadith: "As for Isma'il, he was generous with the blood of himself." ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz asked a Jew who had become Muslim about this, and he said: "Indeed a Jew knows it, but they envy you, O Arabs." The two horns of the ram were hung in the Kaʿba. Al-Asmaʿi asked Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla about the sacrificed one, and he said: "O Asmaʿi, where has your reason strayed from you? When was Isaac in Mecca? And he is the one who built the House with his father, and the place of sacrifice is in Mecca." End of quote.

God described him with patience in His saying ﴿And Isma'il and Idris and Dhu al-Kifl, each of them was among the patient﴾ [al-Anbiya': 85], which is his patience over the slaughter. And with truthfulness of promise in His saying ﴿Indeed he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam: 54], because he promised his father from himself patience over the slaughter, and fulfilled it. Al-Tabari mentioned that Ibn ʿAbbas said: the sacrificed one is Isma'il, and the Jews claim that it is Isaac, and the Jews lied. Among the strongest evidences used is that God gave Ibrahim good news of Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob. So if the sacrificed one were Isaac, then that announcement would not correspond to reality, and that is impossible in God's announcements, may He be exalted.

A group went to the view that the sacrificed one is Isaac, among them al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, Ibn Masʿud, ʿAli, ʿAtaʾ, ʿIkrima, Kaʿb, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, and Ibn ʿAbbas in one narration. And the command to sacrifice him was in Syria (al-Sham). ʿAtaʾ and Muqatil said: in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was also said: in the Hijaz, and he came with his father upon al-Buraq. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and Ibn ʿAbbas in one narration said: the command to sacrifice him was in Syria, at the Maqam (the Station of Ibrahim). Ibn ʿAbbas said: the good news in His saying ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac﴾ is the good news of his prophethood. They said: God informed of His friend Ibrahim, when he migrated to Syria, that he asked Him for a son, then He followed that good news with a gentle boy, then He mentioned his vision of slaughtering that boy who had been announced. This is indicated by the letter of Jacob to Joseph, peace be upon them both: "From Jacob, Israel of God, son of Isaac, sacrificed one of God, son of Ibrahim, friend of God." Whoever makes the sacrificed one Isaac makes this good news a good news of his prophethood, as we mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas. They said: it is not permissible for God to give him good news of both his birth and his prophethood together, because the testing by slaughtering him would not be valid while he knows that he will be a prophet. Whoever makes him Isma'il makes the good news about his son Isaac. The word *nabiyyan* ("a prophet") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) (p-372), which is a *hal muqaddara* (a state that is future with respect to the time of the main verb). If Isaac is the sacrificed one, and this good news was of the birth of Isaac, then al-Zamakhshari raised this as a question. He said: If you say: there is a difference between this and His saying ﴿Enter it, abiding forever﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. That is because the one entered exists together with the entering, but abiding forever does not exist together with both, so you estimated two estimates for the abiding, and it was correct. But the thing given good news of is not like that, since it is known at the time the good news exists, and the non-existence of the one given good news necessitates the non-existence of its state, because a state is an ornament that subsists only with its bearer. This one given good news, who is Isaac, when he came into existence, prophethood was not yet present with his existence, but was delayed from him for a long period. So how can he be made a prophet as a state to be estimated? A state is a description of the doer and the object at the time the act exists from or upon them. So abiding forever, though it is not their description at the time of entering Paradise, its estimate is their description, because the meaning is: estimating abiding forever. But prophethood is not like that, since there is no way for it to be existent at the time of the existence of the good news of Isaac, because Isaac does not exist. I say: this is a question fine in its thread and narrow in its path. What resolves the problem is that it is necessary to estimate an omitted genitive construction, which is His saying ﴿And We gave him good news﴾ with the existence of Isaac as a prophet, meaning: that he would come into existence with his prophethood estimated. So the governing element of the state is the existence, not the act of giving good news. By this, the parallel to His saying ﴿Enter it, abiding forever﴾ [al-Zumar: 73] returns. ﴿From among the righteous﴾ is a second state, and its coming is for the sake of praise and commendation, because every prophet must be among the righteous. End of quote.

﴿And We blessed him and Isaac﴾, meaning We poured upon them both the blessings of religion and of this world, and by bringing forth the prophets of the Children of Israel from his loins.

﴿And among their offspring is one who does good and one who clearly wrongs himself﴾. In this there is a warning to the Jews, and to whoever was among their offspring who did not believe in Muhammad ﷺ. In it there is also evidence that a righteous person may beget a wicked one, and no defect or deficiency attaches to him because of that.

[p. 368]

﴿He said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me.﴾ ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy.﴾ ﴿And when he reached with him [the age of] exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast."﴾ ﴿And when they had both submitted and he put him down upon his forehead,﴾ ﴿We called to him, "O Abraham,﴾ ﴿you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this was the clear trial.﴾ ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ ﴿And We left for him [favorable mention] among later generations:﴾ ﴿"Peace upon Abraham."﴾ ﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ ﴿And We gave him good tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are doers of good and those who clearly wrong themselves.﴾ ﴿And We certainly bestowed favor upon Moses and Aaron.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 114] ﴿And We saved them and their people from the great distress.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 115] ﴿And We helped them, so they were the victors.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 116] ﴿And We gave them the clear Book.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 117] ﴿And We guided them to the straight path.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 118] ﴿And We left for them [favorable mention] among later generations:﴾ [Al-Saffat: 119] ﴿"Peace upon Moses and Aaron."﴾ [Al-Saffat: 120] ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 121] ﴿Indeed, they were among Our believing servants.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 122] ﴿And indeed, Elias was among the messengers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 123] ﴿When he said to his people, "Will you not fear Allah?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 124] ﴿Do you call upon Baal and leave the best of creators,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 125] ﴿Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your first forefathers?"﴾ [Al-Saffat: 126] ﴿But they denied him, so indeed, they will be brought [to punishment].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 127] ﴿Except the chosen servants of Allah.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 128] ﴿And We left for him [favorable mention] among later generations:﴾ [Al-Saffat: 129] ﴿"Peace upon the family of Yasin."﴾ [Al-Saffat: 130] ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 131] ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 132] ﴿And indeed, Lot was among the messengers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 133] ﴿When We saved him and his family, all of them,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 134] ﴿except an old woman among those who remained behind.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 135] ﴿Then We destroyed the others.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 136] ﴿And indeed, you pass by them in the morning﴾ [Al-Saffat: 137] ﴿and at night. Then will you not reason?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 138] ﴿And indeed, Jonah was among the messengers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 139] ﴿When he fled to the laden ship.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 140] ﴿And he drew lots and was among the losers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 141] ﴿Then the fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 142] ﴿And had he not been of those who exalt [Allah],﴾ [Al-Saffat: 143] ﴿he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 144] ﴿So We cast him onto the open land while he was ill.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 145] ﴿And We caused to grow over him a gourd vine.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 146] ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 147] ﴿And they believed, so We let them enjoy [worldly life] for a time.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 148] ﴿So ask them, "Does your Lord have daughters while they have sons?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 149] ﴿Or did We create the angels female while they were witnesses?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 150] ﴿Unquestionably, it is from their own falsehood that they say,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 151] ﴿"Allah has begotten," and indeed, they are liars.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 152] ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 153] ﴿What is [wrong] with you? How do you judge?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 154] ﴿Will you not be reminded?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 155] ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 156] ﴿Then bring your Book, if you should be truthful.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 157] ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship. But the jinn know that they will be brought [to punishment].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 158] ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they describe,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 159] ﴿except the chosen servants of Allah.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 160] ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship﴾ [Al-Saffat: 161] ﴿cannot lead [anyone] astray,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 162] ﴿except one who is to burn in Hell.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 163] ﴿And there is none of us but that he has a known position.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 164] ﴿And indeed, we are those who line up [in ranks].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 165] ﴿And indeed, we are those who exalt [Allah].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 166] ﴿And indeed, they were saying,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 167] ﴿"If we had with us a reminder from the former peoples,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 168] ﴿we would have been sincere servants of Allah."﴾ [Al-Saffat: 169] ﴿But they disbelieved in it, so they will come to know.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 170] ﴿And Our word had already preceded for Our servants, the messengers,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 171] ﴿that indeed they would be the victorious.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 172] ﴿And indeed, Our soldiers—they will be the victors.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 173] ﴿So turn away from them for a time.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 174] ﴿And observe them, for they will see.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 175] ﴿Then is it Our punishment they are hastening?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 176] ﴿But when it descends in their courtyard, evil is the morning of those who were warned.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 177] ﴿So turn away from them for a time.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 178] ﴿And observe, for they will see.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 179] ﴿Exalted is your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 180] ﴿And peace upon the messengers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 181] ﴿And praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 182]

Talla al-rajulu al-rajula: he threw him down on his side; it was also said: he placed him down with force. Sa'ida ibn Huwba said:
"And he laid him down for the forehead and the mouth."

Al-jabinan: the two sides of the forehead on either side. The plural of jabin as ajbun is anomalous; its regular form in the paucal would be ajbina, like kathib and akthiba, and in the plural jabanat and jubun, like kuthubat and kutub.

Al-dhabh (sacrifice): the name of what is slaughtered, like al-ri'y (pasture) is the name of what is grazed.

Abaqa: he fled. Sahama: he cast lots. Al-mudhda': the overturned one. Al-hut: the fish, a known creature.

Alama: he did what one is blamed for. The poet said:
"How many a blameworthy one was not struck with blame, and how many a wrongdoer has no sin."

Al-ara': open, spacious land with no trees and no known landmarks. The poet said:
"I raised a leg whose stumbling I do not fear, and I cast off my garments into the wide open land."

Al-yaqtin: yafil (a pattern) like al-yafsid, from qatana: he remained in the place. It refers to plants that do not stand on a stalk of wood, such as melon, colocynth and cucumber vines. Al-sahah: the courtyard; its plural is sukh. The poet said:
"Thus it was the same whether they did not let their camels graze, or they let them graze and the courtyards were dusty."

[p. 369]

﴿He said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me.﴾ ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy.﴾ ﴿And when he reached with him [the age of] exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast."﴾ ﴿And when they had both submitted and he put him down upon his forehead,﴾ ﴿We called to him, "O Abraham,﴾ ﴿you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this was the clear trial.﴾ ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ ﴿And We left for him [favorable mention] among later generations:﴾ ﴿"Peace upon Abraham."﴾ ﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ ﴿And We gave him good tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are doers of good and those who clearly wrong themselves.﴾.

When Allah saved him from them and from the fire into which they threw him, he resolved to part from them. He expressed his migration to the land of Syria as going to his Lord, as he said: ﴿Indeed, I am migrating to my Lord﴾ [Al-Ankabut: 26], so that he could worship his Lord freely and supplicate to Him without meeting anyone who would disturb him. He emigrated from the land of Babil (Babylon), from the kingdom of Namrud (Nimrod), to Syria. It was also said: to the land of Egypt. The view of those who say that his going does not mean emigration, but rather meeting Allah after being burned, believing that he would die in the fire, is far-fetched; they say he said this before being thrown into the fire. As for ﴿He will guide me﴾, it means to Paradise, as Qatada held; because his saying ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous﴾ refutes this view, since one who believes he will die in the fire would not pray that Allah grant him a righteous son. ("He will guide me") means He will grant me success in what is good for me.

﴿From among the righteous﴾ means a son who will be counted among the righteous. The word hibah (gift) is mostly used for a child, though it has also come for a brother, as in His saying ﴿And We gave him, from Our mercy, his brother Aaron as a prophet﴾ [Maryam: 53]. The good tidings included that the child would be male, that he would reach the age of puberty, and that he would be described as forbearing. What forbearance is greater than his saying, when his father had presented the sacrifice to him: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast﴾.

﴿When he reached with him [the age of] exertion﴾: between this clause and the one before it there is an omitted element, whose sense is: so a child was born to him and grew up.

﴿When he reached﴾ means that he reached the point of walking with his father in his affairs and needs. Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ibn Zayd said: al-sa'y here means work, worship and assistance. Qatada said: al-sa'y is walking on foot, meaning exertion with full capacity. On this al-Zamakhshari said: it cannot be connected to balagha (reached) in the sense that both of them reached the limit of exertion together, nor to al-sa'y, because its origin is a verbal noun which cannot precede what depends on it. He denied that it is an explanation, as if, when he said ﴿When he reached with him the exertion﴾, meaning the limit at which he could exert himself, it was asked: "With whom?" and he answered: "With his father." The reason for specifying the father is that he was the gentlest of people and the most compassionate toward him and toward others, and he would not impose on him the kind of demand that would be hard for him, since he had not yet become firm in his speech and his father did not require him to return. At that time he was thirteen years old. End of quote.

﴿He said, "O my son"﴾: a call of tenderness and compassion.

﴿Indeed, I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you﴾, meaning by a command from Allah, and this is indicated by ﴿do as you are commanded﴾. The dreams of prophets are revelation, like wakefulness. His mentioning the dream to him was a way of making him bear that great trial. He consulted him with the words ﴿so see what you think﴾, although it was a binding command from Allah, so that he would know what he had in him for accepting this great test, would strengthen him if he grew anxious, would prepare his soul to face this trial, and would calm his soul regarding what was unavoidable, since being surprised by a trial before one is aware of it is harder on the soul. What he saw was in a dream and not in wakefulness, like the dream of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and the dream of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of entering the Sacred Mosque; this shows that the states of the prophets, in wakefulness and in sleep, are equal in truthfulness and mutually supporting. It is said: when the angels gave the good tidings of a forbearing boy, he said: "Then he is the one to be sacrificed to Allah." When he reached the limit of exertion with him, it was said to him: "Fulfil your vow." It is said: on the night of Tarwiyah he saw someone saying to him: "Allah commands you to sacrifice this son of yours." When he woke in the morning, he reflected on it throughout the day until evening, wondering whether this dream was from Allah; hence the day was named Tarwiyah (reflection). When he saw the same thing the following evening, he knew it was from Allah; hence the day was named Arafah (knowledge). Then he saw the same in the third night, and he resolved to slaughter him; hence it was named the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr).

The majority of reciters read (ترى) "tara" with a fatha on the ta and the ra. Abdullah (Ibn Mas'ud), al-Aswad ibn Yazid, Ibn Wathhab, Talha, al-A'mash, Mujahid, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with a damma on the ta and a kasra on the ra. Al-Dahhak and al-A'mash also read it with a damma on the ta and a fatha on the ra. The first is from opinion (al-ra'y); the second means: what do you show me and what do you present so that I may consider it? The third means: what is it that comes to your imagination and falls into your heart? (انظر) is suspended, and (ماذا) is an interrogative. If (ذا) is a relative pronoun meaning "that which," then (ما) is the subject, and the verb after (ذا) is its relative clause. If (ذا) is part of a compound, then it is in the position of an object of the verb after it. The clause, together with the interrogative that is the object of the verb following it, is in the position of an object of (انظر). Since the father's address was (يا بني) out of tenderness, the son addressed him as (يا أبت) out of reverence and honor.

﴿Do as you are commanded﴾: meaning do what you are commanded to do. The object has been omitted, though it is in the accusative case; the original is ما تؤمر به, then the particle was dropped and the pronoun became attached in the accusative, so its deletion was permitted because the conditions for deletion are present. Al-Zamakhshari said: or ما أمرك, with the verbal noun attached to the object that has no named agent; there is disagreement over this. Is it held that a verbal noun that governs can be formed in the passive so that what follows it becomes an object without a named agent, or is that not so?

﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast﴾: the speech of one who has been given forbearance, patience, and obedience to the command of Allah, and contentment with what Allah has decreed.

**Commentary of Abu Hayyan (al-Bahr al-Muhit) on surah 37, verses 99–113 (part 2 of 2):**

﴿When they had both submitted﴾, meaning, to the command of God. It is said: "istaslama" and "salama" have the same meaning. The majority read *aslama*. ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud), ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Jaʿfar ibn Muhammad, al-Aʿmash and al-Thawri read *sallama*, meaning they entrusted the matter to Him in His decree and His destiny. It is also read *istaslama*, in three readings. Qatada said, regarding *aslama*, that "this one submitted his son, and this one submitted himself," making *aslama* transitive. Others made it intransitive, meaning: they both yielded to the command of God and humbled themselves before Him.

﴿And he laid him down upon his forehead﴾, meaning he cast him down on one of his sides upon the ground, while carrying out the matter with patience and resolve. This took place at the rock that is in Mina. Al-Hasan said it was at the spot overlooking the mosque of Mina. Al-Dahhak said it was at the place of sacrifice where sacrifices are made today.

The answer to *lamma* ("when") is omitted and is to be supplied after ﴿and he laid him down upon his forehead﴾, meaning: We gave them a great reward. This was said by some of the Basran grammarians. Or it is to be supplied after ﴿the vision﴾, meaning: what happened, which speech conveys but which description cannot encompass, of their rejoicing and their praising God for what He bestowed upon them, in many words that al-Zamakhshari mentioned in his customary oratorical manner. Or it is to be supplied before ﴿and he laid him down﴾, its estimate being ﴿When they had both submitted and he laid him down﴾. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, and it is in their view like the words of Imru' al-Qays:

*So when we passed through the courtyard of the tribe and he turned aside*

The Kufans said: the answer is affirmative, and it is ﴿We called out to him﴾, with the *waw* being extra. A group said: it is ﴿and he laid him down﴾, with the *waw* being extra. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned in the story of Ibrahim and his son, and what passed between them of words and deeds, detailed accounts, the correctness of which God knows best; they may be found in his book. The *an* (that) is explanatory, meaning ﴿you have fulfilled the vision﴾. Zayd ibn ʿAli read *wa-nadaynahu qad saddaqta* ("and We called out to him, you have fulfilled"), omitting *an*. It is also read *sadaqta*, with the *dal* lightened. Fayyad read *al-Riyya*, with a kasra on the *ra'* and assimilation, and *taṣdiq al-ru'ya* (the confirmation of the vision). Al-Zamakhshari said: He exerted his utmost effort and did what the slaughterer does: laying him down on his side and drawing the blade across his throat. But God, glorified is He, brought about what prevented the blade from passing through it, and this does not detract from Ibrahim's act. Do you not see that he is not called disobedient or negligent? Rather he is called obedient and striving, as if the blade had passed through and cut the veins, and let the blood flow. This is not a case of abrogation (*naskh*, the cancellation of a ruling) affecting the one commanded before the act, nor before the time of the act, in any way, as some minds might leap to, until one becomes occupied with speech about it. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ may mean with your heart, in the sense: your vision was in your sight a true vision from God, and you acted according to it when you believed in it and held its truth. It may also mean: you confirmed in your heart what the vision produced in your soul, as if he said: you have fulfilled its right through action. End of quote.

﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the good-doers﴾. This is a reason for the granting of the relief that God bestowed upon them after hardship, and the attainment of their desire after despair.

﴿Indeed, this﴾, meaning what Ibrahim was commanded to do, namely the slaughter of his son, ﴿was surely the manifest trial﴾, meaning the clear test in which the sincere are distinguished from others. Or it was the clear tribulation, whose difficulty is such that no tribulation is harder than it.

﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it was the ram that Abel offered, which was accepted from him, and which was grazing in Paradise until Isma'il was ransomed with it. Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan also said: he was ransomed with a mountain goat that came down upon him from the *sarw* (a tree). The majority said: it was a white ram, with curved horns, of a fine shape, and it was described as great. Mujahid said: because it was accepted with certainty. ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd said: because a tradition (*sunna*) was established through it, and it became an enduring religious practice until the end of time. al-Hasan ibn al-Fadl said: because it was from God. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: because it was not from lineage, but from creation (*al-takwin*). Ibn ʿAbbas and Ibn Jubayr said: its greatness was that it was one of the rams of Paradise, pastured there for forty autumns. In His saying ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice﴾ there is evidence that Ibrahim did not slaughter his son, since he was ransomed. A group said: the slaughter took place and then he was restored. Ibn ʿAtiyya said: this is a manifest lie. Another group said: Ibrahim did not see in his dream only the passing of the blade, so he assumed it was a complete slaughter and carried it out accordingly. When what he saw occurred, the abrogation occurred. He said: there is no disagreement, since Ibrahim, peace be upon him, passed the blade over the throat of his son and it did not cut. End of quote. What the Qur'an indicates is that He ﴿laid him down upon his forehead﴾ only, and it is not reported in any authentic hadith that "he passed the blade over the throat of his son."

﴿And We left for him among later generations﴾ up to ﴿the believers﴾. Its parallel was explained earlier, at the end of the story of Noah, before the story of Ibrahim here. Here He said "thus," without "indeed" (*inna*), being content with the mention of that before and after.

﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous﴾. The apparent meaning is that this is a good news different from that earlier good news. The gentle boy promised to Ibrahim is Isma'il, and he is the one who was sacrificed, not Isaac. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, Muʿawiya ibn Abi Sufyan, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb al-Qurazi, al-Shaʿbi, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and a group of the Successors (*tabiʿun*). They relied on the apparent sense of these verses, and on his saying, peace be upon him: "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones." And on the saying of a Bedouin to him: "O son of the two sacrificed ones," and he smiled, peace be upon him, meaning Isma'il and his father ʿAbdullah. ʿAbd al-Muttalib had vowed to sacrifice one of his sons, and the lot fell upon ʿAbdullah, but his maternal uncles prevented it and said to him: ransom your son with a hundred camels, so he ransomed him with them. And in what God revealed to Musa in a long hadith: "As for Isma'il, he was generous with the blood of himself." ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz asked a Jew who had become Muslim about this, and he said: "Indeed a Jew knows it, but they envy you, O Arabs." The two horns of the ram were hung in the Kaʿba. Al-Asmaʿi asked Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla about the sacrificed one, and he said: "O Asmaʿi, where has your reason strayed from you? When was Isaac in Mecca? And he is the one who built the House with his father, and the place of sacrifice is in Mecca." End of quote.

God described him with patience in His saying ﴿And Isma'il and Idris and Dhu al-Kifl, each of them was among the patient﴾ [al-Anbiya': 85], which is his patience over the slaughter. And with truthfulness of promise in His saying ﴿Indeed he was true to his promise﴾ [Maryam: 54], because he promised his father from himself patience over the slaughter, and fulfilled it. Al-Tabari mentioned that Ibn ʿAbbas said: the sacrificed one is Isma'il, and the Jews claim that it is Isaac, and the Jews lied. Among the strongest evidences used is that God gave Ibrahim good news of Isaac, and Isaac begot Jacob. So if the sacrificed one were Isaac, then that announcement would not correspond to reality, and that is impossible in God's announcements, may He be exalted.

A group went to the view that the sacrificed one is Isaac, among them al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, Ibn Masʿud, ʿAli, ʿAtaʾ, ʿIkrima, Kaʿb, ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, and Ibn ʿAbbas in one narration. And the command to sacrifice him was in Syria (al-Sham). ʿAtaʾ and Muqatil said: in Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was also said: in the Hijaz, and he came with his father upon al-Buraq. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr and Ibn ʿAbbas in one narration said: the command to sacrifice him was in Syria, at the Maqam (the Station of Ibrahim). Ibn ʿAbbas said: the good news in His saying ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac﴾ is the good news of his prophethood. They said: God informed of His friend Ibrahim, when he migrated to Syria, that he asked Him for a son, then He followed that good news with a gentle boy, then He mentioned his vision of slaughtering that boy who had been announced. This is indicated by the letter of Jacob to Joseph, peace be upon them both: "From Jacob, Israel of God, son of Isaac, sacrificed one of God, son of Ibrahim, friend of God." Whoever makes the sacrificed one Isaac makes this good news a good news of his prophethood, as we mentioned from Ibn ʿAbbas. They said: it is not permissible for God to give him good news of both his birth and his prophethood together, because the testing by slaughtering him would not be valid while he knows that he will be a prophet. Whoever makes him Isma'il makes the good news about his son Isaac. The word *nabiyyan* ("a prophet") is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (*hal*) (p-372), which is a *hal muqaddara* (a state that is future with respect to the time of the main verb). If Isaac is the sacrificed one, and this good news was of the birth of Isaac, then al-Zamakhshari raised this as a question. He said: If you say: there is a difference between this and His saying ﴿Enter it, abiding forever﴾ [al-Zumar: 73]. That is because the one entered exists together with the entering, but abiding forever does not exist together with both, so you estimated two estimates for the abiding, and it was correct. But the thing given good news of is not like that, since it is known at the time the good news exists, and the non-existence of the one given good news necessitates the non-existence of its state, because a state is an ornament that subsists only with its bearer. This one given good news, who is Isaac, when he came into existence, prophethood was not yet present with his existence, but was delayed from him for a long period. So how can he be made a prophet as a state to be estimated? A state is a description of the doer and the object at the time the act exists from or upon them. So abiding forever, though it is not their description at the time of entering Paradise, its estimate is their description, because the meaning is: estimating abiding forever. But prophethood is not like that, since there is no way for it to be existent at the time of the existence of the good news of Isaac, because Isaac does not exist. I say: this is a question fine in its thread and narrow in its path. What resolves the problem is that it is necessary to estimate an omitted genitive construction, which is His saying ﴿And We gave him good news﴾ with the existence of Isaac as a prophet, meaning: that he would come into existence with his prophethood estimated. So the governing element of the state is the existence, not the act of giving good news. By this, the parallel to His saying ﴿Enter it, abiding forever﴾ [al-Zumar: 73] returns. ﴿From among the righteous﴾ is a second state, and its coming is for the sake of praise and commendation, because every prophet must be among the righteous. End of quote.

﴿And We blessed him and Isaac﴾, meaning We poured upon them both the blessings of religion and of this world, and by bringing forth the prophets of the Children of Israel from his loins.

﴿And among their offspring is one who does good and one who clearly wrongs himself﴾. In this there is a warning to the Jews, and to whoever was among their offspring who did not believe in Muhammad ﷺ. In it there is also evidence that a righteous person may beget a wicked one, and no defect or deficiency attaches to him because of that.

[p. 368]

﴿He said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me.﴾ ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy.﴾ ﴿And when he reached with him [the age of] exertion, he said, "O my son, indeed I have seen in a dream that I am sacrificing you, so see what you think." He said, "O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast."﴾ ﴿And when they had both submitted and he put him down upon his forehead,﴾ ﴿We called to him, "O Abraham,﴾ ﴿you have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, this was the clear trial.﴾ ﴿And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.﴾ ﴿And We left for him [favorable mention] among later generations:﴾ ﴿"Peace upon Abraham."﴾ ﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ ﴿And We gave him good tidings of Isaac, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ ﴿And We blessed him and Isaac. And among their descendants are doers of good and those who clearly wrong themselves.﴾ ﴿And We certainly bestowed favor upon Moses and Aaron.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 114] ﴿And We saved them and their people from the great distress.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 115] ﴿And We helped them, so they were the victors.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 116] ﴿And We gave them the clear Book.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 117] ﴿And We guided them to the straight path.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 118] ﴿And We left for them [favorable mention] among later generations:﴾ [Al-Saffat: 119] ﴿"Peace upon Moses and Aaron."﴾ [Al-Saffat: 120] ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 121] ﴿Indeed, they were among Our believing servants.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 122] ﴿And indeed, Elias was among the messengers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 123] ﴿When he said to his people, "Will you not fear Allah?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 124] ﴿Do you call upon Baal and leave the best of creators,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 125] ﴿Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your first forefathers?"﴾ [Al-Saffat: 126] ﴿But they denied him, so indeed, they will be brought [to punishment].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 127] ﴿Except the chosen servants of Allah.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 128] ﴿And We left for him [favorable mention] among later generations:﴾ [Al-Saffat: 129] ﴿"Peace upon the family of Yasin."﴾ [Al-Saffat: 130] ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 131] ﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 132] ﴿And indeed, Lot was among the messengers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 133] ﴿When We saved him and his family, all of them,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 134] ﴿except an old woman among those who remained behind.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 135] ﴿Then We destroyed the others.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 136] ﴿And indeed, you pass by them in the morning﴾ [Al-Saffat: 137] ﴿and at night. Then will you not reason?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 138] ﴿And indeed, Jonah was among the messengers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 139] ﴿When he fled to the laden ship.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 140] ﴿And he drew lots and was among the losers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 141] ﴿Then the fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 142] ﴿And had he not been of those who exalt [Allah],﴾ [Al-Saffat: 143] ﴿he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 144] ﴿So We cast him onto the open land while he was ill.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 145] ﴿And We caused to grow over him a gourd vine.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 146] ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 147] ﴿And they believed, so We let them enjoy [worldly life] for a time.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 148] ﴿So ask them, "Does your Lord have daughters while they have sons?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 149] ﴿Or did We create the angels female while they were witnesses?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 150] ﴿Unquestionably, it is from their own falsehood that they say,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 151] ﴿"Allah has begotten," and indeed, they are liars.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 152] ﴿Has He chosen daughters over sons?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 153] ﴿What is [wrong] with you? How do you judge?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 154] ﴿Will you not be reminded?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 155] ﴿Or do you have a clear authority?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 156] ﴿Then bring your Book, if you should be truthful.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 157] ﴿And they have made between Him and the jinn a kinship. But the jinn know that they will be brought [to punishment].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 158] ﴿Exalted is Allah above what they describe,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 159] ﴿except the chosen servants of Allah.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 160] ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship﴾ [Al-Saffat: 161] ﴿cannot lead [anyone] astray,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 162] ﴿except one who is to burn in Hell.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 163] ﴿And there is none of us but that he has a known position.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 164] ﴿And indeed, we are those who line up [in ranks].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 165] ﴿And indeed, we are those who exalt [Allah].﴾ [Al-Saffat: 166] ﴿And indeed, they were saying,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 167] ﴿"If we had with us a reminder from the former peoples,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 168] ﴿we would have been sincere servants of Allah."﴾ [Al-Saffat: 169] ﴿But they disbelieved in it, so they will come to know.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 170] ﴿And Our word had already preceded for Our servants, the messengers,﴾ [Al-Saffat: 171] ﴿that indeed they would be the victorious.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 172] ﴿And indeed, Our soldiers—they will be the victors.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 173] ﴿So turn away from them for a time.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 174] ﴿And observe them, for they will see.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 175] ﴿Then is it Our punishment they are hastening?﴾ [Al-Saffat: 176] ﴿But when it descends in their courtyard, evil is the morning of those who were warned.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 177] ﴿So turn away from them for a time.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 178] ﴿And observe, for they will see.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 179] ﴿Exalted is your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 180] ﴿And peace upon the messengers.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 181] ﴿And praise is for Allah, Lord of the worlds.﴾ [Al-Saffat: 182]

Talla al-rajulu al-rajula: he threw him down on his side; it was also said: he placed him down with force. Sa'ida ibn Huwba said:
"And he laid him down for the forehead and the mouth."

Al-jabinan: the two sides of the forehead on either side. The plural of jabin as ajbun is anomalous; its regular form in the paucal would be ajbina, like kathib and akthiba, and in the plural jabanat and jubun, like kuthubat and kutub.

Al-dhabh (sacrifice): the name of what is slaughtered, like al-ri'y (pasture) is the name of what is grazed.

Abaqa: he fled. Sahama: he cast lots. Al-mudhda': the overturned one. Al-hut: the fish, a known creature.

Alama: he did what one is blamed for. The poet said:
"How many a blameworthy one was not struck with blame, and how many a wrongdoer has no sin."

Al-ara': open, spacious land with no trees and no known landmarks. The poet said:
"I raised a leg whose stumbling I do not fear, and I cast off my garments into the wide open land."

Al-yaqtin: yafil (a pattern) like al-yafsid, from qatana: he remained in the place. It refers to plants that do not stand on a stalk of wood, such as melon, colocynth and cucumber vines. Al-sahah: the courtyard; its plural is sukh. The poet said:
