When it was made plural, the nisbah yā' was lightened by deleting one of the two, out of dislike of doubling, so two silent letters met: the yā' in it and the letter of extension that marks the plural. So the latter was deleted because of their meeting, as they said: al-Ashʿarūn, al-Aʿjamūn, al-Khabībūn and al-Muhallabūn. Will you not then use your reason?﴾

﴿الكَرْبِ العَظِيمِ﴾ [the great distress]: the enslavement of the Copts over them, then their fear of Pharaoh's army, then the sea after that. The pronoun in ﴿ونَصَرْناهم﴾ [and We helped them] refers to Moses, Aaron and their people. It has also been said that it refers to Moses and Aaron alone, as an honouring of the two of them by using the plural form. The word (هم) [them] may be a separating pronoun (fasl), meaning it separates and emphasises, or it may be a substitute (badal). The ﴿الكِتابَ المُسْتَبِينَ﴾ [the Book that makes things clear] is the Torah, as God the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which there is guidance and light﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44]. The ﴿الصِّراطَ المُسْتَقِيمَ﴾ [the straight path] is Islam and the law of God.

The majority recited ﴿وإنَّ إلْياسَ﴾ with a hamzah of cutting (hamzat qat') carrying a kasrah. ʿIkrimah and al-Hasan, according to one of the two reports from them, and al-A'raj, Abu Raja', Ibn 'Amir and Ibn Muhaysin recited it with the hamzah of connection (hamzat wasl) on the alif. This allows that they connected the hamzah of cutting, and it allows that his name is Yasa', and that (ال) [al] was prefixed to it, as it was prefixed to al-Yasa' [Elisha]. In the reading of Ubayy and his codex, it is: ﴿وإنَّ إيلِيسَ﴾, with a hamzah carrying a kasrah, followed by a silent yā', followed by a lām carrying a kasrah, followed by a silent yā', followed by a sīn with a fatha. It was also recited: ﴿وإنَّ إدْراسَ﴾, as a dialectal form of Idris, like Ibrahamu for Ibrahim.

﴿أتَدْعُونَ بَعْلًا﴾ [Do you call upon Baal]: that is, do you worship Baal? It is the proper name of an idol they had. This was said by al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd. It has been said that it was made of gold, twenty cubits tall, and had four faces. They were tempted by it and glorified it until they assigned four hundred attendants (sadanah) to serve it and made them into prophets. The devil would enter the belly of Baal and speak with the law of misguidance, and the attendants would memorise it and teach it to the people. They were the people of Baalbek in the lands of al-Sham, and their city was named Baalbek after it. ʿIkrimah and Qatadah said: al-Baʿl means "the lord" in the dialect of Yemen. Ibn ʿAbbas heard a man searching for a lost animal, and a man said to him: "I am its Baʿl" [its owner]. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "God is greatest. Do you call upon Baal?" It is also said: "Who is the Baʿl of this house?", meaning its lord. The meaning according to this is: Do you worship some of the lords and abandon the worship of God? A group said that Baal is the name of a woman who brought them misguidance, and they followed her. The Kufans and Zayd ibn ʿAlī recited ﴿اللَّهَ رَبَّكم ورَبَّ آبائِكُمُ﴾ [God, your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers] in the accusative in all three, as a substitute for ﴿أحْسَنَ﴾ [best], or as an explanatory apposition (ʿaṭf bayan), if we say that the genitive construction of comparison is definite (idafah mahdah). The remaining seven recited them in the nominative, meaning: He is God, or it is a new sentence beginning with a subject, and ﴿رَبُّكم﴾ [your Lord] is its predicate. Yunus ibn Matta (Jonah, son of Matta) was from the Children of Israel. It is related that he was given prophethood at the age of twenty-eight. God sent him to his people, and he invited them to faith, but they opposed him. So he threatened them with punishment, and God informed them of its day, and Yunus set that day for them. Then, when his people saw the signs of the punishment before it reached them, they repented and believed, so God accepted their repentance and turned the punishment away from them. The account of his story has already been explained, and we have repeated a portion of it so that it may clarify what lies between the two mentions. It is said: Yunus was seized by anger, so he fled to board the ship, running away from his people. He described the flight with the word ibaq (fleeing from one's master), since he is a servant of God, and he went out fleeing without permission from God. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that when the ship sailed far out into the sea with Yunus aboard, it stopped moving. Its people said: "Indeed, there is among us someone because of whom God has held the ship back, so let us draw lots." They took a lot for each person, on the condition that whoever's lot floats is the one, and whoever's lot sinks is not him. Yunus's lot floated. They did this three times, and the lot fell upon him each time, so they agreed to throw him overboard. He went to a side of the ship in order to fall from it, but there was a creature of the sea's creatures watching and lying in wait for him. In the story of Yunus, peace be upon him, there are omitted sentences implied here before the mention of his flight to the ship, just as in his story in Surat al-Anbiya' in God's words ﴿when he went off in anger﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] — what follows this — and His words ﴿then he called out in the darkness﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] are also omitted sentences. It is possible that God caused it to grow with a stalk, so that he could shade himself with it and its leaves, as an exception to the usual course of things; so he grew well, healed, and his appearance became good, because the leaves of the gourd are the most beneficial thing for one whose skin has peeled off.

This is shown by ﴿so they believed, and We let them enjoy themselves﴾, and the enjoyment of that community is what angered Yunus, peace be upon him, until he fled. Ibn Abbas and Qatada said: it is another mission after He cast him onto the open shore, and it was to the people of Nineveh, on the side of Mosul. Al-Zamakhshari said: what is meant is his earlier sending to his people, who were the people of Nineveh. It was also said: it is a second sending after the first one that was directed at them, or to others. It was said: they became Muslims and asked him to return to them, but he refused, because a prophet who has emigrated from his people does not return to them to live among them; so he said to them: "Indeed God will send to you a prophet." The majority read ﴿aw﴾ ("or"); Ibn Abbas said it means "bal" ("rather"). It was also said: it means "wa" ("and") and is used with the meaning of "and." Ja'far ibn Muhammad read it likewise. It was said: it is for the ambiguity of the addressee's perspective. Al-Mubarrad and many of the Basran grammarians said: the meaning is according to human perception and estimation, so that whoever is behind them says: they are a hundred thousand or more. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention any other view than this, saying: "or more" in the sight of the beholder: when the observer sees them he says: they are a hundred thousand or more. The purpose is a description of their multitude. The excess was thirty thousand, as said by Ibn Abbas; or seventy thousand, as said by Ibn Jubayr; or twenty thousand, related from Ubayy from the Prophet (ﷺ). If this is authentic, what else is said is invalid.

(﴿So they believed﴾): It is related that they went out with their children, offspring and animals, separated them from their mothers, wailed, cried out, and sincerely turned to God, so God lifted the punishment from them. Enjoyment here means life, and the term (hīn, "a time") refers to their previously decreed appointed terms in eternity; this was said by Qatada and al-Suddi.

The pronoun in ﴿So ask them﴾: al-Zamakhshari said it is conjoined with a similar one at the beginning of the sura, even though the distance between them is great. He commanded His messenger to ask the Quraysh about the basis of their denial of resurrection at first, then continued the speech connecting part of it to part, then commanded that they be asked about the basis of the unjust division. End of quotation. What he said about conjunction is far-fetched.

If they counted the separation by a sentence such as "Eat meat, strike Zayd, and [eat] bread" among the most ugly constructions, how much more so with many sentences and disparate stories? So the view of conjunction is not permissible. Then He informed of them thirdly with the greatest disbelief, which is their claim that He has begotten, so their falsehood reached the attribution of offspring. Yunus ibn Matta (Jonah, son of Matta) was from the Children of Israel. It is related that he was given prophethood at the age of twenty-eight. It is said: Yunus was seized by anger, so he fled to board the ship, running away from his people. He described the flight with the word ibaq (fleeing from one's master), since he is a servant of God, and he went out fleeing without permission from God. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that when the ship sailed far out into the sea with Yunus aboard, it stopped moving. Its people said: "Indeed, there is among us someone because of whom God has held the ship back, so let us draw lots." They took a lot for each person, on the condition that whoever's lot floats is the one, and whoever's lot sinks is not him. Yunus's lot floated. They did this three times, and the lot fell upon him each time, so they agreed to throw him overboard. He went to a side of the ship in order to fall from it, but there was a creature of the sea's creatures watching and lying in wait for him. He moved to the other side, and found it there too, until it circled the vessel while it never left him. He knew that this was from God, so he threw himself towards it, and it swallowed him.

In the story of Yunus, peace be upon him, there are omitted sentences implied here before the mention of his flight to the ship, just as in his story in Surat al-Anbiya' in God's words ﴿when he went off in anger﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] — what follows this — and His words ﴿then he called out in the darkness﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] are also omitted sentences. It is said: Yunus was seized by anger, so he fled to board the ship, running away from his people. He described the flight with the word ibaq (fleeing from one's master), since he is a servant of God, and he went out fleeing without permission from God. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that when the ship sailed far out into the sea with Yunus aboard, it stopped moving. Its people said: "Indeed, there is among us someone because of whom God has held the ship back, so let us draw lots." They took a lot for each person, on the condition that whoever's lot floats is the one, and whoever's lot sinks is not him. Yunus's lot floated. They did this three times, and the lot fell upon him each time, so they agreed to throw him overboard. He went to a side of the ship in order to fall from it, but there was a creature of the sea's creatures watching and lying in wait for him. He moved to the other side, and found it there too, until it circled the vessel while it never left him. He knew that this was from God, so he threw himself towards it, and it swallowed him.

By gathering the accounts together, what was omitted in each one becomes clear.

It was read ﴿wa-huwa muliym﴾ ("while he was blameworthy") with a fatha on the mim (mulīm). Yunus ibn Matta (Jonah, son of Matta) was from the Children of Israel. It is related that he was given prophethood at the age of twenty-eight. God sent him to his people, and he invited them to faith, but they opposed him. So he threatened them with punishment, and God informed them of its day, and Yunus set that day for them. Then, when his people saw the signs of the punishment before it reached them, they repented and believed, so God accepted their repentance and turned the punishment away from them. The account of his story has already been explained, and we have repeated a portion of it so that it may clarify what lies between the two mentions. It is said: Yunus was seized by anger, so he fled to board the ship, running away from his people. He described the flight with the word ibaq (fleeing from one's master), since he is a servant of God, and he went out fleeing without permission from God. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that when the ship sailed far out into the sea with Yunus aboard, it stopped moving. Its people said: "Indeed, there is among us someone because of whom God has held the ship back, so let us draw lots." They took a lot for each person, on the condition that whoever's lot floats is the one, and whoever's lot sinks is not him. Yunus's lot floated. They did this three times, and the lot fell upon him each time, so they agreed to throw him overboard. He went to a side of the ship in order to fall from it, but there was a creature of the sea's creatures watching and lying in wait for him. He moved to the other side, and found it there too, until it circled the vessel while it never left him. He knew that this was from God, so he threw himself towards it, and it swallowed him.

In the story of Yunus, peace be upon him, there are omitted sentences implied here before the mention of his flight to the ship, just as in his story in Surat al-Anbiya' in God's words ﴿when he went off in anger﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] — what follows this — and His words ﴿then he called out in the darkness﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] are also omitted sentences. By gathering the accounts together, what was omitted in each one becomes clear.

﴿Then he cast lots, and he was among the losers﴾: "among the defeated," and its real meaning is "among those slipped away from the position of victory in the drawing of lots." It was read ﴿wa-huwa muliym﴾ ("while he was blameworthy") with a fatha on the mim (mulīm). Its regular form would be malūm, since it derives from lumtuhu, alūmuhu, lawman, so it is of the wāw-type; but it was given the pattern alīm, as they said mashīb and mad'iyy in place of mashūb, and mad'uww, based on shayab and da'a.

﴿Among those who glorify God﴾: among those who remember God with glorification (tasbih) and sanctification (taqdis). The apparent meaning is that He means what was mentioned in His words in Surat al-Anbiya': ﴿then he called out in the darkness: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87]. Ibn Jubayr said: it is His words "Glory be to God." A group said: his glorification is voluntary prayer. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Abu al-'Aliyah said: his prayer in times of ease benefits him in times of hardship. Al-Dahhak ibn Qays said from his pulpit: "Remember God in ease and He will remember you in hardship; indeed Yunus was a servant who remembered God, and when hardship befell him, that benefited him." Almighty and Majestic God said: ﴿So had he not been one of those who glorify God﴾, ﴿he would have remained in its belly until the day they are resurrected﴾. Al-Hasan said: his glorification was his prayer in the belly of the fish. It is related that he would lift the flesh of the fish with his hands, saying: "I will surely build You a place of worship (masjid) where no one has built before me."

It is related that the fish travelled alongside the ship, raising its head to breathe while Yunus glorified God, and it did not leave them until they reached the shore. It then spat him out safe, with nothing of him changed, and so they became Muslims. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿he would have remained in its belly until the day of resurrection﴾ is as follows. Qatada said: the belly of the fish would have been a grave for him until the Day of Resurrection. Various mutually contradictory statements have been made about the length of his stay in the belly of the fish, and we set those aside completely without mention.

Yunus ibn Matta (Jonah, son of Matta) was from the Children of Israel. It is related that he was given prophethood at the age of twenty-eight. God sent him to his people, and he invited them to faith, but they opposed him. So he threatened them with punishment, and God informed them of its day, and Yunus set that day for them. Then, when his people saw the signs of the punishment before it reached them, they repented and believed, so God accepted their repentance and turned the punishment away from them. The account of his story has already been explained, and we have repeated a portion of it so that it may clarify what lies between the two mentions. It is said: Yunus was seized by anger, so he fled to board the ship, running away from his people. He described the flight with the word ibaq (fleeing from one's master), since he is a servant of God, and he went out fleeing without permission from God. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that when the ship sailed far out into the sea with Yunus aboard, it stopped moving. Its people said: "Indeed, there is among us someone because of whom God has held the ship back, so let us draw lots." They took a lot for each person, on the condition that whoever's lot floats is the one, and whoever's lot sinks is not him. Yunus's lot floated. They did this three times, and the lot fell upon him each time, so they agreed to throw him overboard. He went to a side of the ship in order to fall from it, but there was a creature of the sea's creatures watching and lying in wait for him. He moved to the other side, and found it there too, until it circled the vessel while it never left him. He knew that this was from God, so he threw himself towards it, and it swallowed him.

In the story of Yunus, peace be upon him, there are omitted sentences implied here before the mention of his flight to the ship, just as in his story in Surat al-Anbiya' in God's words ﴿when he went off in anger﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] — what follows this — and His words ﴿then he called out in the darkness﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] are also omitted sentences. By gathering the accounts together, what was omitted in each one becomes clear.

﴿Then he cast lots, and he was among the losers﴾: "among the defeated," and its real meaning is "among those slipped away from the position of victory in the drawing of lots." It was read ﴿wa-huwa muliym﴾ ("while he was blameworthy") with a fatha on the mim (mulīm). Its regular form would be malūm, since it derives from lumtuhu, alūmuhu, lawman, so it is of the wāw-type; but it was given the pattern alīm, as they said mashīb and mad'iyy in place of mashūb, and mad'uww, based on shayab and da'a.

﴿Among those who glorify God﴾: among those who remember God with glorification (tasbih) and sanctification (taqdis). The apparent meaning is that He means what was mentioned in His words in Surat al-Anbiya': ﴿then he called out in the darkness: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87]. Ibn Jubayr said: it is His words "Glory be to God." A group said: his glorification is voluntary prayer. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Abu al-'Aliyah said: his prayer in times of ease benefits him in times of hardship. Al-Dahhak ibn Qays said from his pulpit: "Remember God in ease and He will remember you in hardship; indeed Yunus was a servant who remembered God, and when hardship befell him, that benefited him." Almighty and Majestic God said: ﴿So had he not been one of those who glorify God﴾, ﴿he would have remained in its belly until the day they are resurrected﴾. Al-Hasan said: his glorification was his prayer in the belly of the fish. It is related that he would lift the flesh of the fish with his hands, saying: "I will surely build You a place of worship (masjid) where no one has built before me."

It is related that the fish travelled alongside the ship, raising its head to breathe while Yunus glorified God, and it did not leave them until they reached the shore. It then spat him out safe, with nothing of him changed, and so they became Muslims. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿he would have remained in its belly until the day of resurrection﴾ is as follows. Qatada said: the belly of the fish would have been a grave for him until the Day of Resurrection. Various mutually contradictory statements have been made about the length of his stay in the belly of the fish, and we set those aside completely without mention.

﴿While he was ailing﴾: It is related that his body became like the body of a newborn child when it is born; this was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi. Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra and Amr ibn Maymun said: al-yaqtin means specifically the gourd (qar'). It was said: this is the one God caused to grow over him, and it combines several qualities: the coolness of its shade, the smoothness of its touch, the largeness of its leaves, and flies do not approach it. It was said: if water from its leaves is sprinkled on a place, no fly comes near it. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"He caused a gourd to grow over him by mercy from God; had God not been there, he would have found me lost."

It is reported that [the Prophet] said: "Indeed you love the gourd?" He said: "Yes, it is the tree of my brother Yunus." It was also said: it is the banana tree; he covered himself with its leaves, shaded himself with its branches, and broke his fast with its fruit. The meaning of ﴿We caused a tree to grow over him﴾ in Arabic usage is a plant that stands upon a stalk of wood. It is possible that God caused it to grow with a stalk, so that he could shade himself with it and its leaves, as an exception to the usual course of things; so he grew well, healed, and his appearance became good, because the leaves of the gourd are the most beneficial thing for one whose skin has peeled off.

Yunus ibn Matta (Jonah, son of Matta) was from the Children of Israel. It is related that he was given prophethood at the age of twenty-eight. God sent him to his people, and he invited them to faith, but they opposed him. So he threatened them with punishment, and God informed them of its day, and Yunus set that day for them. Then, when his people saw the signs of the punishment before it reached them, they repented and believed, so God accepted their repentance and turned the punishment away from them. The account of his story has already been explained, and we have repeated a portion of it so that it may clarify what lies between the two mentions. It is said: Yunus was seized by anger, so he fled to board the ship, running away from his people. He described the flight with the word ibaq (fleeing from one's master), since he is a servant of God, and he went out fleeing without permission from God. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that when the ship sailed far out into the sea with Yunus aboard, it stopped moving. Its people said: "Indeed, there is among us someone because of whom God has held the ship back, so let us draw lots." They took a lot for each person, on the condition that whoever's lot floats is the one, and whoever's lot sinks is not him. Yunus's lot floated. They did this three times, and the lot fell upon him each time, so they agreed to throw him overboard. He went to a side of the ship in order to fall from it, but there was a creature of the sea's creatures watching and lying in wait for him. He moved to the other side, and found it there too, until it circled the vessel while it never left him. He knew that this was from God, so he threw himself towards it, and it swallowed him.

In the story of Yunus, peace be upon him, there are omitted sentences implied here before the mention of his flight to the ship, just as in his story in Surat al-Anbiya' in God's words ﴿when he went off in anger﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] — what follows this — and His words ﴿then he called out in the darkness﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] are also omitted sentences. By gathering the accounts together, what was omitted in each one becomes clear.

﴿Then he cast lots, and he was among the losers﴾: "among the defeated," and its real meaning is "among those slipped away from the position of victory in the drawing of lots." It was read ﴿wa-huwa muliym﴾ ("while he was blameworthy") with a fatha on the mim (mulīm). Its regular form would be malūm, since it derives from lumtuhu, alūmuhu, lawman, so it is of the wāw-type; but it was given the pattern alīm, as they said mashīb and mad'iyy in place of mashūb, and mad'uww, based on shayab and da'a.

﴿Among those who glorify God﴾: among those who remember God with glorification (tasbih) and sanctification (taqdis). The apparent meaning is that He means what was mentioned in His words in Surat al-Anbiya': ﴿then he called out in the darkness: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87]. Ibn Jubayr said: it is His words "Glory be to God." A group said: his glorification is voluntary prayer. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Abu al-'Aliyah said: his prayer in times of ease benefits him in times of hardship. Al-Dahhak ibn Qays said from his pulpit: "Remember God in ease and He will remember you in hardship; indeed Yunus was a servant who remembered God, and when hardship befell him, that benefited him." Almighty and Majestic God said: ﴿So had he not been one of those who glorify God﴾, ﴿he would have remained in its belly until the day they are resurrected﴾. Al-Hasan said: his glorification was his prayer in the belly of the fish. It is related that he would lift the flesh of the fish with his hands, saying: "I will surely build You a place of worship (masjid) where no one has built before me."

It is related that the fish travelled alongside the ship, raising its head to breathe while Yunus glorified God, and it did not leave them until they reached the shore. It then spat him out safe, with nothing of him changed, and so they became Muslims. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿he would have remained in its belly until the day of resurrection﴾ is as follows. Qatada said: the belly of the fish would have been a grave for him until the Day of Resurrection. Various mutually contradictory statements have been made about the length of his stay in the belly of the fish, and we set those aside completely without mention.

﴿While he was ailing﴾: It is related that his body became like the body of a newborn child when it is born; this was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi. Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra and Amr ibn Maymun said: al-yaqtin means specifically the gourd (qar'). It was said: this is the one God caused to grow over him, and it combines several qualities: the coolness of its shade, the smoothness of its touch, the largeness of its leaves, and flies do not approach it. It was said: if water from its leaves is sprinkled on a place, no fly comes near it. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"He caused a gourd to grow over him by mercy from God; had God not been there, he would have found me lost."

It is reported that [the Prophet] said: "Indeed you love the gourd?" He said: "Yes, it is the tree of my brother Yunus." It was also said: it is the banana tree; he covered himself with its leaves, shaded himself with its branches, and broke his fast with its fruit. The meaning of ﴿We caused a tree to grow over him﴾ in Arabic usage is a plant that stands upon a stalk of wood. It is possible that God caused it to grow with a stalk, so that he could shade himself with it and its leaves, as an exception to the usual course of things; so he grew well, healed, and his appearance became good, because the leaves of the gourd are the most beneficial thing for one whose skin has peeled off.

﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾: The majority said: this mission is the first one, after which he fled, and He mentioned it at the end of the narrative to draw attention to his mission. This is shown by ﴿so they believed, and We let them enjoy themselves﴾, and the enjoyment of that community is what angered Yunus, peace be upon him, until he fled. Ibn Abbas and Qatada said: it is another mission after He cast him onto the open shore, and it was to the people of Nineveh, on the side of Mosul. Al-Zamakhshari said: what is meant is his earlier sending to his people, who were the people of Nineveh. It was also said: it is a second sending after the first one that was directed at them, or to others. It was said: they became Muslims and asked him to return to them, but he refused, because a prophet who has emigrated from his people does not return to them to live among them; so he said to them: "Indeed God will send to you a prophet." Al-Zamakhshari did not mention any other view than this, saying: "or more" in the sight of the beholder: when the observer sees them he says: they are a hundred thousand or more. The purpose is a description of their multitude. Yunus ibn Matta (Jonah, son of Matta) was from the Children of Israel. It is related that he was given prophethood at the age of twenty-eight. God sent him to his people, and he invited them to faith, but they opposed him. So he threatened them with punishment, and God informed them of its day, and Yunus set that day for them. Then, when his people saw the signs of the punishment before it reached them, they repented and believed, so God accepted their repentance and turned the punishment away from them. The account of his story has already been explained, and we have repeated a portion of it so that it may clarify what lies between the two mentions. It is said: Yunus was seized by anger, so he fled to board the ship, running away from his people. He described the flight with the word ibaq (fleeing from one's master), since he is a servant of God, and he went out fleeing without permission from God. It is related from Ibn Mas'ud that when the ship sailed far out into the sea with Yunus aboard, it stopped moving. Its people said: "Indeed, there is among us someone because of whom God has held the ship back, so let us draw lots." They took a lot for each person, on the condition that whoever's lot floats is the one, and whoever's lot sinks is not him. Yunus's lot floated. They did this three times, and the lot fell upon him each time, so they agreed to throw him overboard. He went to a side of the ship in order to fall from it, but there was a creature of the sea's creatures watching and lying in wait for him. He moved to the other side, and found it there too, until it circled the vessel while it never left him. He knew that this was from God, so he threw himself towards it, and it swallowed him.

In the story of Yunus, peace be upon him, there are omitted sentences implied here before the mention of his flight to the ship, just as in his story in Surat al-Anbiya' in God's words ﴿when he went off in anger﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] — what follows this — and His words ﴿then he called out in the darkness﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87] are also omitted sentences. By gathering the accounts together, what was omitted in each one becomes clear.

﴿Then he cast lots, and he was among the losers﴾: "among the defeated," and its real meaning is "among those slipped away from the position of victory in the drawing of lots." It was read ﴿wa-huwa muliym﴾ ("while he was blameworthy") with a fatha on the mim (mulīm). Its regular form would be malūm, since it derives from lumtuhu, alūmuhu, lawman, so it is of the wāw-type; but it was given the pattern alīm, as they said mashīb and mad'iyy in place of mashūb, and mad'uww, based on shayab and da'a.

﴿Among those who glorify God﴾: among those who remember God with glorification (tasbih) and sanctification (taqdis). The apparent meaning is that He means what was mentioned in His words in Surat al-Anbiya': ﴿then he called out in the darkness: "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers"﴾ [al-Anbiya': 87]. Ibn Jubayr said: it is His words "Glory be to God." A group said: his glorification is voluntary prayer. Ibn Abbas, Qatada and Abu al-'Aliyah said: his prayer in times of ease benefits him in times of hardship. Al-Dahhak ibn Qays said from his pulpit: "Remember God in ease and He will remember you in hardship; indeed Yunus was a servant who remembered God, and when hardship befell him, that benefited him." Almighty and Majestic God said: ﴿So had he not been one of those who glorify God﴾, ﴿he would have remained in its belly until the day they are resurrected﴾. Al-Hasan said: his glorification was his prayer in the belly of the fish. It is related that he would lift the flesh of the fish with his hands, saying: "I will surely build You a place of worship (masjid) where no one has built before me."

It is related that the fish travelled alongside the ship, raising its head to breathe while Yunus glorified God, and it did not leave them until they reached the shore. It then spat him out safe, with nothing of him changed, and so they became Muslims. The apparent meaning of His words ﴿he would have remained in its belly until the day of resurrection﴾ is as follows. Qatada said: the belly of the fish would have been a grave for him until the Day of Resurrection. Various mutually contradictory statements have been made about the length of his stay in the belly of the fish, and we set those aside completely without mention.

﴿While he was ailing﴾: It is related that his body became like the body of a newborn child when it is born; this was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi. Ibn Abbas, Abu Hurayra and Amr ibn Maymun said: al-yaqtin means specifically the gourd (qar'). It was said: this is the one God caused to grow over him, and it combines several qualities: the coolness of its shade, the smoothness of its touch, the largeness of its leaves, and flies do not approach it. It was said: if water from its leaves is sprinkled on a place, no fly comes near it. Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt said:

"He caused a gourd to grow over him by mercy from God; had God not been there, he would have found me lost."

It is reported that [the Prophet] said: "Indeed you love the gourd?" He said: "Yes, it is the tree of my brother Yunus." It was also said: it is the banana tree; he covered himself with its leaves, shaded himself with its branches, and broke his fast with its fruit. The meaning of ﴿We caused a tree to grow over him﴾ in Arabic usage is a plant that stands upon a stalk of wood. It is possible that God caused it to grow with a stalk, so that he could shade himself with it and its leaves, as an exception to the usual course of things; so he grew well, healed, and his appearance became good, because the leaves of the gourd are the most beneficial thing for one whose skin has peeled off.

﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾: The majority said: this mission is the first one, after which he fled, and He mentioned it at the end of the narrative to draw attention to his mission. This is shown by ﴿so they believed, and We let them enjoy themselves﴾, and the enjoyment of that community is what angered Yunus, peace be upon him, until he fled. Ibn Abbas and Qatada said: it is another mission after He cast him onto the open shore, and it was to the people of Nineveh, on the side of Mosul. Al-Zamakhshari said: what is meant is his earlier sending to his people, who were the people of Nineveh. It was also said: it is a second sending after the first one that was directed at them, or to others. It was said: they became Muslims and asked him to return to them, but he refused, because a prophet who has emigrated from his people does not return to them to live among them; so he said to them: "Indeed God will send to you a prophet." The majority read ﴿aw﴾ ("or"); Ibn Abbas said it means "bal" ("rather"). It was also said: it means "wa" ("and") and is used with the meaning of "and." Ja'far ibn Muhammad read it likewise. It was said: it is for the ambiguity of the addressee's perspective. Al-Mubarrad and many of the Basran grammarians said: the meaning is according to human perception and estimation, so that whoever is behind them says: they are a hundred thousand or more. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention any other view than this, saying: "or more" in the sight of the beholder: when the observer sees them he says: they are a hundred thousand or more. The purpose is a description of their multitude. The excess was thirty thousand, as said by Ibn Abbas; or seventy thousand, as said by Ibn Jubayr; or twenty thousand, related from Ubayy from the Prophet (ﷺ). If this is authentic, what else is said is invalid.

(﴿So they believed﴾): It is related that they went out with their children, offspring and animals, separated them from their mothers, wailed, cried out, and sincerely turned to God, so God lifted the punishment from them. Enjoyment here means life, and the term (hīn, "a time") refers to their previously decreed appointed terms in eternity; this was said by Qatada and al-Suddi.

The pronoun in ﴿So ask them﴾: al-Zamakhshari said it is conjoined with a similar one at the beginning of the sura, even though the distance between them is great. He commanded His messenger to ask the Quraysh about the basis of their denial of resurrection at first, then continued the speech connecting part of it to part, then commanded that they be asked about the basis of the unjust division. End of quotation. What he said about conjunction is far-fetched.

If they counted the separation by a sentence such as "Eat meat, strike Zayd, and [eat] bread" among the most ugly constructions, how much more so with many sentences and disparate stories? So the view of conjunction is not permissible. The asking here is a question in the manner of rebuke and reproach for their saying falsehood about God, since they attributed females to God in their saying that the angels are God's daughters, while they themselves disliked them, buried them alive, and disdained anyone who mentioned them. They committed three kinds of disbelief: anthropomorphism (tajsim), since begetting is specific to bodies; the exaltation of themselves, since they ascribed the higher of the two kinds to themselves and the other to God Most High; and their belittling of those who are honoured with God, since they made the angels female.

He first began by rebuking them for exalting themselves with His words ﴿For your Lord are the daughters?﴾, and He changed from saying "for your Lord" to "for your Lord" with the omission of attribution to them, because leaving out their attribution beautifies them and honours His prophet by attributing it to him. He then said that ascribing femaleness to the angels requires witnessing, so He denied this to them with ﴿Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?﴾, meaning: We created them while they witnessed nothing of their state, as He said in another place ﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19], and as He said ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves﴾ [al-Kahf: 51]. Then He informed of them thirdly with the greatest disbelief, which is their claim that He has begotten, so their falsehood reached the attribution of offspring. Since this was grave, He said ﴿and indeed they are liars﴾. It is possible that this sentence is specific to their saying "God has begotten" and serves as emphasis for His words ﴿from their own lie﴾; it is also possible that it covers this entire statement. If you say: why did He say "while they were witnesses" and restrict their knowledge to witnessing? I say: it is nothing but mockery and ascribing ignorance to them, like His words ﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 19]. That is because, just as they did not know this through witnessing, they did not know it through knowledge that God placed in their hearts, nor through a truthful report, nor through reasoning or inference. It is also possible that the meaning is that they say this as one who speaks with a settled heart and tranquil soul out of extreme ignorance, as if they had witnessed His creation. Qur'anic reading: ﴿Walad Allah﴾ ("the offspring of God"), that is, the angels are His offspring; walad is a form of fa'al meaning maf'ul, which applies to the singular and plural, masculine and feminine. You say: "This is my child (walad)" and "These are my children." End of quotation.

As for His words ﴿And indeed they are liars﴾, it is a parenthetical sentence between the two statements of disbelief, coming to intensify and emphasize that their saying is from their own falsehood.

﴿Then bring your Book﴾: which was sent down to you with that, as in His words ﴿Have We sent down to them an authority that speaks of what they used to associate?﴾ [al-Rum: 35].

The apparent meaning is that *al-jinnah* refers to the devils (*al-shayatin*), and there are outrageous statements by the disbelievers about this. Among them is that He, exalted is He, intermarried with the chiefs of the jinn, and from them begot the angels, who are a group from the Banu Mudlij. Some of the disbelievers said this directly to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him).

﴿And they have set up between Him and the jinn a kinship. But the jinn know well that they will surely be brought forth.﴾ That is, the devils know that they are brought forth to the command of Allah, to reward and punishment. This is said by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Zamakhshari said: If *al-jinnah* is interpreted as the devils, then the pronoun in ﴿innahum lamuhdarun﴾ may refer to them. The meaning is that the devils know that Allah will bring them to the Fire and punish them, and if they were related to Him, or partners in the obligation of obedience, He would not punish them. It is also said that the pronoun in (*wa-ja'alu*) refers to a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs, and *al-jinnah* means the angels, so called because of their concealment (*ijtinan*) and their being hidden. Al-Zamakhshari also said: He mentioned them with this name to demean them and diminish them, even though they themselves held them in high regard, so that they would not reach the rank of the kinship they attributed to them. In this is an indication that one whose attribute is concealment and hiding, which are attributes of bodies, cannot be a fitting relation to one to whom such things are not permissible. End of quote.

﴿And the jinn know well that they (*annahum*), that is the disbelievers who claim a kinship between the angels and Allah, Exalted is He, will be brought to the Fire, to be punished for what they say.﴾ This knowledge is attributed to those who are claimed to be related to Him, as an exaggeration in refuting those who make the claim. Then Allah, Exalted is He, declared Himself free of the attribute that is not fitting for Him: ﴿except the servants of Allah﴾, for they describe Him by His attributes. As for the phrase "from those brought forth" (*al-muhdarun*), that is, except the servants of Allah, they are saved for the duration of the punishment. The sentence of declaring Him free (*tanzih*) is then a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiradh*) relating to both opinions, and the exception is disconnected (*munqati'*). The apparent view is that the *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is conjunctive, joining "what you worship" to the pronoun in *innakum*, and that the pronoun in *alayhi* refers to (*ma*). The meaning is: Say to them, O Muhammad: "You and what you worship, of idols, are such that you and they dominate (the speech)." The address is made dominant, as you say: "You and Zayd go out against it," meaning against the worship of your deity.

﴿fatinin﴾ means bearers of temptation (*fitnah*) to His servants, except for those whom Allah has decreed in His prior knowledge to be among the people of the Fire. The pronoun in *alayhi* refers to (*ma*) by omitting a noun (*mudaf*) as we have said, that is, against His worship. (*Fatinin*) is given the sense of "bearers of temptation," and (*man*) is its object; the governing element is left free because (*fatinin*) was not taken as an object-taking participle. It is also said that *alayhi* means "with" (*bi*): that is, you are not the ones who, with the one you worship, are tempting, except those for whom the decree has preceded that they will enter the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari made the pronoun in *alayhi* refer to Allah. He said: If you ask, "How can they tempt them against Allah?" I say: They corrupt them against Him by leading them astray and misleading them, from your saying: "So-and-so tempted so-and-so against so-and-so his wife," just as you say: "He corrupted her against him" and "he disappointed her against him." The *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ may also mean "together with" (*ma'a*), like their saying: "Every man and his estate." Just as it is permissible to be silent about "every man and his estate," so it is permissible to be silent about His saying ﴿innakum wa-ma ta'budun﴾, because His saying ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ takes the place of the predicate, since its meaning is "you together with what you worship." The meaning is: you together with your gods, that is, you are their companions and associates, not ceasing to worship them. Then He said ﴿ma antum 'alayhi﴾, that is, "upon what you worship," ﴿bi-fatinin﴾, meaning: inciting or bearing toward the path of temptation and misguidance, except for one who is astray among you. End of quote. That the *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is the *waw* of "together with" is not obvious to the mind, and separating ﴿ma antum 'alayhi bi-fatinin﴾ from ﴿innakum wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is not a good view, because attributing it to them is what comes first to understanding, together with the soundness of the meaning, so one should not turn away from it.

(p-379) Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ablah read (*salu al-jahim*), with a *waw*, and so it is written in the *Kamil* of al-Hudhali. In the book of Ibn Khalawayh, from both of them, it is written (*sala*) without a *waw*; and in the book of Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Hasan read (*salu*) written with a *waw*; and in the book of *al-Lawami'* and the book of al-Zamakhshari, from al-Hasan, it is written (*sala*) without a *waw*. As for the one who keeps the *waw*, it is the sound plural (*jam' salamah*) with the *nun* dropped due to the annexation (*idafah*). It is first treated according to the wording of (*man*) and so is singular, then secondly according to its meaning and so is plural, like His saying: ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]. In (*yaqulu*) it is treated according to the wording of (*man*), and in (*wa-ma hum*) according to the meaning, and the treatment according to the wording and the meaning are combined in one sentence, which is the relative clause, like His saying: ﴿except for one who was a Jew or a Christian﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. And the poet's saying:

*And he woke whoever among you was asleep.*

As for the one who does not keep the *waw*, it is possible that it is a plural and the *waw* was omitted in writing, as it is omitted in pronunciation in pause for the meeting of two unvocalized letters. It is also possible that (*sala*) is singular and its final radical was dropped for lightness, and the case-ending (*i'rab*) was applied to its middle, as was dropped in His saying: ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near﴾ [al-Rahman: 54], and ﴿And His are the ships raised high﴾ [al-Rahman: 24], with the *nun* and *jawar* in the nominative. And they say: *ma balayt bihi balah*, meaning *baliyah* from *balaa*, like *'afiyah* from *'afa*, so the final radical of (*balaytu* and *baliyah*) was dropped. And they say: *balah* and *bal*, with the radical dropped in both. Al-Zamakhshari said: He has directed the two preceding views in a certain way, and made them the first and third, saying: The second is that its origin is *sa'il* (one who is burning) with the metathesis, then it is said *sal* for *sa'il*, like their saying: *shakk* for *sha'ik* (sharp). End of quote.

﴿And there is none of us (*wa-ma minna*), that is, anyone, ﴿except that he has a known station﴾, that is, a station in worship and in ending at the command of Allah, restricted to him and not exceeding it. As it has been narrated: "Some of them are bowing who do not raise their backs, and some are prostrate who do not raise their heads." This is the speech of the angels, and it supports the view of those who said that *al-jinnah* are the angels: they disowned what the disbelievers attributed to them, that they are daughters of Allah, and they informed about their state of servitude and the condition in which they are. In a hadith: "There is not a place in the heaven but there is an angel in it, prostrating or standing and praying." And from Ibn Mas'ud: "There is no spot the width of a span but upon it is the forehead of an angel or his feet." The omission of the subject with (*min*) is fine and eloquent, as has passed in His saying: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book except that he will surely believe in Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 159], that is, "And there is none of the People of the Book who..." The Arabs say: "Among us is one who departed, and among us is one who stayed," meaning: "among us is a group who departed, and among us is a group who stayed." And al-Zamakhshari said: "And there is none of us but that he has a known station," where the qualified noun is omitted and the adjective put in its place, like his saying:

*I am the son of Jala, and the scaler of the passes, by my hand he was among the best archers of mankind.*

End of quote. This is not an omission of the qualified noun with the adjective taking its place, because the omitted *ahad* (anyone) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and *illa lahu maqam ma'lum* (except he has a known station) is its predicate, and because no complete sentence is formed from His saying "And there is none of us anyone." So His saying ﴿except that he has a known station﴾ is the place of the benefit. Even if it is imagined that ﴿except that he has a known station﴾ is in the position of an adjective, they have stated that *illa* (except) cannot be an adjective when its qualified noun is omitted, and that it differs from *ghayr* (other than) when *ghayr* is an adjective in that respect, so that *ghayr* can be more fully used as an adjective while *illa* is less fully usable in this way. This is treated like His saying: *ana ibn Jala*, meaning "the son of a man who departed," and *bi-kaffi kana*, meaning "a man who was." This is, according to the grammarians, among the most objectionable of poetic necessities (*darurat*).

﴿And indeed we are those who stand in rows (*al-saffun*)﴾, that is, placing our feet in prayer, or our wings in the air, or around the Throne, supplicating for the believers. Al-Zahrawi said: It is said that the Muslims have arranged themselves in rows in prayer since this verse was revealed, and no group of the religions arranges itself in rows except the Muslims.

﴿And indeed we are those who glorify (*al-musabbihun*)﴾, that is, those who declare Allah free from what the disbelievers attribute to Him, or those who declare Him free with the words of glorification (*tasbih*), or those who pray. It is appropriate that His saying ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe﴾ be taken as the speech of the angels, so that the sentences follow in sequence and proceed from one speaker. It is as if it were said: "And the angels knew well that those who attribute this are to be brought forth for punishment; and they said, 'Glory be to Allah,' so they declared Him free of that and excepted whoever among the servants of Allah is sincere; and they said to the disbelievers, 'Indeed you and your gods...' to the end." And how could we be related to Him while we are servants before Him, each of us having a station of obedience? And so on, to what they described themselves with of the rank of servitude. It is also said: ﴿And there is none of us except that he has a known station﴾ is from the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: "And there is none of the messengers except that he has a known station on the Day of Resurrection according to his deed," from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾ [al-Isra': 79]. Then he mentioned their deeds, and that they are those who arrange themselves in rows in prayer and who declare Allah free of what the people of misguidance say.

The pronoun in (*la-yaqulun*) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh: ﴿If only we had with us a reminder from the earlier peoples﴾, that is, a book from the books of the earlier peoples to whom the Torah and the Gospel were revealed, ﴿we would have been sincere servants of Allah﴾, and we would not have denied as they denied. ﴿But they disbelieved in it (*fa-kafaru bihi*)﴾, that is, then the Reminder came to them which they used to wish for, and it is the most honorable of reminders, because of its inimitability among the books.

﴿So they will soon know﴾ the outcome of their disbelief, and what retribution will befall them. They emphasized their statement with the lightened *in* and with the *lam*, indicating that they were earnest in that; then there appeared from them denial and intense aversion, like His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89].

﴿And indeed Our word has preceded (*kalimatuna*)﴾. The majority read it in the singular, since it is united in one meaning, so it was expressed in the singular. Al-Dahhak read it in the plural. The intended promise is the victory of the messengers over their enemies in the stations of argument and the battles of war in this world, and their superiority over them in the Hereafter. Al-Hasan said: No prophet was defeated in war, nor was any killed in it.

﴿So turn away from them for a time (*hatta hin*)﴾, that is, for a short period, which is the period of ceasing fighting. From al-Suddi: until the Day of Badr, and al-Tabari preferred this. Qatadah said: until their death. Ibn Zayd said: until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And watch them﴾, that is, look at the outcome of their affair, ﴿for they will soon see﴾ it, and what will befall them of punishment, capture and killing; or they will soon see you and what will be accomplished for you of victory over them and triumph against them. His command to watch them is an indication of a state that is awaited and certain to occur, and that it is near, as if it were between his two eyes so that he sees it. In this is consolation and relief for him, peace be upon him.

﴿Then are they seeking to hasten Our punishment?﴾ An interrogation of reproach.

﴿فَإذا نَزَلَ﴾ [When it descends], that is, the punishment, is like the punishment that descended upon them after he had warned them. They denied it to such a degree that he warned his people and some of their craftsmen of its approach, yet they paid no attention to his warning, did not take precautions against it, and made no plan that would save them, until it came down into their courtyard and launched its raid upon them and cut off their last trace. It was the custom of their raids to attack at dawn, so the raid was called "dawn" even when it occurred at another time. This verse would not be eloquent, nor would it have the striking beauty that makes it pleasing and makes its meaning settle in the soul and nature, except that it comes in the manner of a figurative expression (tamthil), as al-Zamakhshari (the Qur'an commentator and grammarian) said. The majority of readers recited نَزَلَ in the active voice (مَبْنِيًّا لِلْفاعِلِ), while Ibn Mas'ud recited it in the passive voice (مَبْنِيًّا لِلْمَفْعُولِ). In the passive reading, ساحَتِهِمْ (their courtyard) is the substitute for the subject (القائِمُ مَقامَ الفاعِلِ). The expression نَزَلَ ساحَةَ فُلانٍ (it descended upon the courtyard of so-and-so) is used for whatever comes upon a person, whether good or evil. سُوءُ الصَّباحِ (the evil of the morning) is used for the arrival of raids and calamities, like the words of the one crying out: يا صَباحاهُ (Alas, my morning!). The ruling of ساءَ (sā'a, "evil is") here is the ruling of بِئْسَ (bi'sa, "evil is"). ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited فَبِئْسَ (fa-bi'sa). The thing being condemned is omitted; its implied meaning is: "Evil is the morning of those who were warned, their morning."

﴿وتَوَلَّ عَنْهم حَتّى حِينٍ﴾ [And turn away from them for a time]. He repeated the command to turn away, to console him (ʿalayhi al-salam), to comfort him, and to emphasize the certainty of the appointed time. He did not restrict the command with seeing (al-ibsar), as he had restricted it in the first instance. This was either because he was satisfied with it in the first instance and omitted it for brevity, or because leaving it unrestricted allows the mind to range over what the seeing relates to: the various kinds of joys for him, and the various kinds of troubles for them. It was also said: the first refers to the punishment of this world, and the later refers to the punishment of the Hereafter.

God, exalted is He, concluded this surah by declaring Himself free from what the polytheists describe, and He attributed the Lord to His Prophet, honoring him by this attribution and by addressing him. Then He attributed the Lord to might (al-ʿizza), which is the created might that belongs to the prophets and believers. The jurists said likewise, on the basis that it is something nurtured (marbūbah, created and sustained). Muhammad ibn Sahnun and others said: whoever swears by the might of God, intending His might that is created among His servants, which is the one in His saying ﴿رَبِّ العِزَّةِ﴾ [the Lord of Might], then it is not an oath (yamin). Al-Zamakhshari said: the Lord is attributed to might because He is specifically characterized by it, as if it were said "the Possessor of might," just as you say "companion of truthfulness" because he is specifically characterized by truthfulness. End of quote. On this view, an oath by the might of God is binding, because it is one of His attributes. He said: it is also possible that it means there is no might for any of the kings or others except that He is its Lord and Owner, in accordance with His saying ﴿وتُعِزُّ مَن تَشاءُ﴾ [and You exalt whom You will] [Ali Imran: 26].

It is related from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: "Whoever wishes to be measured with the fullest measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let the last of his words when he rises from his assembly be: (Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might) to the end of the surah."

(p-378)

The apparent meaning is that *al-jinnah* refers to the devils (*al-shayatin*), and there are outrageous statements by the disbelievers about this. Among them is that He, exalted is He, intermarried with the chiefs of the jinn, and from them begot the angels, who are a group from the Banu Mudlij. Some of the disbelievers said this directly to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him).

﴿And they have set up between Him and the jinn a kinship. But the jinn know well that they will surely be brought forth.﴾ That is, the devils know that they are brought forth to the command of Allah, to reward and punishment. This is said by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Zamakhshari said: If *al-jinnah* is interpreted as the devils, then the pronoun in ﴿innahum lamuhdarun﴾ may refer to them. The meaning is that the devils know that Allah will bring them to the Fire and punish them, and if they were related to Him, or partners in the obligation of obedience, He would not punish them. It is also said that the pronoun in (*wa-ja'alu*) refers to a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs, and *al-jinnah* means the angels, so called because of their concealment (*ijtinan*) and their being hidden. Al-Zamakhshari also said: He mentioned them with this name to demean them and diminish them, even though they themselves held them in high regard, so that they would not reach the rank of the kinship they attributed to them. In this is an indication that one whose attribute is concealment and hiding, which are attributes of bodies, cannot be a fitting relation to one to whom such things are not permissible. End of quote.

﴿And the jinn know well that they (*annahum*), that is the disbelievers who claim a kinship between the angels and Allah, Exalted is He, will be brought to the Fire, to be punished for what they say.﴾ This knowledge is attributed to those who are claimed to be related to Him, as an exaggeration in refuting those who make the claim. Then Allah, Exalted is He, declared Himself free of the attribute that is not fitting for Him: ﴿except the servants of Allah﴾, for they describe Him by His attributes. As for the phrase "from those brought forth" (*al-muhdarun*), that is, except the servants of Allah, they are saved for the duration of the punishment. The sentence of declaring Him free (*tanzih*) is then a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiradh*) relating to both opinions, and the exception is disconnected (*munqati'*). The apparent view is that the *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is conjunctive, joining "what you worship" to the pronoun in *innakum*, and that the pronoun in *alayhi* refers to (*ma*). The meaning is: Say to them, O Muhammad: "You and what you worship, of idols, are such that you and they dominate (the speech)." The address is made dominant, as you say: "You and Zayd go out against it," meaning against the worship of your deity.

﴿fatinin﴾ means bearers of temptation (*fitnah*) to His servants, except for those whom Allah has decreed in His prior knowledge to be among the people of the Fire. The pronoun in *alayhi* refers to (*ma*) by omitting a noun (*mudaf*) as we have said, that is, against His worship. (*Fatinin*) is given the sense of "bearers of temptation," and (*man*) is its object; the governing element is left free because (*fatinin*) was not taken as an object-taking participle. It is also said that *alayhi* means "with" (*bi*): that is, you are not the ones who, with the one you worship, are tempting, except those for whom the decree has preceded that they will enter the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari made the pronoun in *alayhi* refer to Allah. He said: If you ask, "How can they tempt them against Allah?" I say: They corrupt them against Him by leading them astray and misleading them, from your saying: "So-and-so tempted so-and-so against so-and-so his wife," just as you say: "He corrupted her against him" and "he disappointed her against him." The *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ may also mean "together with" (*ma'a*), like their saying: "Every man and his estate." Just as it is permissible to be silent about "every man and his estate," so it is permissible to be silent about His saying ﴿innakum wa-ma ta'budun﴾, because His saying ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ takes the place of the predicate, since its meaning is "you together with what you worship." The meaning is: you together with your gods, that is, you are their companions and associates, not ceasing to worship them. Then He said ﴿ma antum 'alayhi﴾, that is, "upon what you worship," ﴿bi-fatinin﴾, meaning: inciting or bearing toward the path of temptation and misguidance, except for one who is astray among you. End of quote. That the *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is the *waw* of "together with" is not obvious to the mind, and separating ﴿ma antum 'alayhi bi-fatinin﴾ from ﴿innakum wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is not a good view, because attributing it to them is what comes first to understanding, together with the soundness of the meaning, so one should not turn away from it.
