﴿And indeed we are those who glorify (*al-musabbihun*)﴾, that is, those who declare Allah free from what the disbelievers attribute to Him, or those who declare Him free with the words of glorification (*tasbih*), or those who pray. It is appropriate that His saying ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe﴾ be taken as the speech of the angels, so that the sentences follow in sequence and proceed from one speaker. It is as if it were said: "And the angels knew well that those who attribute this are to be brought forth for punishment; and they said, 'Glory be to Allah,' so they declared Him free of that and excepted whoever among the servants of Allah is sincere; and they said to the disbelievers, 'Indeed you and your gods...' to the end." And how could we be related to Him while we are servants before Him, each of us having a station of obedience? And so on, to what they described themselves with of the rank of servitude. It is also said: ﴿And there is none of us except that he has a known station﴾ is from the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: "And there is none of the messengers except that he has a known station on the Day of Resurrection according to his deed," from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾ [al-Isra': 79]. Then he mentioned their deeds, and that they are those who arrange themselves in rows in prayer and who declare Allah free of what the people of misguidance say.

The pronoun in (*la-yaqulun*) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh: ﴿If only we had with us a reminder from the earlier peoples﴾, that is, a book from the books of the earlier peoples to whom the Torah and the Gospel were revealed, ﴿we would have been sincere servants of Allah﴾, and we would not have denied as they denied. ﴿But they disbelieved in it (*fa-kafaru bihi*)﴾, that is, then the Reminder came to them which they used to wish for, and it is the most honorable of reminders, because of its inimitability among the books.

﴿So they will soon know﴾ the outcome of their disbelief, and what retribution will befall them. They emphasized their statement with the lightened *in* and with the *lam*, indicating that they were earnest in that; then there appeared from them denial and intense aversion, like His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89].

﴿And indeed Our word has preceded (*kalimatuna*)﴾. The majority read it in the singular, since it is united in one meaning, so it was expressed in the singular. Al-Dahhak read it in the plural. The intended promise is the victory of the messengers over their enemies in the stations of argument and the battles of war in this world, and their superiority over them in the Hereafter. Al-Hasan said: No prophet was defeated in war, nor was any killed in it.

﴿So turn away from them for a time (*hatta hin*)﴾, that is, for a short period, which is the period of ceasing fighting. From al-Suddi: until the Day of Badr, and al-Tabari preferred this. Qatadah said: until their death. Ibn Zayd said: until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And watch them﴾, that is, look at the outcome of their affair, ﴿for they will soon see﴾ it, and what will befall them of punishment, capture and killing; or they will soon see you and what will be accomplished for you of victory over them and triumph against them. His command to watch them is an indication of a state that is awaited and certain to occur, and that it is near, as if it were between his two eyes so that he sees it. In this is consolation and relief for him, peace be upon him.

﴿Then are they seeking to hasten Our punishment?﴾ An interrogation of reproach.

﴿فَإذا نَزَلَ﴾ [When it descends], that is, the punishment, is like the punishment that descended upon them after he had warned them. They denied it to such a degree that he warned his people and some of their craftsmen of its approach, yet they paid no attention to his warning, did not take precautions against it, and made no plan that would save them, until it came down into their courtyard and launched its raid upon them and cut off their last trace. It was the custom of their raids to attack at dawn, so the raid was called "dawn" even when it occurred at another time. This verse would not be eloquent, nor would it have the striking beauty that makes it pleasing and makes its meaning settle in the soul and nature, except that it comes in the manner of a figurative expression (tamthil), as al-Zamakhshari (the Qur'an commentator and grammarian) said. The majority of readers recited نَزَلَ in the active voice (مَبْنِيًّا لِلْفاعِلِ), while Ibn Mas'ud recited it in the passive voice (مَبْنِيًّا لِلْمَفْعُولِ). In the passive reading, ساحَتِهِمْ (their courtyard) is the substitute for the subject (القائِمُ مَقامَ الفاعِلِ). The expression نَزَلَ ساحَةَ فُلانٍ (it descended upon the courtyard of so-and-so) is used for whatever comes upon a person, whether good or evil. سُوءُ الصَّباحِ (the evil of the morning) is used for the arrival of raids and calamities, like the words of the one crying out: يا صَباحاهُ (Alas, my morning!). The ruling of ساءَ (sā'a, "evil is") here is the ruling of بِئْسَ (bi'sa, "evil is"). ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited فَبِئْسَ (fa-bi'sa). The thing being condemned is omitted; its implied meaning is: "Evil is the morning of those who were warned, their morning."

﴿وتَوَلَّ عَنْهم حَتّى حِينٍ﴾ [And turn away from them for a time]. He repeated the command to turn away, to console him (ʿalayhi al-salam), to comfort him, and to emphasize the certainty of the appointed time. He did not restrict the command with seeing (al-ibsar), as he had restricted it in the first instance. This was either because he was satisfied with it in the first instance and omitted it for brevity, or because leaving it unrestricted allows the mind to range over what the seeing relates to: the various kinds of joys for him, and the various kinds of troubles for them. It was also said: the first refers to the punishment of this world, and the later refers to the punishment of the Hereafter.

God, exalted is He, concluded this surah by declaring Himself free from what the polytheists describe, and He attributed the Lord to His Prophet, honoring him by this attribution and by addressing him. Then He attributed the Lord to might (al-ʿizza), which is the created might that belongs to the prophets and believers. The jurists said likewise, on the basis that it is something nurtured (marbūbah, created and sustained). Muhammad ibn Sahnun and others said: whoever swears by the might of God, intending His might that is created among His servants, which is the one in His saying ﴿رَبِّ العِزَّةِ﴾ [the Lord of Might], then it is not an oath (yamin). Al-Zamakhshari said: the Lord is attributed to might because He is specifically characterized by it, as if it were said "the Possessor of might," just as you say "companion of truthfulness" because he is specifically characterized by truthfulness. End of quote. On this view, an oath by the might of God is binding, because it is one of His attributes. He said: it is also possible that it means there is no might for any of the kings or others except that He is its Lord and Owner, in accordance with His saying ﴿وتُعِزُّ مَن تَشاءُ﴾ [and You exalt whom You will] [Ali Imran: 26].

It is related from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: "Whoever wishes to be measured with the fullest measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let the last of his words when he rises from his assembly be: (Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might) to the end of the surah."

(p-378)

The apparent meaning is that *al-jinnah* refers to the devils (*al-shayatin*), and there are outrageous statements by the disbelievers about this. Among them is that He, exalted is He, intermarried with the chiefs of the jinn, and from them begot the angels, who are a group from the Banu Mudlij. Some of the disbelievers said this directly to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him).

﴿And they have set up between Him and the jinn a kinship. But the jinn know well that they will surely be brought forth.﴾ That is, the devils know that they are brought forth to the command of Allah, to reward and punishment. This is said by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Zamakhshari said: If *al-jinnah* is interpreted as the devils, then the pronoun in ﴿innahum lamuhdarun﴾ may refer to them. The meaning is that the devils know that Allah will bring them to the Fire and punish them, and if they were related to Him, or partners in the obligation of obedience, He would not punish them. It is also said that the pronoun in (*wa-ja'alu*) refers to a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs, and *al-jinnah* means the angels, so called because of their concealment (*ijtinan*) and their being hidden. Al-Zamakhshari also said: He mentioned them with this name to demean them and diminish them, even though they themselves held them in high regard, so that they would not reach the rank of the kinship they attributed to them. In this is an indication that one whose attribute is concealment and hiding, which are attributes of bodies, cannot be a fitting relation to one to whom such things are not permissible. End of quote.

﴿And the jinn know well that they (*annahum*), that is the disbelievers who claim a kinship between the angels and Allah, Exalted is He, will be brought to the Fire, to be punished for what they say.﴾ This knowledge is attributed to those who are claimed to be related to Him, as an exaggeration in refuting those who make the claim. Then Allah, Exalted is He, declared Himself free of the attribute that is not fitting for Him: ﴿except the servants of Allah﴾, for they describe Him by His attributes. As for the phrase "from those brought forth" (*al-muhdarun*), that is, except the servants of Allah, they are saved for the duration of the punishment. The sentence of declaring Him free (*tanzih*) is then a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiradh*) relating to both opinions, and the exception is disconnected (*munqati'*). The apparent view is that the *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is conjunctive, joining "what you worship" to the pronoun in *innakum*, and that the pronoun in *alayhi* refers to (*ma*). The meaning is: Say to them, O Muhammad: "You and what you worship, of idols, are such that you and they dominate (the speech)." The address is made dominant, as you say: "You and Zayd go out against it," meaning against the worship of your deity.

﴿fatinin﴾ means bearers of temptation (*fitnah*) to His servants, except for those whom Allah has decreed in His prior knowledge to be among the people of the Fire. The pronoun in *alayhi* refers to (*ma*) by omitting a noun (*mudaf*) as we have said, that is, against His worship. (*Fatinin*) is given the sense of "bearers of temptation," and (*man*) is its object; the governing element is left free because (*fatinin*) was not taken as an object-taking participle. It is also said that *alayhi* means "with" (*bi*): that is, you are not the ones who, with the one you worship, are tempting, except those for whom the decree has preceded that they will enter the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari made the pronoun in *alayhi* refer to Allah. He said: If you ask, "How can they tempt them against Allah?" I say: They corrupt them against Him by leading them astray and misleading them, from your saying: "So-and-so tempted so-and-so against so-and-so his wife," just as you say: "He corrupted her against him" and "he disappointed her against him." The *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ may also mean "together with" (*ma'a*), like their saying: "Every man and his estate." Just as it is permissible to be silent about "every man and his estate," so it is permissible to be silent about His saying ﴿innakum wa-ma ta'budun﴾, because His saying ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ takes the place of the predicate, since its meaning is "you together with what you worship." The meaning is: you together with your gods, that is, you are their companions and associates, not ceasing to worship them. Then He said ﴿ma antum 'alayhi﴾, that is, "upon what you worship," ﴿bi-fatinin﴾, meaning: inciting or bearing toward the path of temptation and misguidance, except for one who is astray among you. End of quote. That the *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is the *waw* of "together with" is not obvious to the mind, and separating ﴿ma antum 'alayhi bi-fatinin﴾ from ﴿innakum wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is not a good view, because attributing it to them is what comes first to understanding, together with the soundness of the meaning, so one should not turn away from it.

(p-379) Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ablah read (*salu al-jahim*), with a *waw*, and so it is written in the *Kamil* of al-Hudhali. In the book of Ibn Khalawayh, from both of them, it is written (*sala*) without a *waw*; and in the book of Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Hasan read (*salu*) written with a *waw*; and in the book of *al-Lawami'* and the book of al-Zamakhshari, from al-Hasan, it is written (*sala*) without a *waw*. As for the one who keeps the *waw*, it is the sound plural (*jam' salamah*) with the *nun* dropped due to the annexation (*idafah*). It is first treated according to the wording of (*man*) and so is singular, then secondly according to its meaning and so is plural, like His saying: ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]. In (*yaqulu*) it is treated according to the wording of (*man*), and in (*wa-ma hum*) according to the meaning, and the treatment according to the wording and the meaning are combined in one sentence, which is the relative clause, like His saying: ﴿except for one who was a Jew or a Christian﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. And the poet's saying:

*And he woke whoever among you was asleep.*

As for the one who does not keep the *waw*, it is possible that it is a plural and the *waw* was omitted in writing, as it is omitted in pronunciation in pause for the meeting of two unvocalized letters. It is also possible that (*sala*) is singular and its final radical was dropped for lightness, and the case-ending (*i'rab*) was applied to its middle, as was dropped in His saying: ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near﴾ [al-Rahman: 54], and ﴿And His are the ships raised high﴾ [al-Rahman: 24], with the *nun* and *jawar* in the nominative. And they say: *ma balayt bihi balah*, meaning *baliyah* from *balaa*, like *'afiyah* from *'afa*, so the final radical of (*balaytu* and *baliyah*) was dropped. And they say: *balah* and *bal*, with the radical dropped in both. Al-Zamakhshari said: He has directed the two preceding views in a certain way, and made them the first and third, saying: The second is that its origin is *sa'il* (one who is burning) with the metathesis, then it is said *sal* for *sa'il*, like their saying: *shakk* for *sha'ik* (sharp). End of quote.

﴿And there is none of us (*wa-ma minna*), that is, anyone, ﴿except that he has a known station﴾, that is, a station in worship and in ending at the command of Allah, restricted to him and not exceeding it. As it has been narrated: "Some of them are bowing who do not raise their backs, and some are prostrate who do not raise their heads." This is the speech of the angels, and it supports the view of those who said that *al-jinnah* are the angels: they disowned what the disbelievers attributed to them, that they are daughters of Allah, and they informed about their state of servitude and the condition in which they are. In a hadith: "There is not a place in the heaven but there is an angel in it, prostrating or standing and praying." And from Ibn Mas'ud: "There is no spot the width of a span but upon it is the forehead of an angel or his feet." The omission of the subject with (*min*) is fine and eloquent, as has passed in His saying: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book except that he will surely believe in Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 159], that is, "And there is none of the People of the Book who..." The Arabs say: "Among us is one who departed, and among us is one who stayed," meaning: "among us is a group who departed, and among us is a group who stayed." And al-Zamakhshari said: "And there is none of us but that he has a known station," where the qualified noun is omitted and the adjective put in its place, like his saying:

*I am the son of Jala, and the scaler of the passes, by my hand he was among the best archers of mankind.*

End of quote. This is not an omission of the qualified noun with the adjective taking its place, because the omitted *ahad* (anyone) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and *illa lahu maqam ma'lum* (except he has a known station) is its predicate, and because no complete sentence is formed from His saying "And there is none of us anyone." So His saying ﴿except that he has a known station﴾ is the place of the benefit. Even if it is imagined that ﴿except that he has a known station﴾ is in the position of an adjective, they have stated that *illa* (except) cannot be an adjective when its qualified noun is omitted, and that it differs from *ghayr* (other than) when *ghayr* is an adjective in that respect, so that *ghayr* can be more fully used as an adjective while *illa* is less fully usable in this way. This is treated like His saying: *ana ibn Jala*, meaning "the son of a man who departed," and *bi-kaffi kana*, meaning "a man who was." This is, according to the grammarians, among the most objectionable of poetic necessities (*darurat*).

﴿And indeed we are those who stand in rows (*al-saffun*)﴾, that is, placing our feet in prayer, or our wings in the air, or around the Throne, supplicating for the believers. Al-Zahrawi said: It is said that the Muslims have arranged themselves in rows in prayer since this verse was revealed, and no group of the religions arranges itself in rows except the Muslims.

﴿And indeed we are those who glorify (*al-musabbihun*)﴾, that is, those who declare Allah free from what the disbelievers attribute to Him, or those who declare Him free with the words of glorification (*tasbih*), or those who pray. It is appropriate that His saying ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe﴾ be taken as the speech of the angels, so that the sentences follow in sequence and proceed from one speaker. It is as if it were said: "And the angels knew well that those who attribute this are to be brought forth for punishment; and they said, 'Glory be to Allah,' so they declared Him free of that and excepted whoever among the servants of Allah is sincere; and they said to the disbelievers, 'Indeed you and your gods...' to the end." And how could we be related to Him while we are servants before Him, each of us having a station of obedience? And so on, to what they described themselves with of the rank of servitude. It is also said: ﴿And there is none of us except that he has a known station﴾ is from the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: "And there is none of the messengers except that he has a known station on the Day of Resurrection according to his deed," from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾ [al-Isra': 79]. Then he mentioned their deeds, and that they are those who arrange themselves in rows in prayer and who declare Allah free of what the people of misguidance say.

The pronoun in (*la-yaqulun*) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh: ﴿If only we had with us a reminder from the earlier peoples﴾, that is, a book from the books of the earlier peoples to whom the Torah and the Gospel were revealed, ﴿we would have been sincere servants of Allah﴾, and we would not have denied as they denied. ﴿But they disbelieved in it (*fa-kafaru bihi*)﴾, that is, then the Reminder came to them which they used to wish for, and it is the most honorable of reminders, because of its inimitability among the books.

﴿So they will soon know﴾ the outcome of their disbelief, and what retribution will befall them. They emphasized their statement with the lightened *in* and with the *lam*, indicating that they were earnest in that; then there appeared from them denial and intense aversion, like His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89].

﴿And indeed Our word has preceded (*kalimatuna*)﴾. The majority read it in the singular, since it is united in one meaning, so it was expressed in the singular. Al-Dahhak read it in the plural. The intended promise is the victory of the messengers over their enemies in the stations of argument and the battles of war in this world, and their superiority over them in the Hereafter. Al-Hasan said: No prophet was defeated in war, nor was any killed in it.

﴿So turn away from them for a time (*hatta hin*)﴾, that is, for a short period, which is the period of ceasing fighting. From al-Suddi: until the Day of Badr, and al-Tabari preferred this. Qatadah said: until their death. Ibn Zayd said: until the Day of Resurrection.

In this is consolation and relief for him, peace be upon him.

﴿Then are they seeking to hasten Our punishment?﴾ An interrogation of reproach.

﴿فَإذا نَزَلَ﴾ [When it descends], that is, the punishment, is like the punishment that descended upon them after he had warned them. ﴿fatinin﴾ means bearers of temptation (*fitnah*) to His servants, except for those whom Allah has decreed in His prior knowledge to be among the people of the Fire. The pronoun in *alayhi* refers to (*ma*) by omitting a noun (*mudaf*) as we have said, that is, against His worship. (*Fatinin*) is given the sense of "bearers of temptation," and (*man*) is its object; the governing element is left free because (*fatinin*) was not taken as an object-taking participle. It is also said that *alayhi* means "with" (*bi*): that is, you are not the ones who, with the one you worship, are tempting, except those for whom the decree has preceded that they will enter the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari made the pronoun in *alayhi* refer to Allah. He said: If you ask, "How can they tempt them against Allah?" I say: They corrupt them against Him by leading them astray and misleading them, from your saying: "So-and-so tempted so-and-so against so-and-so his wife," just as you say: "He corrupted her against him" and "he disappointed her against him." The *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ may also mean "together with" (*ma'a*), like their saying: "Every man and his estate." Just as it is permissible to be silent about "every man and his estate," so it is permissible to be silent about His saying ﴿innakum wa-ma ta'budun﴾, because His saying ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ takes the place of the predicate, since its meaning is "you together with what you worship." The meaning is: you together with your gods, that is, you are their companions and associates, not ceasing to worship them. Then He said ﴿ma antum 'alayhi﴾, that is, "upon what you worship," ﴿bi-fatinin﴾, meaning: inciting or bearing toward the path of temptation and misguidance, except for one who is astray among you. End of quote. That the *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is the *waw* of "together with" is not obvious to the mind, and separating ﴿ma antum 'alayhi bi-fatinin﴾ from ﴿innakum wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is not a good view, because attributing it to them is what comes first to understanding, together with the soundness of the meaning, so one should not turn away from it.

(p-379) Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ablah read (*salu al-jahim*), with a *waw*, and so it is written in the *Kamil* of al-Hudhali. In the book of Ibn Khalawayh, from both of them, it is written (*sala*) without a *waw*; and in the book of Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Hasan read (*salu*) written with a *waw*; and in the book of *al-Lawami'* and the book of al-Zamakhshari, from al-Hasan, it is written (*sala*) without a *waw*. As for the one who keeps the *waw*, it is the sound plural (*jam' salamah*) with the *nun* dropped due to the annexation (*idafah*). It is first treated according to the wording of (*man*) and so is singular, then secondly according to its meaning and so is plural, like His saying: ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]. In (*yaqulu*) it is treated according to the wording of (*man*), and in (*wa-ma hum*) according to the meaning, and the treatment according to the wording and the meaning are combined in one sentence, which is the relative clause, like His saying: ﴿except for one who was a Jew or a Christian﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. And the poet's saying:

*And he woke whoever among you was asleep.*

As for the one who does not keep the *waw*, it is possible that it is a plural and the *waw* was omitted in writing, as it is omitted in pronunciation in pause for the meeting of two unvocalized letters. It is also possible that (*sala*) is singular and its final radical was dropped for lightness, and the case-ending (*i'rab*) was applied to its middle, as was dropped in His saying: ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near﴾ [al-Rahman: 54], and ﴿And His are the ships raised high﴾ [al-Rahman: 24], with the *nun* and *jawar* in the nominative. And they say: *ma balayt bihi balah*, meaning *baliyah* from *balaa*, like *'afiyah* from *'afa*, so the final radical of (*balaytu* and *baliyah*) was dropped. And they say: *balah* and *bal*, with the radical dropped in both. Al-Zamakhshari said: He has directed the two preceding views in a certain way, and made them the first and third, saying: The second is that its origin is *sa'il* (one who is burning) with the metathesis, then it is said *sal* for *sa'il*, like their saying: *shakk* for *sha'ik* (sharp). End of quote.

﴿And there is none of us (*wa-ma minna*), that is, anyone, ﴿except that he has a known station﴾, that is, a station in worship and in ending at the command of Allah, restricted to him and not exceeding it. As it has been narrated: "Some of them are bowing who do not raise their backs, and some are prostrate who do not raise their heads." This is the speech of the angels, and it supports the view of those who said that *al-jinnah* are the angels: they disowned what the disbelievers attributed to them, that they are daughters of Allah, and they informed about their state of servitude and the condition in which they are. In a hadith: "There is not a place in the heaven but there is an angel in it, prostrating or standing and praying." And from Ibn Mas'ud: "There is no spot the width of a span but upon it is the forehead of an angel or his feet." The omission of the subject with (*min*) is fine and eloquent, as has passed in His saying: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book except that he will surely believe in Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 159], that is, "And there is none of the People of the Book who..." The Arabs say: "Among us is one who departed, and among us is one who stayed," meaning: "among us is a group who departed, and among us is a group who stayed." And al-Zamakhshari said: "And there is none of us but that he has a known station," where the qualified noun is omitted and the adjective put in its place, like his saying:

*I am the son of Jala, and the scaler of the passes, by my hand he was among the best archers of mankind.*

End of quote. This is not an omission of the qualified noun with the adjective taking its place, because the omitted *ahad* (anyone) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and *illa lahu maqam ma'lum* (except he has a known station) is its predicate, and because no complete sentence is formed from His saying "And there is none of us anyone." So His saying ﴿except that he has a known station﴾ is the place of the benefit. Even if it is imagined that ﴿except that he has a known station﴾ is in the position of an adjective, they have stated that *illa* (except) cannot be an adjective when its qualified noun is omitted, and that it differs from *ghayr* (other than) when *ghayr* is an adjective in that respect, so that *ghayr* can be more fully used as an adjective while *illa* is less fully usable in this way. This is treated like His saying: *ana ibn Jala*, meaning "the son of a man who departed," and *bi-kaffi kana*, meaning "a man who was." This is, according to the grammarians, among the most objectionable of poetic necessities (*darurat*).

﴿And indeed we are those who stand in rows (*al-saffun*)﴾, that is, placing our feet in prayer, or our wings in the air, or around the Throne, supplicating for the believers. Al-Zahrawi said: It is said that the Muslims have arranged themselves in rows in prayer since this verse was revealed, and no group of the religions arranges itself in rows except the Muslims.

﴿And indeed we are those who glorify (*al-musabbihun*)﴾, that is, those who declare Allah free from what the disbelievers attribute to Him, or those who declare Him free with the words of glorification (*tasbih*), or those who pray. It is appropriate that His saying ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe﴾ be taken as the speech of the angels, so that the sentences follow in sequence and proceed from one speaker. It is as if it were said: "And the angels knew well that those who attribute this are to be brought forth for punishment; and they said, 'Glory be to Allah,' so they declared Him free of that and excepted whoever among the servants of Allah is sincere; and they said to the disbelievers, 'Indeed you and your gods...' to the end." And how could we be related to Him while we are servants before Him, each of us having a station of obedience? And so on, to what they described themselves with of the rank of servitude. It is also said: ﴿And there is none of us except that he has a known station﴾ is from the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: "And there is none of the messengers except that he has a known station on the Day of Resurrection according to his deed," from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾ [al-Isra': 79]. Then he mentioned their deeds, and that they are those who arrange themselves in rows in prayer and who declare Allah free of what the people of misguidance say.

The pronoun in (*la-yaqulun*) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh: ﴿If only we had with us a reminder from the earlier peoples﴾, that is, a book from the books of the earlier peoples to whom the Torah and the Gospel were revealed, ﴿we would have been sincere servants of Allah﴾, and we would not have denied as they denied. ﴿But they disbelieved in it (*fa-kafaru bihi*)﴾, that is, then the Reminder came to them which they used to wish for, and it is the most honorable of reminders, because of its inimitability among the books.

﴿So they will soon know﴾ the outcome of their disbelief, and what retribution will befall them. They emphasized their statement with the lightened *in* and with the *lam*, indicating that they were earnest in that; then there appeared from them denial and intense aversion, like His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89].

﴿And indeed Our word has preceded (*kalimatuna*)﴾. The majority read it in the singular, since it is united in one meaning, so it was expressed in the singular. Al-Dahhak read it in the plural. The intended promise is the victory of the messengers over their enemies in the stations of argument and the battles of war in this world, and their superiority over them in the Hereafter. Al-Hasan said: No prophet was defeated in war, nor was any killed in it.

﴿So turn away from them for a time (*hatta hin*)﴾, that is, for a short period, which is the period of ceasing fighting. From al-Suddi: until the Day of Badr, and al-Tabari preferred this. Qatadah said: until their death. Ibn Zayd said: until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And watch them﴾, that is, look at the outcome of their affair, ﴿for they will soon see﴾ it, and what will befall them of punishment, capture and killing; or they will soon see you and what will be accomplished for you of victory over them and triumph against them. His command to watch them is an indication of a state that is awaited and certain to occur, and that it is near, as if it were between his two eyes so that he sees it. In this is consolation and relief for him, peace be upon him.

﴿Then are they seeking to hasten Our punishment?﴾ An interrogation of reproach.

﴿فَإذا نَزَلَ﴾ [When it descends], that is, the punishment, is like the punishment that descended upon them after he had warned them. They denied it to such a degree that he warned his people and some of their craftsmen of its approach, yet they paid no attention to his warning, did not take precautions against it, and made no plan that would save them, until it came down into their courtyard and launched its raid upon them and cut off their last trace. It was the custom of their raids to attack at dawn, so the raid was called "dawn" even when it occurred at another time. This verse would not be eloquent, nor would it have the striking beauty that makes it pleasing and makes its meaning settle in the soul and nature, except that it comes in the manner of a figurative expression (tamthil), as al-Zamakhshari (the Qur'an commentator and grammarian) said. The majority of readers recited نَزَلَ in the active voice (مَبْنِيًّا لِلْفاعِلِ), while Ibn Mas'ud recited it in the passive voice (مَبْنِيًّا لِلْمَفْعُولِ). In the passive reading, ساحَتِهِمْ (their courtyard) is the substitute for the subject (القائِمُ مَقامَ الفاعِلِ). The expression نَزَلَ ساحَةَ فُلانٍ (it descended upon the courtyard of so-and-so) is used for whatever comes upon a person, whether good or evil. سُوءُ الصَّباحِ (the evil of the morning) is used for the arrival of raids and calamities, like the words of the one crying out: يا صَباحاهُ (Alas, my morning!). The ruling of ساءَ (sā'a, "evil is") here is the ruling of بِئْسَ (bi'sa, "evil is"). ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited فَبِئْسَ (fa-bi'sa). The thing being condemned is omitted; its implied meaning is: "Evil is the morning of those who were warned, their morning."

﴿وتَوَلَّ عَنْهم حَتّى حِينٍ﴾ [And turn away from them for a time]. He repeated the command to turn away, to console him (ʿalayhi al-salam), to comfort him, and to emphasize the certainty of the appointed time. He did not restrict the command with seeing (al-ibsar), as he had restricted it in the first instance. This was either because he was satisfied with it in the first instance and omitted it for brevity, or because leaving it unrestricted allows the mind to range over what the seeing relates to: the various kinds of joys for him, and the various kinds of troubles for them. It was also said: the first refers to the punishment of this world, and the later refers to the punishment of the Hereafter.

God, exalted is He, concluded this surah by declaring Himself free from what the polytheists describe, and He attributed the Lord to His Prophet, honoring him by this attribution and by addressing him. Then He attributed the Lord to might (al-ʿizza), which is the created might that belongs to the prophets and believers. The jurists said likewise, on the basis that it is something nurtured (marbūbah, created and sustained). Muhammad ibn Sahnun and others said: whoever swears by the might of God, intending His might that is created among His servants, which is the one in His saying ﴿رَبِّ العِزَّةِ﴾ [the Lord of Might], then it is not an oath (yamin). Al-Zamakhshari said: the Lord is attributed to might because He is specifically characterized by it, as if it were said "the Possessor of might," just as you say "companion of truthfulness" because he is specifically characterized by truthfulness. End of quote. On this view, an oath by the might of God is binding, because it is one of His attributes. He said: it is also possible that it means there is no might for any of the kings or others except that He is its Lord and Owner, in accordance with His saying ﴿وتُعِزُّ مَن تَشاءُ﴾ [and You exalt whom You will] [Ali Imran: 26].

It is related from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: "Whoever wishes to be measured with the fullest measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let the last of his words when he rises from his assembly be: (Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might) to the end of the surah."

(p-378)

The apparent meaning is that *al-jinnah* refers to the devils (*al-shayatin*), and there are outrageous statements by the disbelievers about this. Among them is that He, exalted is He, intermarried with the chiefs of the jinn, and from them begot the angels, who are a group from the Banu Mudlij. Some of the disbelievers said this directly to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him).

﴿And they have set up between Him and the jinn a kinship. But the jinn know well that they will surely be brought forth.﴾ That is, the devils know that they are brought forth to the command of Allah, to reward and punishment. This is said by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Zamakhshari said: If *al-jinnah* is interpreted as the devils, then the pronoun in ﴿innahum lamuhdarun﴾ may refer to them. The meaning is that the devils know that Allah will bring them to the Fire and punish them, and if they were related to Him, or partners in the obligation of obedience, He would not punish them. It is also said that the pronoun in (*wa-ja'alu*) refers to a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs, and *al-jinnah* means the angels, so called because of their concealment (*ijtinan*) and their being hidden. Al-Zamakhshari also said: He mentioned them with this name to demean them and diminish them, even though they themselves held them in high regard, so that they would not reach the rank of the kinship they attributed to them. In this is an indication that one whose attribute is concealment and hiding, which are attributes of bodies, cannot be a fitting relation to one to whom such things are not permissible. End of quote.

﴿And the jinn know well that they (*annahum*), that is the disbelievers who claim a kinship between the angels and Allah, Exalted is He, will be brought to the Fire, to be punished for what they say.﴾ This knowledge is attributed to those who are claimed to be related to Him, as an exaggeration in refuting those who make the claim. Then Allah, Exalted is He, declared Himself free of the attribute that is not fitting for Him: ﴿except the servants of Allah﴾, for they describe Him by His attributes. As for the phrase "from those brought forth" (*al-muhdarun*), that is, except the servants of Allah, they are saved for the duration of the punishment. The sentence of declaring Him free (*tanzih*) is then a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiradh*) relating to both opinions, and the exception is disconnected (*munqati'*). The apparent view is that the *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is conjunctive, joining "what you worship" to the pronoun in *innakum*, and that the pronoun in *alayhi* refers to (*ma*). The meaning is: Say to them, O Muhammad: "You and what you worship, of idols, are such that you and they dominate (the speech)." The address is made dominant, as you say: "You and Zayd go out against it," meaning against the worship of your deity.

﴿fatinin﴾ means bearers of temptation (*fitnah*) to His servants, except for those whom Allah has decreed in His prior knowledge to be among the people of the Fire. The pronoun in *alayhi* refers to (*ma*) by omitting a noun (*mudaf*) as we have said, that is, against His worship. (*Fatinin*) is given the sense of "bearers of temptation," and (*man*) is its object; the governing element is left free because (*fatinin*) was not taken as an object-taking participle. It is also said that *alayhi* means "with" (*bi*): that is, you are not the ones who, with the one you worship, are tempting, except those for whom the decree has preceded that they will enter the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari made the pronoun in *alayhi* refer to Allah. He said: If you ask, "How can they tempt them against Allah?" I say: They corrupt them against Him by leading them astray and misleading them, from your saying: "So-and-so tempted so-and-so against so-and-so his wife," just as you say: "He corrupted her against him" and "he disappointed her against him." The *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ may also mean "together with" (*ma'a*), like their saying: "Every man and his estate." Just as it is permissible to be silent about "every man and his estate," so it is permissible to be silent about His saying ﴿innakum wa-ma ta'budun﴾, because His saying ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ takes the place of the predicate, since its meaning is "you together with what you worship." The meaning is: you together with your gods, that is, you are their companions and associates, not ceasing to worship them. Then He said ﴿ma antum 'alayhi﴾, that is, "upon what you worship," ﴿bi-fatinin﴾, meaning: inciting or bearing toward the path of temptation and misguidance, except for one who is astray among you. End of quote. That the *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is the *waw* of "together with" is not obvious to the mind, and separating ﴿ma antum 'alayhi bi-fatinin﴾ from ﴿innakum wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is not a good view, because attributing it to them is what comes first to understanding, together with the soundness of the meaning, so one should not turn away from it.

﴿So turn away from them for a time (*hatta hin*)﴾, that is, for a short period, which is the period of ceasing fighting. From al-Suddi: until the Day of Badr, and al-Tabari preferred this. Qatadah said: until their death. Ibn Zayd said: until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And watch them﴾, that is, look at the outcome of their affair, ﴿for they will soon see﴾ it, and what will befall them of punishment, capture and killing; or they will soon see you and what will be accomplished for you of victory over them and triumph against them. His command to watch them is an indication of a state that is awaited and certain to occur, and that it is near, as if it were between his two eyes so that he sees it. In this is consolation and relief for him, peace be upon him.

﴿Then are they seeking to hasten Our punishment?﴾ An interrogation of reproach.

﴿فَإذا نَزَلَ﴾ [When it descends], that is, the punishment, is like the punishment that descended upon them after he had warned them. They denied it to such a degree that he warned his people and some of their craftsmen of its approach, yet they paid no attention to his warning, did not take precautions against it, and made no plan that would save them, until it came down into their courtyard and launched its raid upon them and cut off their last trace. It was the custom of their raids to attack at dawn, so the raid was called "dawn" even when it occurred at another time. This verse would not be eloquent, nor would it have the striking beauty that makes it pleasing and makes its meaning settle in the soul and nature, except that it comes in the manner of a figurative expression (tamthil), as al-Zamakhshari (the Qur'an commentator and grammarian) said. The majority of readers recited نَزَلَ in the active voice (مَبْنِيًّا لِلْفاعِلِ), while Ibn Mas'ud recited it in the passive voice (مَبْنِيًّا لِلْمَفْعُولِ). In the passive reading, ساحَتِهِمْ (their courtyard) is the substitute for the subject (القائِمُ مَقامَ الفاعِلِ). The expression نَزَلَ ساحَةَ فُلانٍ (it descended upon the courtyard of so-and-so) is used for whatever comes upon a person, whether good or evil. سُوءُ الصَّباحِ (the evil of the morning) is used for the arrival of raids and calamities, like the words of the one crying out: يا صَباحاهُ (Alas, my morning!). The ruling of ساءَ (sā'a, "evil is") here is the ruling of بِئْسَ (bi'sa, "evil is"). ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited فَبِئْسَ (fa-bi'sa). The thing being condemned is omitted; its implied meaning is: "Evil is the morning of those who were warned, their morning."

﴿وتَوَلَّ عَنْهم حَتّى حِينٍ﴾ [And turn away from them for a time]. He repeated the command to turn away, to console him (ʿalayhi al-salam), to comfort him, and to emphasize the certainty of the appointed time. He did not restrict the command with seeing (al-ibsar), as he had restricted it in the first instance. This was either because he was satisfied with it in the first instance and omitted it for brevity, or because leaving it unrestricted allows the mind to range over what the seeing relates to: the various kinds of joys for him, and the various kinds of troubles for them. It was also said: the first refers to the punishment of this world, and the later refers to the punishment of the Hereafter.

God, exalted is He, concluded this surah by declaring Himself free from what the polytheists describe, and He attributed the Lord to His Prophet, honoring him by this attribution and by addressing him. Then He attributed the Lord to might (al-ʿizza), which is the created might that belongs to the prophets and believers. The jurists said likewise, on the basis that it is something nurtured (marbūbah, created and sustained). Muhammad ibn Sahnun and others said: whoever swears by the might of God, intending His might that is created among His servants, which is the one in His saying ﴿رَبِّ العِزَّةِ﴾ [the Lord of Might], then it is not an oath (yamin). Al-Zamakhshari said: the Lord is attributed to might because He is specifically characterized by it, as if it were said "the Possessor of might," just as you say "companion of truthfulness" because he is specifically characterized by truthfulness. End of quote. On this view, an oath by the might of God is binding, because it is one of His attributes. He said: it is also possible that it means there is no might for any of the kings or others except that He is its Lord and Owner, in accordance with His saying ﴿وتُعِزُّ مَن تَشاءُ﴾ [and You exalt whom You will] [Ali Imran: 26].

It is related from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: "Whoever wishes to be measured with the fullest measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let the last of his words when he rises from his assembly be: (Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might) to the end of the surah."

(p-378)

The apparent meaning is that *al-jinnah* refers to the devils (*al-shayatin*), and there are outrageous statements by the disbelievers about this. Among them is that He, exalted is He, intermarried with the chiefs of the jinn, and from them begot the angels, who are a group from the Banu Mudlij. Some of the disbelievers said this directly to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him).

﴿And they have set up between Him and the jinn a kinship. But the jinn know well that they will surely be brought forth.﴾ That is, the devils know that they are brought forth to the command of Allah, to reward and punishment. This is said by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Zamakhshari said: If *al-jinnah* is interpreted as the devils, then the pronoun in ﴿innahum lamuhdarun﴾ may refer to them. The meaning is that the devils know that Allah will bring them to the Fire and punish them, and if they were related to Him, or partners in the obligation of obedience, He would not punish them. It is also said that the pronoun in (*wa-ja'alu*) refers to a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs, and *al-jinnah* means the angels, so called because of their concealment (*ijtinan*) and their being hidden. Al-Zamakhshari also said: He mentioned them with this name to demean them and diminish them, even though they themselves held them in high regard, so that they would not reach the rank of the kinship they attributed to them. In this is an indication that one whose attribute is concealment and hiding, which are attributes of bodies, cannot be a fitting relation to one to whom such things are not permissible. End of quote.

﴿And the jinn know well that they (*annahum*), that is the disbelievers who claim a kinship between the angels and Allah, Exalted is He, will be brought to the Fire, to be punished for what they say.﴾ This knowledge is attributed to those who are claimed to be related to Him, as an exaggeration in refuting those who make the claim. Then Allah, Exalted is He, declared Himself free of the attribute that is not fitting for Him: ﴿except the servants of Allah﴾, for they describe Him by His attributes. As for the phrase "from those brought forth" (*al-muhdarun*), that is, except the servants of Allah, they are saved for the duration of the punishment. The sentence of declaring Him free (*tanzih*) is then a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiradh*) relating to both opinions, and the exception is disconnected (*munqati'*). The apparent view is that the *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is conjunctive, joining "what you worship" to the pronoun in *innakum*, and that the pronoun in *alayhi* refers to (*ma*). The meaning is: Say to them, O Muhammad: "You and what you worship, of idols, are such that you and they dominate (the speech)." The address is made dominant, as you say: "You and Zayd go out against it," meaning against the worship of your deity.

﴿fatinin﴾ means bearers of temptation (*fitnah*) to His servants, except for those whom Allah has decreed in His prior knowledge to be among the people of the Fire. The pronoun in *alayhi* refers to (*ma*) by omitting a noun (*mudaf*) as we have said, that is, against His worship. (*Fatinin*) is given the sense of "bearers of temptation," and (*man*) is its object; the governing element is left free because (*fatinin*) was not taken as an object-taking participle. It is also said that *alayhi* means "with" (*bi*): that is, you are not the ones who, with the one you worship, are tempting, except those for whom the decree has preceded that they will enter the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari made the pronoun in *alayhi* refer to Allah. He said: If you ask, "How can they tempt them against Allah?" I say: They corrupt them against Him by leading them astray and misleading them, from your saying: "So-and-so tempted so-and-so against so-and-so his wife," just as you say: "He corrupted her against him" and "he disappointed her against him." The *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ may also mean "together with" (*ma'a*), like their saying: "Every man and his estate." Just as it is permissible to be silent about "every man and his estate," so it is permissible to be silent about His saying ﴿innakum wa-ma ta'budun﴾, because His saying ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ takes the place of the predicate, since its meaning is "you together with what you worship." The meaning is: you together with your gods, that is, you are their companions and associates, not ceasing to worship them. Then He said ﴿ma antum 'alayhi﴾, that is, "upon what you worship," ﴿bi-fatinin﴾, meaning: inciting or bearing toward the path of temptation and misguidance, except for one who is astray among you. End of quote. That the *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is the *waw* of "together with" is not obvious to the mind, and separating ﴿ma antum 'alayhi bi-fatinin﴾ from ﴿innakum wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is not a good view, because attributing it to them is what comes first to understanding, together with the soundness of the meaning, so one should not turn away from it.

(p-379) Al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Ablah read (*salu al-jahim*), with a *waw*, and so it is written in the *Kamil* of al-Hudhali. In the book of Ibn Khalawayh, from both of them, it is written (*sala*) without a *waw*; and in the book of Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Hasan read (*salu*) written with a *waw*; and in the book of *al-Lawami'* and the book of al-Zamakhshari, from al-Hasan, it is written (*sala*) without a *waw*. As for the one who keeps the *waw*, it is the sound plural (*jam' salamah*) with the *nun* dropped due to the annexation (*idafah*). It is first treated according to the wording of (*man*) and so is singular, then secondly according to its meaning and so is plural, like His saying: ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah and the Last Day," but they are not believers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]. In (*yaqulu*) it is treated according to the wording of (*man*), and in (*wa-ma hum*) according to the meaning, and the treatment according to the wording and the meaning are combined in one sentence, which is the relative clause, like His saying: ﴿except for one who was a Jew or a Christian﴾ [al-Baqarah: 111]. And the poet's saying:

*And he woke whoever among you was asleep.*

As for the one who does not keep the *waw*, it is possible that it is a plural and the *waw* was omitted in writing, as it is omitted in pronunciation in pause for the meeting of two unvocalized letters. It is also possible that (*sala*) is singular and its final radical was dropped for lightness, and the case-ending (*i'rab*) was applied to its middle, as was dropped in His saying: ﴿And the fruit of the two gardens is near﴾ [al-Rahman: 54], and ﴿And His are the ships raised high﴾ [al-Rahman: 24], with the *nun* and *jawar* in the nominative. And they say: *ma balayt bihi balah*, meaning *baliyah* from *balaa*, like *'afiyah* from *'afa*, so the final radical of (*balaytu* and *baliyah*) was dropped. And they say: *balah* and *bal*, with the radical dropped in both. Al-Zamakhshari said: He has directed the two preceding views in a certain way, and made them the first and third, saying: The second is that its origin is *sa'il* (one who is burning) with the metathesis, then it is said *sal* for *sa'il*, like their saying: *shakk* for *sha'ik* (sharp). End of quote.

﴿And there is none of us (*wa-ma minna*), that is, anyone, ﴿except that he has a known station﴾, that is, a station in worship and in ending at the command of Allah, restricted to him and not exceeding it. As it has been narrated: "Some of them are bowing who do not raise their backs, and some are prostrate who do not raise their heads." This is the speech of the angels, and it supports the view of those who said that *al-jinnah* are the angels: they disowned what the disbelievers attributed to them, that they are daughters of Allah, and they informed about their state of servitude and the condition in which they are. In a hadith: "There is not a place in the heaven but there is an angel in it, prostrating or standing and praying." And from Ibn Mas'ud: "There is no spot the width of a span but upon it is the forehead of an angel or his feet." The omission of the subject with (*min*) is fine and eloquent, as has passed in His saying: ﴿And there is none of the People of the Book except that he will surely believe in Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 159], that is, "And there is none of the People of the Book who..." The Arabs say: "Among us is one who departed, and among us is one who stayed," meaning: "among us is a group who departed, and among us is a group who stayed." And al-Zamakhshari said: "And there is none of us but that he has a known station," where the qualified noun is omitted and the adjective put in its place, like his saying:

*I am the son of Jala, and the scaler of the passes, by my hand he was among the best archers of mankind.*

End of quote. This is not an omission of the qualified noun with the adjective taking its place, because the omitted *ahad* (anyone) is the subject (*mubtada'*), and *illa lahu maqam ma'lum* (except he has a known station) is its predicate, and because no complete sentence is formed from His saying "And there is none of us anyone." So His saying ﴿except that he has a known station﴾ is the place of the benefit. Even if it is imagined that ﴿except that he has a known station﴾ is in the position of an adjective, they have stated that *illa* (except) cannot be an adjective when its qualified noun is omitted, and that it differs from *ghayr* (other than) when *ghayr* is an adjective in that respect, so that *ghayr* can be more fully used as an adjective while *illa* is less fully usable in this way. This is treated like His saying: *ana ibn Jala*, meaning "the son of a man who departed," and *bi-kaffi kana*, meaning "a man who was." This is, according to the grammarians, among the most objectionable of poetic necessities (*darurat*).

﴿And indeed we are those who stand in rows (*al-saffun*)﴾, that is, placing our feet in prayer, or our wings in the air, or around the Throne, supplicating for the believers. Al-Zahrawi said: It is said that the Muslims have arranged themselves in rows in prayer since this verse was revealed, and no group of the religions arranges itself in rows except the Muslims.

﴿And indeed we are those who glorify (*al-musabbihun*)﴾, that is, those who declare Allah free from what the disbelievers attribute to Him, or those who declare Him free with the words of glorification (*tasbih*), or those who pray. It is appropriate that His saying ﴿Glory be to Allah above what they describe﴾ be taken as the speech of the angels, so that the sentences follow in sequence and proceed from one speaker. It is as if it were said: "And the angels knew well that those who attribute this are to be brought forth for punishment; and they said, 'Glory be to Allah,' so they declared Him free of that and excepted whoever among the servants of Allah is sincere; and they said to the disbelievers, 'Indeed you and your gods...' to the end." And how could we be related to Him while we are servants before Him, each of us having a station of obedience? And so on, to what they described themselves with of the rank of servitude. It is also said: ﴿And there is none of us except that he has a known station﴾ is from the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: "And there is none of the messengers except that he has a known station on the Day of Resurrection according to his deed," from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾ [al-Isra': 79]. Then he mentioned their deeds, and that they are those who arrange themselves in rows in prayer and who declare Allah free of what the people of misguidance say.

The pronoun in (*la-yaqulun*) refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh: ﴿If only we had with us a reminder from the earlier peoples﴾, that is, a book from the books of the earlier peoples to whom the Torah and the Gospel were revealed, ﴿we would have been sincere servants of Allah﴾, and we would not have denied as they denied. ﴿But they disbelieved in it (*fa-kafaru bihi*)﴾, that is, then the Reminder came to them which they used to wish for, and it is the most honorable of reminders, because of its inimitability among the books.

﴿So they will soon know﴾ the outcome of their disbelief, and what retribution will befall them. They emphasized their statement with the lightened *in* and with the *lam*, indicating that they were earnest in that; then there appeared from them denial and intense aversion, like His saying: ﴿So when there came to them what they recognized, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 89].

﴿And indeed Our word has preceded (*kalimatuna*)﴾. The majority read it in the singular, since it is united in one meaning, so it was expressed in the singular. Al-Dahhak read it in the plural. The intended promise is the victory of the messengers over their enemies in the stations of argument and the battles of war in this world, and their superiority over them in the Hereafter. Al-Hasan said: No prophet was defeated in war, nor was any killed in it.

﴿So turn away from them for a time (*hatta hin*)﴾, that is, for a short period, which is the period of ceasing fighting. From al-Suddi: until the Day of Badr, and al-Tabari preferred this. Qatadah said: until their death. Ibn Zayd said: until the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And watch them﴾, that is, look at the outcome of their affair, ﴿for they will soon see﴾ it, and what will befall them of punishment, capture and killing; or they will soon see you and what will be accomplished for you of victory over them and triumph against them. His command to watch them is an indication of a state that is awaited and certain to occur, and that it is near, as if it were between his two eyes so that he sees it. In this is consolation and relief for him, peace be upon him.

﴿Then are they seeking to hasten Our punishment?﴾ An interrogation of reproach.

﴿فَإذا نَزَلَ﴾ [When it descends], that is, the punishment, is like the punishment that descended upon them after he had warned them. They denied it to such a degree that he warned his people and some of their craftsmen of its approach, yet they paid no attention to his warning, did not take precautions against it, and made no plan that would save them, until it came down into their courtyard and launched its raid upon them and cut off their last trace. It was the custom of their raids to attack at dawn, so the raid was called "dawn" even when it occurred at another time. This verse would not be eloquent, nor would it have the striking beauty that makes it pleasing and makes its meaning settle in the soul and nature, except that it comes in the manner of a figurative expression (tamthil), as al-Zamakhshari (the Qur'an commentator and grammarian) said. The majority of readers recited نَزَلَ in the active voice (مَبْنِيًّا لِلْفاعِلِ), while Ibn Mas'ud recited it in the passive voice (مَبْنِيًّا لِلْمَفْعُولِ). In the passive reading, ساحَتِهِمْ (their courtyard) is the substitute for the subject (القائِمُ مَقامَ الفاعِلِ). The expression نَزَلَ ساحَةَ فُلانٍ (it descended upon the courtyard of so-and-so) is used for whatever comes upon a person, whether good or evil. سُوءُ الصَّباحِ (the evil of the morning) is used for the arrival of raids and calamities, like the words of the one crying out: يا صَباحاهُ (Alas, my morning!). The ruling of ساءَ (sā'a, "evil is") here is the ruling of بِئْسَ (bi'sa, "evil is"). ʿAbdullah (Ibn Mas'ud) recited فَبِئْسَ (fa-bi'sa). The thing being condemned is omitted; its implied meaning is: "Evil is the morning of those who were warned, their morning."

﴿وتَوَلَّ عَنْهم حَتّى حِينٍ﴾ [And turn away from them for a time]. He repeated the command to turn away, to console him (ʿalayhi al-salam), to comfort him, and to emphasize the certainty of the appointed time. He did not restrict the command with seeing (al-ibsar), as he had restricted it in the first instance. This was either because he was satisfied with it in the first instance and omitted it for brevity, or because leaving it unrestricted allows the mind to range over what the seeing relates to: the various kinds of joys for him, and the various kinds of troubles for them. It was also said: the first refers to the punishment of this world, and the later refers to the punishment of the Hereafter.

God, exalted is He, concluded this surah by declaring Himself free from what the polytheists describe, and He attributed the Lord to His Prophet, honoring him by this attribution and by addressing him. Then He attributed the Lord to might (al-ʿizza), which is the created might that belongs to the prophets and believers. The jurists said likewise, on the basis that it is something nurtured (marbūbah, created and sustained). Muhammad ibn Sahnun and others said: whoever swears by the might of God, intending His might that is created among His servants, which is the one in His saying ﴿رَبِّ العِزَّةِ﴾ [the Lord of Might], then it is not an oath (yamin). Al-Zamakhshari said: the Lord is attributed to might because He is specifically characterized by it, as if it were said "the Possessor of might," just as you say "companion of truthfulness" because he is specifically characterized by truthfulness. End of quote. On this view, an oath by the might of God is binding, because it is one of His attributes. He said: it is also possible that it means there is no might for any of the kings or others except that He is its Lord and Owner, in accordance with His saying ﴿وتُعِزُّ مَن تَشاءُ﴾ [and You exalt whom You will] [Ali Imran: 26].

It is related from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: "Whoever wishes to be measured with the fullest measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let the last of his words when he rises from his assembly be: (Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might) to the end of the surah."

(p-378)

The apparent meaning is that *al-jinnah* refers to the devils (*al-shayatin*), and there are outrageous statements by the disbelievers about this. Among them is that He, exalted is He, intermarried with the chiefs of the jinn, and from them begot the angels, who are a group from the Banu Mudlij. Some of the disbelievers said this directly to Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him).

﴿And they have set up between Him and the jinn a kinship. But the jinn know well that they will surely be brought forth.﴾ That is, the devils know that they are brought forth to the command of Allah, to reward and punishment. This is said by Ibn 'Atiyyah. Al-Zamakhshari said: If *al-jinnah* is interpreted as the devils, then the pronoun in ﴿innahum lamuhdarun﴾ may refer to them. The meaning is that the devils know that Allah will bring them to the Fire and punish them, and if they were related to Him, or partners in the obligation of obedience, He would not punish them. It is also said that the pronoun in (*wa-ja'alu*) refers to a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh and the Arabs, and *al-jinnah* means the angels, so called because of their concealment (*ijtinan*) and their being hidden. Al-Zamakhshari also said: He mentioned them with this name to demean them and diminish them, even though they themselves held them in high regard, so that they would not reach the rank of the kinship they attributed to them. In this is an indication that one whose attribute is concealment and hiding, which are attributes of bodies, cannot be a fitting relation to one to whom such things are not permissible. End of quote.

﴿And the jinn know well that they (*annahum*), that is the disbelievers who claim a kinship between the angels and Allah, Exalted is He, will be brought to the Fire, to be punished for what they say.﴾ This knowledge is attributed to those who are claimed to be related to Him, as an exaggeration in refuting those who make the claim. Then Allah, Exalted is He, declared Himself free of the attribute that is not fitting for Him: ﴿except the servants of Allah﴾, for they describe Him by His attributes. As for the phrase "from those brought forth" (*al-muhdarun*), that is, except the servants of Allah, they are saved for the duration of the punishment. The sentence of declaring Him free (*tanzih*) is then a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiradh*) relating to both opinions, and the exception is disconnected (*munqati'*). The apparent view is that the *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is conjunctive, joining "what you worship" to the pronoun in *innakum*, and that the pronoun in *alayhi* refers to (*ma*). The meaning is: Say to them, O Muhammad: "You and what you worship, of idols, are such that you and they dominate (the speech)." The address is made dominant, as you say: "You and Zayd go out against it," meaning against the worship of your deity.

﴿fatinin﴾ means bearers of temptation (*fitnah*) to His servants, except for those whom Allah has decreed in His prior knowledge to be among the people of the Fire. The pronoun in *alayhi* refers to (*ma*) by omitting a noun (*mudaf*) as we have said, that is, against His worship. (*Fatinin*) is given the sense of "bearers of temptation," and (*man*) is its object; the governing element is left free because (*fatinin*) was not taken as an object-taking participle. It is also said that *alayhi* means "with" (*bi*): that is, you are not the ones who, with the one you worship, are tempting, except those for whom the decree has preceded that they will enter the Fire. Al-Zamakhshari made the pronoun in *alayhi* refer to Allah. He said: If you ask, "How can they tempt them against Allah?" I say: They corrupt them against Him by leading them astray and misleading them, from your saying: "So-and-so tempted so-and-so against so-and-so his wife," just as you say: "He corrupted her against him" and "he disappointed her against him." The *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ may also mean "together with" (*ma'a*), like their saying: "Every man and his estate." Just as it is permissible to be silent about "every man and his estate," so it is permissible to be silent about His saying ﴿innakum wa-ma ta'budun﴾, because His saying ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ takes the place of the predicate, since its meaning is "you together with what you worship." The meaning is: you together with your gods, that is, you are their companions and associates, not ceasing to worship them. Then He said ﴿ma antum 'alayhi﴾, that is, "upon what you worship," ﴿bi-fatinin﴾, meaning: inciting or bearing toward the path of temptation and misguidance, except for one who is astray among you. End of quote. That the *waw* in ﴿wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is the *waw* of "together with" is not obvious to the mind, and separating ﴿ma antum 'alayhi bi-fatinin﴾ from ﴿innakum wa-ma ta'budun﴾ is not a good view, because attributing it to them is what comes first to understanding, together with the soundness of the meaning, so one should not turn away from it.
